Hypothesis: Pressure-dependent hysteresis in H2 adsorption in Co(1,4-benzenedipyrazolate) (Co(BDP)) is a nonequilibrium scanning-isotherm phenomenon arising from (i) a μ(P,T)-dependent *thermodynamic bistability* between host conformers (open ↔ constricted and intermediate/gating geometries) and (ii) a finite free-energy barrier along a physically identifiable gating coordinate that makes host interconversion slow on experimental timescales. Rigid-lattice GCMC fails because it samples only a single host topology and thus cannot represent competing adsorption grand potentials Ωα(μ,T) nor the barrier-controlled interconversion rates that produce metastability. A statistically rigorous semigrand/expanded-ensemble framework—where host switches satisfy detailed balance with respect to Δ[β(Fhost,α + Ωα(μ,T))] and where pressure enters only via μ(P,T) for the gas reservoir—combined with an explicit kinetic model (barrier-derived rates or calibrated attempt frequencies) will reproduce (a) the temperature-dependent hysteresis width and (b) its rate dependence, while separating equilibrium coexistence (ΔΩ ≈ 0) from kinetic trapping (ΔG‡ controls loop opening).
Plan:
Step 0 — Define scope, observables, and experimental anchors
• Target observables: (1) adsorption/desorption scanning isotherms N(P,T) exhibiting hysteresis width ΔP(T), (2) microstate probabilities pα(P,T) for host states, (3) isosteric heat qst(N) and its state-resolved decomposition, (4) rate dependence of loop area versus scan rate (if experimental data exist; otherwise propose simulated scan-rate series).
• Working conditions: P = 10^-2–100 bar; T = 20–100 K; H2 treated as quantum-corrected (see Step 4).

Step 1 — Build and validate a *gating pathway* (beyond two minima)
1.1 Host structural set and collective variable (CV)
• Start from reported Co(BDP) crystallographic structures (open and contracted if available) and optimize with periodic DFT including dispersion (e.g., PBE-D3/SCAN+rVV10) to obtain consistent cell parameters and elastic response.
• Define a physically motivated gating CV, s, tied to the known hinge-like pyrazolate/metal node motion and pore accessibility, e.g.:
  – s = minimum window diameter (pore aperture) computed from a Voronoi-based probe, and/or
  – s = cell metric combination capturing breathing (e.g., b/a ratio or a specific Co–N–N–Co hinge angle), and
  – include a secondary CV if needed (e.g., torsion of benzenedipyrazolate) to avoid hidden barriers.
1.2 Free-energy profile of the empty host
• Compute the host-only free-energy along s: Fhost(s,T) using umbrella sampling in NVT (or NσT if constant-stress is later enabled) with harmonic restraints on s; use WHAM/MBAR to reconstruct Fhost(s,T) and identify minima (open, constricted) and at least one intermediate saddle/metastable basin.
• Validate that the identified pathway reproduces experimentally observed lattice changes (ΔV/V, key distances/angles) within uncertainty.

Step 2 — Define a detailed-balance-preserving semigrand/expanded ensemble for adsorption with host states
2.1 Discrete-state semigrand model (baseline)
• Represent the host as a set of K discrete microstates α ∈ {open, intermediate1,…,constricted} obtained by selecting representative structures along s (e.g., 3–6 states spanning the gating coordinate).
• For each α, define:
  – Fhost,α(T): Helmholtz free energy of the empty host in state α (from Step 1, including vibrational contributions via quasi-harmonic or thermodynamic integration as feasible),
  – Ωα(μ,T): grand potential of H2 in host state α at chemical potential μ and temperature T.
• Semigrand partition function:
  Z(μ,T) = Σα exp[-β Fhost,α(T)] · Ξα(μ,T)
  with Ξα(μ,T) = ΣN exp(βμN) Qα(N,T) and Ωα = -kT ln Ξα.
• Host-switch move α→α′ acceptance (expanded-ensemble Metropolis) ensuring detailed balance:
  acc(α→α′) = min{1, exp[-β(ΔFhost + ΔΩ(μ,T))] · (gα/gα′)}
  where gα are optional bias/weight factors used for flat-histogram sampling (set gα=1 for unbiased, or determine gα via Wang–Landau/transition-matrix).
• Pressure enters only through μ(P,T) of the H2 reservoir (EOS-consistent fugacity; Step 5). No explicit mechanical pressure is assumed unless Step 3.3 is activated.
2.2 Continuous-CV benchmark (flexible-lattice reference)
• Implement a parallel “continuous s” approach for validation: hybrid GCMC + biased sampling in s (e.g., grand-canonical Wang–Landau in (N,s) or μVT + umbrella in s), yielding Ω(μ,T;s) and allowing comparison of discrete-state reduction versus continuous landscape.

Step 3 — Preserve equilibrium while enabling controlled nonequilibrium hysteresis (kinetics)
3.1 Separate *equilibrium* from *scanning isotherms*
• First compute equilibrium isotherms by allowing adequate host switching (flat-histogram in α or s) to obtain the true thermodynamic uptake N_eq(P,T) and locate coexistence (ΔΩ between basins).
• Then generate hysteresis via a kinetic protocol (3.2 or 3.3) that mimics finite-time experiments.
3.2 Barrier-derived transition rates + kinetic Monte Carlo (preferred for physical rigor)
• From Step 1 (host-only) and Step 2 (adsorbate-coupled), compute the μ-dependent free-energy surface:
  G(s;μ,T) = Fhost(s,T) + Ω(μ,T;s)
  Determine ΔG‡open→constricted(μ,T) and ΔG‡constricted→open(μ,T) (barrier heights to the dividing surface).
• Convert barriers into transition rates using, e.g., Eyring/Arrhenius form:
  kα→α′(μ,T) = κ(T) (kBT/h) exp[-βΔG‡α→α′(μ,T)]
  with transmission factor κ(T) bounded/estimated; perform sensitivity analysis on κ.
• Couple these rates to adsorption equilibration within each host state (assumed fast relative to host switching, consistent with diffusion-controlled hysteresis), and propagate scanning isotherms using kinetic Monte Carlo while stepping μ(t) corresponding to experimental pressure ramp P(t).
3.3 Attempt-frequency calibration option (if barrier extraction is uncertain)
• If ΔG‡ is hard to converge, calibrate an effective host-switch attempt frequency ν such that simulated loop widths match one experimental reference condition, then predict ΔP(T) across other T and scan rates. Crucially, acceptance probabilities remain detailed-balance-correct (Step 2); only dynamics (attempt schedule) is tuned.
3.4 Avoid artificial hysteresis collapse
• Enforce a timescale hierarchy explicitly: (i) within-state GCMC equilibrates N at fixed α, (ii) α-switch proposals occur with rate consistent with kα→α′. Do not use aggressive expanded-ensemble switching when generating scanning curves; reserve it for equilibrium free energies.

Step 4 — Interaction models and cryogenic quantum corrections for H2
4.1 Host–guest force field
• Start from a validated MOF force field (e.g., UFF4MOF or DREIDING/QuickFF-style parameters) but re-parameterize key nonbonded terms against periodic DFT reference data:
  – H2 binding energies and geometries at representative sites (pore wall, near Co nodes, in constricted windows) using dispersion-corrected DFT.
  – Ensure framework partial charges are consistent (REPEAT/DFT-DDEC) and stable across α states.
4.2 H2 quantum effects at 20–100 K
• Include quantum corrections to H2–host interactions via Feynman–Hibbs effective potentials (second-order) as a baseline; benchmark selected points with path-integral GCMC (small cells/selected states) to quantify error bars.
• Treat H2 as quantum-corrected LJ/point quadrupole if needed; verify sensitivity of uptake and qst to the correction method.
4.3 Uncertainty propagation
• Propagate uncertainties from (i) force-field parameters, (ii) Fhost(s) reconstruction, and (iii) μ(P,T) EOS into predicted hysteresis width using ensemble reweighting/bootstrapping.

Step 5 — Thermodynamic consistency: μ(P,T) from EOS/fugacity
• Convert (P,T) to chemical potential using a consistent H2 equation of state and fugacity coefficient φ:
  μ(P,T) = μ°(T) + kT ln(f/f°), with f = φ(P,T)P.
• Use the same EOS in all simulations and report it explicitly; confirm low-P ideal-gas limit and high-P corrections up to 100 bar.

Step 6 — Deliverables and validation tests
• Validation A (equilibrium): reproduce reported qualitative/quantitative trends: increase of hysteresis pressure width with T (as observed in Co(BDP) literature) and correct order-of-magnitude uptake.
• Validation B (mechanism): show that hysteresis onset aligns with regions where G(s;μ,T) is bistable and ΔG‡ is large; demonstrate microstate trapping (pα depends on scan direction).
• Validation C (predictive tests): predict how modifying ligand rigidity (virtual stiffening of hinge torsions) or metal substitution (Co→Ni/Fe in a hypothetical parameter sweep) changes ΔG‡ and thus hysteresis width—offering design rules.

Step 7 — Explicit optional extension: constant-stress host (only if needed)
• If evidence suggests external mechanical pressure or anisotropic stress impacts gating beyond μ-coupling, implement an NσT (constant-stress) framework MD/MC component to obtain Fhost,α(σ,T). Otherwise, keep the model strictly μ,T-driven to maintain ensemble correctness and avoid ambiguous “(μ,P,T)”.
Feasibility:
Statistical mechanics rigor (addresses ensemble critique): The proposal replaces the ambiguous “(μ,P,T)” notion with a semigrand/expanded-ensemble formulation in which pressure affects adsorption only through μ(P,T) (via fugacity/EOS). Host-switch acceptance is defined by Δ[β(Fhost,α + Ωα(μ,T))], preserving detailed balance. Optional biasing (Wang–Landau/transition-matrix) is explicitly separated into equilibrium free-energy estimation rather than being conflated with kinetics.

Mechanistic completeness (addresses two-minima limitation): Instead of restricting flexibility to two DFT minima, the plan constructs and validates a gating coordinate s and reconstructs Fhost(s,T), ensuring at least one intermediate/saddle region is captured. A continuous-CV benchmark is included to test whether a discrete-state reduction is adequate.

Kinetic interpretability (addresses metastability/hysteresis critique): Hysteresis is generated via a physically grounded kinetic layer: barriers ΔG‡(μ,T) from G(s;μ,T) are converted to rates and propagated with kinetic Monte Carlo under controlled μ(t) ramps. This prevents the common artifact where frequent host-switch moves collapse hysteresis toward equilibrium. A fallback calibration of attempt frequency is included but constrained by detailed-balance-correct acceptance and validated by predicting temperature/scan-rate dependence beyond the calibration point.

Force-field/quantum credibility (addresses interaction-model risk): The interaction model is validated against periodic DFT binding data for multiple host states and includes explicit quantum corrections appropriate for 20–100 K (Feynman–Hibbs; spot-check with path-integral GCMC). The plan includes uncertainty propagation so that agreement/disagreement with experiment can be interpreted quantitatively rather than being potentially fortuitous.

Computational practicality: Each component is standard in contemporary adsorption/flexible-MOF workflows—(i) periodic DFT pathway/umbrella sampling for Fhost(s), (ii) state-resolved GCMC for Ωα(μ,T), (iii) expanded-ensemble methods for equilibrium, and (iv) kMC for scanning isotherms—yet their integration is novel specifically for diffusion-controlled hysteresis in Co(BDP).
Critique: Technically ambitious and largely well-engineered: the expanded-ensemble formalism is correctly framed (pressure enters via μ; host-switch acceptance uses Δ[Fhost+Ω]), and the equilibrium vs scanning separation is a strong point that addresses a common failure mode (artificial hysteresis collapse). The main weaknesses are (i) practical identifiability of a single/few CV(s) that genuinely parameterize the Co(BDP) gate without hidden slow modes—this is acknowledged but not operationally de-risked (clear criteria for CV sufficiency and convergence diagnostics are missing); (ii) the barrier-to-rate mapping is underdetermined for a crystalline framework (Eyring/κ assumptions, dynamical prefactor, and coupling to adsorbate rearrangement may dominate at 20–100 K), so the kMC layer risks becoming semi-empirical despite detailed-balance-correct thermodynamics; and (iii) the plan mixes force-field GCMC with DFT-derived host free energies/barriers, but does not specify a consistency strategy (e.g., how elastic/phonon contributions and adsorbate-induced stress are reconciled across α, or when constant-stress effects become non-negligible). Evidence grounding is solid and stays within adsorption/stat mech/quantum corrections without irrelevant excursions. Rationale is strong: it targets a recognized bottleneck (rigid-lattice GCMC cannot represent competing host grand potentials or kinetic trapping) with a structurally modified sampling framework plus kinetics.

Hypothesis: A covalently asymmetric (Janus) UiO-type Zr6O8-cluster MOF membrane can be engineered so that only the feed-facing crystallite exterior is rendered persistently superhydrophobic, while the internal transport network and permeate-facing surface remain comparatively polar. This will be achieved by (i) enforcing true one-sided node chemistry via a confinement control that blocks through-thickness solvent/polymer wicking and (ii) limiting Zr–carboxylate coordination to an ultrathin, surface-confined grafted layer (telechelic COOH–PCL–COOH) that is subsequently end-capped with long alkyl chains (C8–C18) to minimize surface energy and stabilize a Cassie–Baxter state on a micro/nano-rough MOF crystal topography. Mechanistically, water exclusion will be governed by a quantified breakthrough-pressure (Laplace) criterion using measured effective pore radii of the feed-side intercrystallite openings that water ‘sees’, while oil permeation will proceed primarily through the percolating intercrystallite meso/macro-porosity (not UiO intrinsic micropores), with UiO micropores contributing mainly to sorption/affinity and secondary flow. The refined strategy directly addresses key failure modes: (1) polymer infiltration/pore blocking is prevented by temporary pore filling (removable infiltrant) and by solvent/size selection that discourages MOF wetting and grain-boundary penetration; (2) Zr6–OH/–OH2 chemical state is controlled by strictly anhydrous, non-nucleophilic base conditions and bounded by defect-density control and “no-linker-exchange” sentinel experiments; (3) Cassie-state persistence is validated under realistic pressure fluctuations and surfactant contamination by comparing measured water entry pressure against the Laplace-predicted threshold and by monitoring dynamic wetting hysteresis; (4) Zr–OOC graft retention is bounded by pH/salt/shear aging and a competitive ligand challenge (acetate/benzoate), tracked quantitatively by surface-sensitive spectroscopy and organic loading metrics.
Plan:
Step 1 — Membrane architecture selection, pore-family mapping baseline, and defect control
1.1 MOF choice & defect-density bracket: Prepare (a) UiO-67 and (b) defect-engineered UiO-66 (missing-linker controlled via modulator equivalents; target two levels, e.g., low-defect and high-defect) as polycrystalline layers on porous supports (alumina for chemical robustness; PVDF as polymeric comparator). Record missing-linker signatures (TGA mass loss, 1H NMR of digested samples, and Zr/O ratios by XPS) to quantify node –OH/–OH2 density as graftable sites.
1.2 Roughness engineering (intentional micro/nano hierarchy): Use seeded growth with controlled secondary nucleation to generate a top surface composed of microcrystallites (0.2–2 µm) decorated by nanocrystallites (20–200 nm). Quantify roughness by AFM (Ra, Rz) and SEM image analysis.
1.3 Baseline pore-family transport map (pre-functionalization):
  • Permporometry (dry N2 or He with a condensing vapor such as water or alcohol depending on instrument) to resolve active flow constrictions.
  • Gas permeance (N2, CO2) to infer Knudsen/viscous regimes.
  • Liquid intrusion/cryoporometry (or mercury intrusion if available) to quantify meso/macro pore size distribution of intercrystallite pathways.
  Output: Identify whether flux is dominated by intercrystallite meso/macro pores (expected for membranes) vs intrinsic micropores; set a quantitative baseline “effective pore radius” (reff) relevant for water entry.

Step 2 — Confinement control strategy (beyond one-sided exposure) to prevent polymer infiltration and Janus loss
2.1 Temporary permeate-side pore filling (“removable infiltrant mask”): Prior to grafting, fill the membrane/support pore network from the permeate side with a removable, nonreactive, nonpolar infiltrant that (i) is immiscible with the grafting solvent and (ii) does not coordinate Zr. Two candidate classes:
  • Perfluorinated oil (e.g., a low-viscosity PFPE) for chemical inertness; or
  • Solidifiable alkane/wax (e.g., n-hexadecane) introduced warm, then cooled to immobilize.
  Acceptance criteria: infiltrant must reduce through-thickness solvent uptake (gravimetric solvent uptake <10% of unfilled control over grafting time window) and be removable post-grafting by mild heating/vacuum or extraction with a nonreactive solvent that does not strip the graft.
2.2 Feed-side-only exposure cell with edge sealing: Mount membrane in a diffusion cell where (i) only the feed face is contacted by grafting solution, (ii) the membrane perimeter is sealed (chemical-resistant epoxy or compression gasket) to eliminate lateral edge wicking, and (iii) a defined hydrostatic head is applied on the feed side while the permeate side is kept at zero head (or slight positive backpressure) to oppose convective penetration.
2.3 Timed penetration diagnostics (mandatory): After exposure times t = 5, 15, 60, 240 min, quench, wash, remove infiltrant, and perform cross-sectional ToF-SIMS line scans and/or depth profiling for PCL fragments (e.g., CxHyOz− signatures) and alkyl fragments after end-capping, complemented by angle-resolved XPS (C 1s ester vs carboxylate, Zr 3d). Define a quantitative “Janus factor” J = (organic signal at top 1–3 µm feed side)/(organic signal at mid-plane/permeate side). Target J ≥ 10 for success; if J < 5, tighten confinement (increase infiltrant viscosity/solidification, reduce grafting time, change solvent).

Step 3 — Surface-confined coordination-grafting chemistry with controlled Zr6–OH state and minimized linker exchange
3.1 Anhydrous conditioning to stabilize node chemistry: Pre-dry membranes (vacuum, 120–150 °C, time per MOF stability) to minimize residual water. Transfer under dry atmosphere.
3.2 Solvent and base selection to minimize MOF etching/linker exchange:
  • Use anhydrous, low-polarity solvent system that poorly wets UiO micropores yet dissolves PCL (e.g., toluene with a small fraction of dry THF, minimized to the solubility threshold).
  • Replace/benchmark triethylamine with a less nucleophilic, sterically hindered base (e.g., DIPEA) at low equivalents relative to terminal COOH to promote surface carboxylate formation while minimizing any ligand-exchange kinetics at defective nodes.
  • Include a “sentinel linker-loss test”: measure linker content in solution post-grafting by UV/LC (terephthalate/biphenyldicarboxylate signatures) and compare to blank solvent/base exposure.
3.3 Size-exclusion lever: Use COOH–PCL–COOH with Mn selected to discourage deep infiltration into mesopores (e.g., Mn 5–20 kDa; Rg larger than dominant intercrystallite throat size inferred from cryoporometry). If mesopore throats are large, rely on infiltrant mask + shortened exposure + higher-viscosity solvent.
3.4 Grafting protocol (feed-side only): Contact feed side with COOH–PCL–COOH solution (concentration bracket, e.g., 0.5–10 mg/mL) for controlled time (5–60 min), then rinse with dry solvent to remove physisorbed polymer. Target an ultrathin brush regime: verify by ellipsometry on flat UiO-coated witness substrates and by cross-sectional SEM/TEM contrast if feasible.
3.5 Alkyl end-capping (feed side only) to lock low surface energy: Convert remaining terminal –COOH of grafted PCL to C8–C18 esters/amides using EDC/NHS coupling with long-chain alcohols/amines in strictly anhydrous conditions. Systematically vary alkyl chain length (C2, C8, C12, C18) to reproduce the chain-length/hydrophobicity trend (Asset 1) and establish a design rule.
3.6 Optional PDA primer (feed side only, pore-safe): If adhesion/retention is insufficient under shear, apply sub-10 nm polydopamine on only the outermost feed surface using very short deposition time and dilute dopamine, followed by immediate rinse. Confirm no significant pore blocking by permporometry shift (<10% reduction in dominant constriction radius). PDA is strictly optional and only retained if it improves graft retention without transport penalty (Asset 2).

Step 4 — Quantitative wetting + breakthrough-pressure framework and Cassie-state persistence under real feeds
4.1 Wetting metrics on both faces: Measure static/advancing/receding WCA, contact angle hysteresis, and sliding angle. Target feed-side WCA >150° with low hysteresis; permeate side substantially lower.
4.2 Breakthrough-pressure model (water entry pressure): Use measured effective pore radii (reff) of the relevant feed-side openings (from permporometry/cryoporometry) and the apparent contact angle θapp on the feed side to compute ΔPbreak ≈ −(2 γLV cosθapp)/reff, with γLV for water and corrected “effective θ” derived from Cassie–Baxter fits using roughness/solid fraction estimates. Use this to set an operating safety margin: require ΔPbreak ≥ 3× expected transmembrane pressure fluctuations during gravity/crossflow.
4.3 Challenge feeds to validate Cassie persistence:
  • Surfactant-stabilized emulsions (e.g., SDS/Tween at low–moderate concentrations) to deliberately lower interfacial tension and probe failure.
  • Variable oils (hexane, toluene, diesel surrogate) to test viscosity and affinity effects.
  Record dynamic wetting evolution (WCA vs time), water intrusion (breakthrough events), and flux changes.

Step 5 — Transport mechanism assignment: distinguish micropore vs intercrystallite pathway contributions
5.1 Correlate flux with pore-family metrics: After each functionalization condition, re-run permporometry and cryoporometry/intrusion to detect shifts in active constrictions. If intrinsic micropore uptake is altered (N2 sorption drop) but permporometry/mesopore metrics remain stable, assign separation flux to intercrystallite network; if permporometry constrictions shrink significantly, diagnose polymer infiltration/pore blocking.
5.2 Micropore accessibility control: Collect N2 sorption (or CO2 at 273 K) and compare to pristine UiO. Define an acceptable loss threshold (e.g., <30% micropore surface area loss) to ensure chemistry is surface-confined rather than bulk pore-filling.

Step 6 — Separation testing with mechanistic controls and failure-mode triggers
6.1 Performance tests: Gravity-driven and low-pressure crossflow oil/water separation; report flux, rejection, and stability over cycles.
6.2 Mechanistic controls:
  • Fully functionalized (both sides) vs Janus-only vs unfunctionalized.
  • With vs without infiltrant mask (quantifies confinement necessity).
  • Chain length series (C2→C18) as low-surface-energy control (Asset 1).
6.3 In situ visualization: Confocal microscopy with dyed water/oil to observe wetting front and detect any through-thickness water invasion.

Step 7 — Graft stability/retention: pH/salt/shear aging + competitive ligand challenge
7.1 Aging protocol: Prolonged crossflow under saline (0–3.5 wt% NaCl), pH 2–12 cycles, and defined shear rates. Periodically measure WCA, sliding angle, and flux.
7.2 Spectroscopic retention tracking: Monitor Zr–OOC coordination (ATR-FTIR COO− asym/sym; XPS O 1s/C 1s deconvolution) and quantify organic loading (TGA; ToF-SIMS intensity normalization) before/after aging.
7.3 Competitive ligand challenge: Expose feed side to acetate/benzoate solutions (concentration series) under controlled conditions to bound reversibility of Zr–carboxylate anchoring. Pass criterion: minimal loss of feed-side organic signature and maintained breakthrough pressure; failure triggers redesign (e.g., introduce secondary anchoring via PDA or switch to less labile anchoring chemistry while preserving MOF-native node binding).

Go/No-Go decision rules (explicit failure-mode-driven)
• If cross-sectional ToF-SIMS shows mid-plane/permeate polymer signal >20% of feed-side signal (J < 5): strengthen confinement (better edge sealing, more viscous/solid infiltrant, shorten exposure, reduce THF fraction, increase Mn).
• If permporometry shows dominant constriction radius decreases >25% post-grafting: reduce grafting density/time or lower Mn; validate with N2 sorption recovery.
• If measured ΔPbreak is below expected operating pressure (or collapses under surfactant feeds): increase chain length, increase roughness hierarchy, or reduce solid fraction to favor Cassie state; re-fit Cassie–Baxter parameters.
• If ligand challenge strips graft: add secondary anchoring (PDA primer) or move to bifunctional anchoring strategy while keeping feed-side confinement.
Feasibility:
1) Confinement is made verifiable and controllable, not assumed. The temporary permeate-side pore-filling infiltrant plus edge sealing/backpressure directly targets the reviewer-identified wicking pathway (grain boundaries/support pores) that a diffusion cell alone cannot eliminate. The required outcome (high Janus factor J from cross-sectional ToF-SIMS/XPS line scans after timed exposures) converts “one-sided exposure” into a quantitative, falsifiable design criterion.

2) Node chemistry risk under base is bounded by anhydrous processing, solvent polarity control, sterically hindered base selection, and explicit “sentinel” linker-loss assays to detect etching/linker exchange—especially important at missing-linker sites. Defect density is treated as a tunable variable (grafting site density) rather than an uncontrolled liability.

3) Transport is assigned to pore families with measurements that can distinguish mechanisms. The plan explicitly maps active flow constrictions (permporometry) and intercrystallite meso/macro porosity (cryoporometry/intrusion) before and after grafting, while separately tracking intrinsic microporosity (gas sorption). This addresses the underdetermined question of which pore family carries the separation flux and provides a pore-blocking diagnostic.

4) Cassie–Baxter wetting is coupled to a quantitative breakthrough-pressure framework. By computing and then experimentally challenging ΔPbreak under realistic pressure fluctuations and surfactant-lowered interfacial tension, the proposal tests Cassie-state persistence rather than inferring it from high contact angle alone (Assets 1 and 3 support the roughness + low-surface-energy route to superhydrophobicity).

5) Graft retention is treated as a chemical stability problem with bounds. Tracking Zr–OOC signatures and organic loading after pH/salt/shear aging, plus a competitive ligand challenge (acetate/benzoate), provides an explicit reversibility window for Zr–carboxylate anchoring and a trigger for secondary anchoring (PDA) if needed (Asset 2).
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in execution detail and in converting typical failure modes (wicking, pore blocking, Cassie collapse, Zr–carboxylate lability) into measurable, go/no-go criteria. The confinement strategy (removable infiltrant + sealed cell + timed depth profiling) is a credible advance over standard asymmetric exposure. However, several core risks remain under-specified quantitatively: (i) the infiltrant mask could itself alter intercrystallite connectivity or leave residues that artifactually inflate WCA/ΔPbreak unless stringent mass-balance/chemical verification is added; (ii) the Laplace model depends critically on which “reff” governs water entry in a hierarchically rough, chemically heterogeneous polycrystal—permporometry/cryoporometry may not isolate the true, pressure-limiting throat at the feed surface, and surfactant-lowered γ and dynamic intrusion can invalidate a static θ-based criterion; (iii) the assumption that UiO intrinsic micropores play only a secondary role in oil transport is plausible but not yet pinned to a quantitative resistance model (series/parallel resistances) or to tracer/partitioning data, so mechanistic attribution may remain ambiguous; (iv) Zr–carboxylate grafting under base in mixed solvents is still at meaningful risk of defect-mediated ligand exchange/etching, and the proposed ‘sentinel linker-loss’ assay may miss solid-phase rearrangements unless paired with crystallinity/defect evolution metrics (PXRD line broadening, pair distribution/total scattering, or quantitative digestion-NMR before/after). Overall, methodological rigor is high, but the mechanistic proof structure needs tighter identification of the true water-entry constriction and more definitive discrimination of flow pathways and node-chemistry evolution.

Hypothesis: Defectivity in HKUST-1 can be transformed into a *chemically programmable and verifiable distribution* of Cu-site adsorption energetics by introducing a defect-selective, thermochemically validated node-ligand “fuse” whose exchange selectivity and cleavage outcome are explicitly gated before energetic mapping. The central mechanistic premise is that defect-capped Cu2 paddlewheels (monocarboxylate/solvent-terminated) exhibit measurably higher ligand lability and altered Cu–O bond asymmetry relative to intact BTC-bridged nodes; this difference can be exploited by post-synthetic node–ligand exchange (PSNLE) using isotopically/element-tagged, sterically biased diacids that are kinetically excluded from fully bridged nodes. Upon global heating within a narrowly defined scission window—pre-validated on molecular Cu2(O2CR)4 analogs—the fuse undergoes a known bond-cleavage reaction that yields fragments with demonstrably weak Cu affinity or volatility, producing a stoichiometrically bounded fraction of accessible open metal sites (OMS). The resulting framework contains three *chemically defined* Cu microenvironments: (i) pristine OMS, (ii) fuse-adjacent strained paddlewheels with perturbed Cu–O metrics, and (iii) residual capped defects. These populations generate a predictable broadening and reshaping of the coverage-dependent isosteric heat of adsorption Qst(θ), which is directly quantified by orthogonal OMS titration and microcalorimetry. Because analytes partition differently among these Cu-site classes based on Lewis basicity, quadrupole moment, and hydration competition, the engineered Qst(θ) landscape encodes analyte identity into reproducible calorimetric and optical sensing signatures that are thermodynamically normalized against transport and humidity effects.
Plan:
Phase 0 – Hard selectivity-and-outcome gate (mandatory before Qst mapping):
0.1 Defect-selective PSNLE proof using tagged fuses: Synthesize two sterically differentiated, isotopically/element-tagged diacid fuses: (A) 13C-labeled, ortho-disubstituted aromatic diacid (carboxylates labeled at C=O) and (B) F-tagged aliphatic/aromatic diacid with CF3 reporter groups. Perform PSNLE under rigorously buffered, low-water conditions (≤50 ppm H2O, neutral to mildly basic additives to suppress BTC protonation). Quantify exchange at defect caps vs intact BTC nodes by (i) digestion + quantitative 1H/13C NMR mass balance, (ii) solid-state 13C CP/MAS NMR (tag incorporation vs BTC signal retention), and (iii) XPS/F 1s mapping for spatially averaged incorporation. Controls include pristine HKUST-1, defect-rich HKUST-1 without PSNLE, and intentional BTC displacement benchmarks. Acceptance criterion: ≥80% of incorporated tag attributable to defect caps with ≤5% BTC loss.
0.2 Molecular scission validation on Cu2 paddlewheel analogs: Prepare Cu2(O2CR)4 model complexes bearing the candidate fuse as one or two ligands. Perform variable-temperature TGA–MS, solution NMR, and IR to identify cleavage temperature, products, and kinetics. Independently measure Cu–fragment binding constants (ITC or competitive ligand exchange) to confirm weak binding (ΔGbind ≳ −5 kJ mol−1) or volatility under activation conditions. Reject fuse designs whose fragments persist as strong monocarboxylate caps.
0.3 Net OMS yield verification post-cleavage: Apply the validated heating protocol to fuse-exchanged HKUST-1 and confirm a net decrease in monocarboxylate equivalents by post-activation digestion NMR and TGA. Only materials passing 0.1–0.3 proceed.

Phase 1 – Defect-engineered HKUST-1 library:
1.1 Synthesize HKUST-1 with controlled defect densities via coordination modulation (formic, acetic, benzoic acids spanning pKa/sterics), maintaining comparable crystal sizes through seeded growth. Quantify defect caps by digestion NMR, TGA, DRIFTS, and Cu K-edge XAS.

Phase 2 – Fuse installation and chemistry-defined heat transformation:
2.1 Perform PSNLE using the pre-approved fuse under conditions proven selective in Phase 0. Tune fuse loading (0–100% of defect caps) by stoichiometry and time.
2.2 Apply global thermal activation within the validated scission window (e.g., 90–140 °C under vacuum/inert). Track cleavage in situ by TGA–MS and DRIFTS; monitor Cu coordination changes by XAS and EPR (screening for Cu(I) as a failure mode).

Phase 3 – Orthogonal OMS quantification and site assignment:
3.1 Quantify accessible OMS directly using CO titration microcalorimetry (initial heats), CO-IR (νCO shifts/intensity), and NO adsorption EPR/IR as an independent site count. Correlate OMS fraction with digestion-NMR-derived cap loss.
3.2 Assign Cu microenvironments by combining OMS counts with EXAFS-constrained models and probe-molecule IR (CO, pyridine).

Phase 4 – Energetic landscape mapping:
4.1 Measure multi-temperature adsorption isotherms (CO2, NH3/pyridine, H2O, VOCs). Derive Qst(θ) and validate low-coverage values by differential microcalorimetry.
4.2 Construct a 2D map of Qst(θ) as a function of initial defectivity and fuse loading; fit data to multi-site Langmuir/Temkin models to extract fractions and characteristic heats of each Cu-site class.

Phase 5 – Sensing with thermodynamic normalization:
5.1 Calorimetric sensing: Integrate thin films of controlled thickness onto membrane calorimeters. Normalize heat-release transients by independently measured uptake (QCM/gravimetric).
5.2 Optical sensing: Monitor diffuse-reflectance UV–vis/NIR changes associated with Cu paddlewheel ligand-field perturbations. Correlate signal magnitude/kinetics with OMS fraction and Qst descriptors.
5.3 Stability envelope: Perform water co-adsorption isotherms and accelerated humidity cycling; track PXRD, N2 sorption, XANES edge position, and persistence of Qst(θ) to define operational limits where hydrolysis is negligible.
Feasibility: The revised plan directly addresses reviewer-identified failure modes by inserting a quantitative selectivity-and-outcome gate before any energetic mapping. Defect-selective PSNLE is no longer assumed but proven via isotopic/element tagging and mass balance that explicitly bounds BTC displacement. Fuse chemistry is de-risked by prior validation on molecular Cu2 paddlewheel analogs, ensuring that cleavage products are weakly binding or volatile and that OMS generation is stoichiometrically meaningful rather than empirically inferred. OMS formation is quantified by chemisorption-based titration (CO/NO) orthogonal to EXAFS, providing a direct metric that anchors Qst(θ) heterogeneity to real site counts. Finally, sensor translation is normalized against uptake and bounded by humidity-stability protocols, decoupling thermodynamics from transport and degradation artifacts. Together, these measures convert the original concept from a plausible but empirical tuning strategy into a chemically constrained, mechanistically interpretable platform where defect chemistry, heat-triggered coordination changes, adsorption energetics, and sensing outputs are causally linked.
Critique: The proposal is unusually rigorous in gating assumptions (defect-selective exchange and cleavage outcome) before claiming energetic programmability, and it uses appropriate orthogonal readouts (digestion NMR mass balance, SSNMR/XPS tags, TGA–MS/DRIFTS, XAS/EPR, CO/NO titration, microcalorimetry). The main weaknesses are (i) the central selectivity premise remains chemically underdetermined: steric exclusion alone is not a reliable discriminator between defective and intact HKUST-1 nodes given framework breathing/solvation and possible BTC decoordination under exchange conditions; (ii) the acceptance criterion “≥80% tag at defect caps with ≤5% BTC loss” may be incompatible with detectable incorporation levels and with the kinetics of exchange in a microporous solid (risk of false positives from surface-only exchange); (iii) the scission window (90–140 °C) is optimistic for many bond-cleavage chemistries and may overlap with solvent loss, defect reorganization, or Cu(II) → Cu(I) redox pathways, confounding causal attribution of OMS generation; (iv) the mapping from three hypothesized Cu microenvironments to a deconvolvable multi-site Qst(θ) is not guaranteed—Qst(θ) can be dominated by adsorbate–adsorbate interactions, pore-filling, and residual water, making site-fraction extraction non-identifiable without stronger constraints; and (v) the sensing claim that signatures can be “thermodynamically normalized against transport and humidity effects” is directionally correct but underspecified—humidity competition and partial hydrolysis can change both site counts and optical baselines, breaking normalization unless explicitly modeled and independently measured in situ.

Hypothesis: Zn‑PYI1 can be transformed into a crystallinity‑retaining, permanently porous metalloenzyme‑mimetic by a two-layer catalytic architecture that explicitly de-risks Zn‑carboxylate fragility: (i) a topotactic, low‑fraction solvent‑assisted linker exchange (SALE) installs a latent, inward-facing carbonyl handle on an isoreticular PYI strut while preserving the primary organocatalyst geometry enforced by the Zn-carboxylate lattice; (ii) a water-activity–controlled dynamic covalent manifold (preferentially oxime/hydrazone; imine as a secondary route) programs an adaptive second-sphere microenvironment (H-bonding + Brønsted acid/base + polarity) around the fixed PYI site. Mechanistically, the lattice provides a rigid first-sphere “active-site frame” (crystallinity) that fixes the relative positioning of photoredox (triphenylamine) and organocatalyst (PYI) motifs, while the reversible C=N chemistry acts as an error-correcting, self-healing second sphere that can (a) pre-organize aldehyde/enamine formation, (b) electrostatically and H-bond stabilize the enamine–radical-cation coupled transition state in photoinduced asymmetric α-alkylation, and (c) suppress nonselective solution pathways by increasing internal effective molarity and restricting radical diffusion/recombination. The refined approach overcomes the reviewers’ chemistry–structure interface concerns by (1) avoiding strong aqueous acid for deprotection (switch to MOF-compatible carbonyl unmasking and/or direct carbonyl-linker exchange), (2) operating under quantified low water activity (Karl Fischer–verified solvents; molecular sieves; buffered catalysts), and (3) replacing unquantified “self-sorting” with a measurable selectivity hierarchy (competitive uptake/isotherms + in-pore speciation by ssNMR/XPS) that predicts which amines occupy which fraction of carbonyl sites as a function of pKa, size, and diffusion. Catalytic gains are predicted to correlate with a defined pocket-density parameter (ρpocket = xexchange × θC=N loading) and with site-isolation metrics proving pore-internal turnover dominates over external surface catalysis.
Plan:
Step 0 — Define quantitative go/no-go gates (mandatory derisking milestones)
0.1. Crystallinity gate (all postsynthetic steps): PXRD similarity index ≥ 0.90 vs parent (peak positions within ±0.05° 2θ; no new dominant phases), and (where crystals permit) unit-cell volume change |ΔV| ≤ 3% by SCXRD or Le Bail refinement.
0.2. Permanent porosity gate: BET surface area retention ≥ 70% of parent Zn‑PYI1 after each critical step (post-SALE; post-carbonyl unmasking; post-pocket installation), and micropore volume retention ≥ 65% (NLDFT).
0.3. Chemical stability gate: Zn leaching during any treatment or catalysis ≤ 1.0 wt% of total Zn per cycle (ICP‑MS of supernatants), and carboxylate-linker loss/defect increase limited to ≤ 5% relative change by quantitative digest NMR mass balance (total linker:Zn ratio) plus TGA consistency.
0.4. Internal-site catalysis gate: (i) external poisoning reduces activity ≤ 20% (internal remains), while (ii) pore blocking reduces activity ≥ 60% (internal required), and (iii) initial rate shows weak particle-size dependence consistent with internal diffusion control only beyond a defined size regime (see Step 3.4).

Step 1 — Baseline reproduction and controls (structure–function anchor)
1.1. Synthesize Zn‑PYI1 and activate under literature-consistent conditions; prepare three particle-size cuts (e.g., ~0.5–1 µm, 2–5 µm, 20–50 µm) by controlled crystallization/sonication/sieving; measure size distributions (SEM + laser diffraction).
1.2. Baseline characterization: PXRD, N2/Ar sorption (BET, NLDFT), CO2 (273 K) for ultramicropore access, TGA, and photocatalytic asymmetric α‑alkylation benchmarking under fixed photon flux (actinometry), fixed stirring, identical catalyst mass and optical path. Record: initial rates, yields, ee, quantum yield (apparent), and recyclability (≥5 cycles).
1.3. Establish homogeneous and “physical mixture” controls: (i) homogeneous PYI organocatalyst + triphenylamine analogue (if available) + amine additives; (ii) physical mixture of parent Zn‑PYI1 with the same amine additives not tethered; these define the non-confinement baseline.

Step 2 — Linker editing with explicit SCSC derisking (SALE fraction control)
2.1. Linker design options (choose primary + contingency):
  - Primary path A (avoid post-exchange acid deprotection): synthesize an isoreticular PYI-derived dicarboxylate linker bearing a directly accessible aldehyde (L‑CHO) but electronically deactivated toward side reactions (e.g., aromatic aldehyde separated by a short alkyl spacer to reduce coordination interference) and lacking extra donor atoms.
  - Contingency path B (latent carbonyl, MOF-compatible unmasking): synthesize L‑Acetal (acetal-protected aldehyde) OR L‑Diol precursor that can be oxidized in-pore to aldehyde under neutral conditions (e.g., TEMPO/bleach-type oxidations are excluded; instead use mild, non-aqueous oxidants compatible with Zn-carboxylates; final selection determined by stability screen in Step 2.5).
  - Nonreactive control linker L‑Me (steric/electronic analog lacking carbonyl reactivity).
2.2. SALE protocol (topotactic constraints): perform SALE on activated Zn‑PYI1 in non-coordinating solvent (e.g., chlorinated solvent/alkane + minimal polar co-solvent as required for linker solubility; exclude DMF/strong amide donors if they increase lability) at 40–70 °C with low linker concentration to minimize dissolution–reprecipitation. Target xexchange = 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20.
2.3. Time-course sampling to prove topotaxy: collect aliquots at multiple time points; quantify exchange fraction by digest 1H NMR (integral ratios of native vs introduced linker), and verify crystallinity retention by high-resolution PXRD; accept only conditions meeting gates 0.1–0.3.
2.4. Defect quantification and lattice lability check: (i) total scattering/PDF before/after SALE to detect local Zn–O distortions; (ii) thermogravimetry/digest NMR for linker:Zn stoichiometry; (iii) quantify any increase in missing-linker defects indirectly via increased uptake of a defect-probe (e.g., small polar probe gas vs parent) while ensuring micropore retention.
2.5. Carbonyl-handle viability screen (small-scale stability matrix): expose SALE materials to candidate unmasking/activation conditions in sealed vials with controlled water activity (aw) and quantify: PXRD similarity, BET retention, and Zn leaching. Only one protocol is promoted to full workflow:
  - Validated protocol requirement: demonstrate ≥70% BET retention and ≤1 wt% Zn loss after 24 h treatment.

Step 2b — Carbonyl activation/unmasking with water-activity control (explicit protocol + contingency)
2b.1. If direct L‑CHO is used: skip deprotection and proceed to pocket formation.
2b.2. If acetal deprotection is required (contingency, only if Step 2.5 passes): perform acetal hydrolysis under strictly controlled low aw using anhydrous alcohol solvent pre-dried to <200 ppm H2O (Karl Fischer), 3Å molecular sieves, and catalytic, non-coordinating Brønsted acid at minimal loading (screen: 0.1–1 mol% relative to acetal sites). Keep crystals solvent-filled at all times; avoid vacuum drying until after neutralization and thorough solvent exchange.
2b.3. If any deprotection condition violates gates: pivot to oxime/hydrazone strategy using a carbonyl that does not require acid (direct L‑CHO), or pivot to in-pore formation of oxime/hydrazone from a ketone handle that is installed directly.

Step 3 — Pocket programming with quantified “assembly rules” (replace qualitative self-sorting)
3.1. Choose dynamic covalent bond type based on stability matrix:
  - Preferred: oxime or hydrazone formation (greater hydrolytic stability than imines; still reversible under mild conditions), using aminooxy or hydrazide residues as second-sphere “modules”.
  - Secondary: imines only if Step 2.5 shows stability under required aw and pH window.
3.2. Define pocket-density parameter and loading control:
  - ρpocket = xexchange × θC=N, where θC=N is fractional conversion of carbonyl sites to C=N adduct (quantified by digest NMR and ssNMR integration).
  - Target θC=N levels: 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 at each xexchange to decouple “how many handles” from “how fully occupied”.
3.3. Quantify competitive uptake/selectivity (mandatory):
  - Measure single-component uptake isotherms in solvent (or vapor, if feasible) for each amine/aminooxy module to obtain apparent partition coefficients (Kpore).
  - Perform competitive uptake experiments (binary/ternary mixtures) and determine selectivity factors Sij = (qi/qj)pore / (Ci/Cj)solution. Use these Sij values to design mixtures that predictably enrich a desired module near the carbonyl handles.
3.4. Replace “self-sorting triad” with rule-based assembly:
  - Construct a minimal “His-like” module (aminoimidazole derivative via C=N chemistry), an “Asp/Glu-like” anionic/polar module (carboxylate/sulfonate-bearing aminooxy/hydrazide), and a “Ser-like” H-bond donor module (aminoalcohol aminooxy/hydrazide).
  - Assembly strategy A (sequential with equilibrium reset): install module 1 to partial θ, wash/exchange, then module 2, then module 3; leverage reversibility by applying a mild catalyst (buffered) to allow error correction, followed by solvent exchange to freeze composition.
  - Assembly strategy B (competitive mixture with predicted outcome): use the measured Sij and diffusion/size data to set feed ratios that target a specified internal composition (e.g., 1:1:1 occupancy within ±10%).
  - Heterogeneity assessment (mandatory): ssNMR (13C/15N CP/MAS) lineshape/broadening analysis to estimate distribution of C=N environments; corroborate with XPS N 1s deconvolution and, where possible, spatial mapping (e.g., micro-FTIR mapping across single crystals) to rule out shell-only functionalization.
3.5. Optional locking step (only after best dynamic pocket identified): reduce C=N adducts to secondary amines under rigorously screened mild conditions (small-scale first), ensuring gates 0.1–0.3 remain satisfied. Maintain an unreduced series to compare “dynamic vs static” function.

Step 4 — Internal-site proof: discriminate pore vs external surface catalysis (mandatory)
4.1. External-site selective poisoning: graft/block external surface with a bulky, non-penetrating reagent that binds/quenches accessible basic sites (size-excluded from pores), then test catalytic activity. Pass criterion: ≤20% loss vs unpoisoned sample.
4.2. Pore-blocking experiment: introduce a bulky, pore-occupying but catalytically inert guest that is known to enter the channels and reduce free volume (quantify by sorption decrease). Pass criterion: ≥60% loss in initial rate and/or ee collapse consistent with loss of confinement.
4.3. Particle-size dependence: compare initial rates and ee across size cuts at identical loading and photon flux. Internal catalysis expectation: (i) rates decrease with increasing crystal size if diffusion-limited; (ii) if external sites dominated, rates scale with external area and show stronger size dependence even when pores are blocked. Use these trends with Thiele-modulus-style interpretation to support internal turnover.
4.4. Leaching/homogeneous contribution test: hot filtration (or light-off filtration) and continuation of reaction in filtrate; require ≤5% additional conversion in filtrate over matched time.

Step 5 — Structure–function correlations tied to quantitative descriptors (address reviewer request)
5.1. Correlate catalytic metrics (kobs, yield, ee, apparent quantum yield) against: xexchange, θC=N, ρpocket, BET/micropore volume, diffusion proxy (uptake kinetics), and heterogeneity metrics (ssNMR linewidth/peak ratios).
5.2. Mechanism probes with decision outcomes:
  - Water/protic additive sensitivity mapped vs dynamic bond type (oxime/hydrazone vs imine) to verify that performance changes track C=N equilibrium rather than framework degradation.
  - H-bond/acid–base perturbation: add competitive H-bond acceptors/donors; quantify changes in ee/rate to infer second-sphere involvement.
  - Photophysics: transient absorption/EPR (if available) to compare radical lifetimes/back-electron transfer rates vs ρpocket; link improved ee to altered radical persistence within pores.
5.3. Confinement beyond size-selectivity: site-isolation metric by comparing turnover frequency normalized to internal functional loading (from digest NMR) and showing super-linear dependence of ee (or rate) on ρpocket consistent with cooperative pocket effects rather than additive external catalysis.

Step 6 — Stability, recyclability, and self-healing demonstration
6.1. Multi-cycle tests (≥8 cycles) with PXRD + sorption after cycles 1, 3, 5, 8; enforce gates 0.1–0.3.
6.2. Compare dynamic vs locked pockets: dynamic materials should show partial recovery of activity/ee after deliberate perturbation (e.g., brief exposure to competitive binder then removal), whereas locked pockets should not—directly testing “enzyme-like adaptivity”.
Feasibility:
This revision directly addresses the reviewers’ three feasibility risks with explicit quantitative milestones and contingency chemistry.

(1) Framework survivability through carbonyl unmasking and C=N chemistry: The plan no longer depends on repeated aqueous/acidic treatments as a default. The primary route installs an already-unmasked aldehyde (L‑CHO) via low-fraction SALE to minimize lattice stress. If protection is unavoidable, unmasking is screened in a water-activity–controlled matrix (Karl Fischer thresholds; molecular sieves; minimal acid) with pass/fail gates for PXRD similarity (≥0.90), BET retention (≥70%), and Zn leaching (≤1 wt%). This gatekeeping converts “SCSC asserted” into a decision-controlled workflow that stops before irreversible damage.

(2) Water/acid management vs permanent porosity: Dynamic covalent assembly is shifted to oxime/hydrazone as the preferred manifold because it is generally more hydrolytically robust than imines while still reversible enough for error-correction; imines are retained as a secondary option only if stability gates are met. Permanent porosity is protected by keeping pores solvent-filled during transformations, using gentle activation (e.g., scCO2 when needed), and requiring micropore volume retention ≥65% after each critical step.

(3) Pocket assembly rules and heterogeneity control: “Self-sorting” is replaced with measurable selectivity factors (competitive uptake/isotherms) and a defined pocket-density descriptor (ρpocket = xexchange × θC=N). Heterogeneity is not assumed away: ssNMR lineshape analysis + XPS speciation + (where feasible) spatially resolved vibrational mapping are specified to detect shell-only functionalization or broad distributions of C=N environments. These measurements feed back into assembly strategy (sequential vs competitive) and into catalysis correlations.

Internal-site proof and confinement controls are upgraded beyond size-selectivity: a paired external-poisoning vs pore-blocking logic with explicit pass thresholds, particle-size dependence across three size cuts, and leaching/hot-filtration criteria together establish whether turnover occurs predominantly within pores. Finally, structure–function correlation is enforced by mapping rate/ee vs (xexchange, θC=N, ρpocket, diffusion proxies, and heterogeneity metrics), enabling a reviewer-satisfying link between pocket geometry/spacing and catalytic outcomes.

This derisking logic is consistent with prior demonstrations that (i) multivariate postsynthetic modifications can preserve crystallinity/porosity when reactions are chosen to match framework stability windows (Assets 1–2), and (ii) Zn‑PYI MOFs deliver synergistic catalysis when cooperative functions are integrated rather than physically mixed (Asset 3). The revised plan adopts the same integration principle while adding conservative stability gates and fallback chemistries to keep Zn‑carboxylate integrity central rather than assumed.
Critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-engineered for Zn‑carboxylate fragility: it defines hard go/no-go gates (PXRD similarity, BET/micropore retention, Zn leaching, defect mass balance) and includes credible internal-site validation (paired external poisoning/pore blocking, size cuts, hot filtration). The main scientific risk is that the central mechanistic claim—second-sphere modules stabilizing an enamine–radical-cation coupled transition state and suppressing radical diffusion/recombination—remains under-specified in terms of measurable, discriminating observables. Several proposed probes (ssNMR/XPS lineshapes, uptake selectivities) establish composition and heterogeneity, but they do not directly verify the hypothesized H-bond/electrostatic organization at the reactive intermediate stage. Additionally, topotactic SALE at low exchange fractions is plausible, yet the plan underestimates practical linker-solubility/transport constraints and the possibility that even ‘non-coordinating’ solvents and mild heat can induce partial dissolution–recrystallization in Zn-carboxylate MOFs; the PDF/stoichiometry checks help, but the criteria may not fully distinguish subtle recrystallization from true SCSC. Finally, the pocket-density descriptor (ρpocket = xexchange × θC=N) is useful but incomplete: it ignores spatial correlations (clustering vs isolation) and local microenvironment distributions, which can dominate catalysis/ee in confined photoredox where exciton/radical migration lengths matter.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that MOF-520 can be converted into a covalently aminated, temperature-swing-optimized CO2 sorbent by (A) node-level phosphonate grafting that proceeds with predictable, quantifiable speciation at the Al-oxo/μ-OH node and (B) subsequent high-yield intrapore coupling to a pore-reactive electrophile (tosylate/mesylate/epoxide/azide) to install sterically shielded diamines as pendant, non-metal-coordinating bases. Mechanistically, the phosphate graft is not treated as a generic ‘handle installation’ but as a controlled node-speciation event: specific mono-/bidentate Al–O–P binding modes partially replace/consume μ-OH/H2O ligation at the Al node without displacing carboxylate linkers, yielding a bound organic tether at a maximum density set by node coordination/charge balance. This pre-organizes diamine sites at a tunable mean spacing (set by P:Al ratio and mixed-graft dilution) while electronically passivating hard Al sites that would otherwise sequester amines via Lewis acid-base coordination. The diamines are tethered through robust covalent bonds (e.g., sulfonamide/β-aminoalcohol/triazole linkages) so they cannot migrate to propagate infinite ammonium–carbamate chains as in diamine–metal-site (dobpdc) systems. Instead, CO2 uptake proceeds through formation of local ion-pair adducts (ammonium–carbamate and/or carbamic acid pairs) whose cooperativity is intentionally truncated by (i) finite cluster size imposed by site spacing/dilution and (ii) steric shielding that raises the free-energy penalty for chain propagation beyond nearest neighbors. This produces an adsorption ‘step’ that is broadened into a process-matched uptake region spanning ~40–90 °C at flue-relevant pCO2 (0.04–0.15 bar), lowering hysteresis and regeneration enthalpy relative to classical cooperative systems while maintaining higher low-pCO2 capacity than pristine MOF-520 physisorption. The hypothesis is falsifiable by (1) node speciation constraints (P:Al limits and Al coordination changes), (2) demonstrably high intrapore coupling conversion to the tethered diamine, and (3) direct distance/mobility measurements showing suppressed long-range amine–amine chain formation correlated with reduced hysteresis and a model-fitted finite-cooperativity parameter.
Plan:
Stage 0 — Pre-registered decision gates (go/no-go)
G0.1 Parent benchmark: synthesize phase-pure MOF-520 and establish baseline: PXRD match; N2 BET at 77 K (parent reference); CO2 isotherms at 25/40/80/110 °C (0–1 bar) and low-pressure CO2 (0–0.2 bar) to define physisorption working capacity.
G0.2 Global go/no-go thresholds (must meet before TSA studies):
  (i) Post-graft BET retention ≥ 70% of parent (hard gate; 60–70% triggers redesign/dilution; <60% stop).
  (ii) Crystallinity retention: synchrotron PXRD peak positions maintained (Δ2θ consistent with <0.2% lattice change) and total scattering/PDF retains node–node correlations; absence of new amorphous halo dominating.
  (iii) Handle-to-amine conversion ≥ 70% by digestion NMR mass balance (see Stage 2); otherwise change electrophile/coupling chemistry.

Stage 1 — Node-level phosphonate grafting with explicit speciation model and quantitative validation
1.1 Node speciation model (pre-defined, testable):
  • Working structural assumption: MOF-520 Al node presents terminal H2O/μ-OH (or hydroxo/aqua) ligation sites accessible for substitution without carboxylate linker displacement.
  • Expected binding modes for R–PO3H2 (as R–PO3^2−/R–PO3H− under conditions):
    - Monodentate Al–O–P (one O bound to one Al, remaining O’s protonated/H-bonded).
    - Bidentate chelating to a single Al (less likely for octahedral Al but possible if a labile site exists).
    - Bidentate bridging (Al–O–P–O–Al) across adjacent Al centers on the node (anticipated dominant under partial deprotonation), consuming two Al coordination sites.
  • Predicted saturation: define an experimental ‘maximum graft density’ as P:Al at plateau; expectation is sub-stoichiometric vs Al due to limited labile sites (target exploration P:Alfeed spanning 0.02–0.30; anticipated plateau region where additional feed does not increase incorporated P).
  • Charge/proton balance: track μ-OH consumption and protonation state by 1H (digestion) and IR (μ-OH attenuation) and by monitoring counterions if used (e.g., tetrabutylammonium phosphonate).

1.2 Reagent set (primary plan avoids alkyl chloride):
  • Primary electrophile-bearing phosphonates to install pore-reactive handles directly:
    (A) R–PO3H2 where R = (CH2)3–OTs (tosylate) or (CH2)3–OMs (mesylate) (high SN2 leaving groups).
    (B) R = (CH2)2–epoxide (glycidyl phosphonate motif) for nucleophilic ring opening.
    (C) R = (CH2)3–N3 (azidopropyl phosphonate) for CuAAC click with alkyne-functional diamines.
  • Mixed-graft dilution phosphonate (inert): methyl- or tert-butyl-phosphonic acid (no electrophile) co-dosed to tune spacing and preserve porosity.

1.3 Grafting conditions (SC–SC not assumed; crystallinity tracked):
  • Solvent screening chosen to minimize framework hydrolysis while enabling phosphonate coordination: dry MeCN or DMF with controlled water activity (e.g., 0–1 vol% H2O), 25–60 °C.
  • Base/activation: mild, non-nucleophilic base (e.g., DIPEA or 2,6-lutidine) to partially deprotonate phosphonic acid and promote Al–O–P formation while limiting Al–carboxylate cleavage.
  • Time-course series (e.g., 0.5, 2, 8, 24 h) to establish kinetics and identify the earliest timepoint meeting BET/crystallinity gates.

1.4 Mandatory quantitative validation of node graft speciation and defect formation:
  • Digestion quantitative NMR (primary quantitation): fully digest MOF in D2SO4/DMSO-d6 or HF/D2O protocol (selected to quantitatively release phosphonate and linker). Use an internal standard (e.g., trimethyl phosphate for 31P; dimethyl sulfone for 1H) to quantify incorporated phosphonate vs linker; report P:Al by combining with ICP-OES (Al, P) on the same digest.
  • ICP-OES/ICP-MS: independent P and Al concentrations to confirm P:Al and exclude surface-only uptake.
  • Solid-state NMR (speciation support, not sole quantitation):
    - 31P MAS to identify bound phosphonate environments (chemical shift distribution).
    - 27Al MAS to detect changes in Al coordination symmetry (octahedral vs distorted sites).
    - 27Al{31P} RESPDOR/REDOR or HMQC (where feasible) to establish direct Al–P proximities consistent with Al–O–P bonding.
  • Total scattering/PDF: compare Al–O/Al–Al correlation peaks pre/post graft; emergence of shortened/lengthened Al–O distances or damped correlations will be used as defect indicators. A ‘defect index’ will be defined as attenuation of medium-range order peaks normalized to low-r peaks.
  • IR/DRIFTS: monitor μ-OH stretch attenuation and P=O/P–O bands as supporting evidence of grafting and OH consumption.

Stage 2 — High-yield intrapore covalent diamine installation using pore-reactive electrophiles; kinetics and mass balance
2.1 Electrophile choice and coupling logic (primary + backups):
  • Primary route 1 (fast SN2): –(CH2)n–OTs/OMs handles + sterically shielded diamine nucleophile to form tethered secondary/tertiary amine linkage (via N-alkylation). Use excess diamine to drive conversion; quench and wash thoroughly.
  • Primary route 2 (epoxide ring opening): glycidyl-phosphonate handles + diamine to give β-aminoalcohol tether (typically high-yield under mild conditions, tolerant of confinement).
  • Primary route 3 (click): azidopropyl-phosphonate handles + alkyne-functionalized diamine (one terminus alkyne-tethered, one terminus free base) via CuAAC, forming a triazole linker (robust; high conversion).
  • Selection criterion: choose the route that achieves ≥70% handle conversion with ≥70% BET retention after tethering.

2.2 Reaction engineering inside pores (explicit kinetics quantification):
  • Perform reactions as time courses (e.g., 0.5, 2, 8, 24 h) at 25–60 °C in MeCN/DMF with controlled water (<0.5 wt%) to suppress hydrolysis of sulfonates.
  • Quantify conversion by digestion NMR: compare residual handle signal (e.g., tosyl aromatic 1H or epoxide 1H/13C features) to newly formed tether signals; confirm with 31P NMR to ensure phosphonate remains bound.
  • Leaving group mass balance:
    - For OTs/OMs: quantify released tosylate/mesylate in washings by ion chromatography (IC) or HPLC-UV (tosylate) to cross-check conversion.
    - For epoxide: quantify disappearance of epoxide functionality by digestion 1H/13C NMR.
  • Elemental analysis (N content) and TGA-MS as orthogonal checks of diamine loading.

2.3 Diamine library (steric gating + tuned basicity; one end tethered, one end free):
  • Bulky primary candidates: 2,2-dimethyl-1,3-propanediamine; N-isopropyl-1,3-propanediamine.
  • Cyclic/sterically constrained: mono-N-alkyl piperazine derivatives (one N tethered; one N free).
  • Include at least one ‘less bulky’ diamine as a control to test the steric-gating hypothesis.

2.4 Spacing control via mixed-grafting (pre-defined series):
  • Prepare three statistically diluted handle densities by co-grafting inert phosphonate + electrophile phosphonate to target incorporated P(handle):P(inert) ratios of ~0.3:0.7, 0.6:0.4, 0.9:0.1 at constant total P (validated by digestion 31P NMR + ICP).
  • This creates a tunable amine site density while holding total phosphonate-induced node modification comparable across samples, decoupling ‘node passivation’ from ‘amine density’.

Stage 3 — Directly measure amine spacing/mobility and connect to finite cooperativity/hysteresis
3.1 Distance constraints (mandatory mechanistic proof):
  • Prepare isotopically labeled subset: 15N-labeled diamine (free amine N) and/or 13C-labeled tether carbon.
  • Use 15N/13C ssNMR with REDOR (e.g., 13C–15N REDOR) to extract average intrapore proximities between tether and amine, and (if feasible) 15N–15N (via spin diffusion proxies) to infer amine–amine distance distributions across different dilution levels.
  • Alternative/backup: low-level nitroxide spin labeling on a fraction of diamines + DEER EPR to obtain distance distributions (nm scale) and assess mobility (temperature-dependent broadening).

3.2 Mobility/rotational barrier probes:
  • Variable-temperature ssNMR line-shape/relaxation (T1/T2) on 13C/15N labels to gauge segmental motion; correlate increased mobility with reduced hysteresis.

Stage 4 — CO2 capture performance under realistic TSA; energetics; binding motif identity
4.1 Adsorption protocol matched to flue gas:
  • Measure CO2 isobars at pCO2 = 0.04, 0.10, 0.15 bar in N2 from 25–120 °C (dry and controlled humidity, e.g., 20–40% RH equivalent using humidified gas blending).
  • Compute process working capacity Δn = n(pCO2, T_ads) − n(pCO2, T_des) with target window T_ads ~ 40–60 °C and T_des ≤ 110 °C.
  • Track hysteresis by adsorption/desorption isobars and quantify loop area as a metric.

4.2 Energetics (parameter extraction for modeling):
  • Adsorption microcalorimetry to obtain Qst versus loading; target moderate Qst at low loading (~45–70 kJ/mol) with diminishing Qst at higher loading if site heterogeneity/finite clustering is achieved.
  • DSC-TGA under CO2/N2 switching to estimate practical regeneration enthalpy and kinetics (mass change vs time at step changes in T and pCO2).

4.3 Binding motif confirmation:
  • Operando DRIFTS/ATR-IR under CO2/N2 with temperature ramps: assign carbamate/carbonyl bands; monitor reversibility and compare across dilution/steric series.
  • 13CO2 dosing + 13C ssNMR to identify carbamate vs carbamic acid signatures and quantify fraction of chemisorbed species.
  • Cycling: ≥500 TSA cycles under humid CO2/N2; track capacity, hysteresis, and amine loss (analyze off-gas by GC-MS; quantify N loss by post-cycling elemental analysis).

Stage 5 — Physically defined model fitting to connect sterics/spacing to isotherm shape and hysteresis
5.1 Model choice (explicit, parameterized by experiments):
  • Fit isobars/isotherms using a finite-cluster cooperative model (Ising/lattice-gas on a diluted lattice): sites correspond to tethered amines; occupation corresponds to CO2-bound ion-pair state.
  • Hamiltonian terms: (i) site energy ε (anchored to microcalorimetry low-loading Qst), (ii) nearest-neighbor coupling J representing propensity for cooperative propagation (expected to decrease with dilution/steric bulk), (iii) maximum cluster size L (or effective correlation length) constrained by measured distance distributions (REDOR/DEER) and dilution fraction.
  • Heterogeneity: include a distribution of ε (Gaussian) to represent local environments induced by mixed grafting; width constrained by 31P chemical shift dispersion and Qst variation.
  • Output parameters reported with uncertainty; demonstrate that reduced hysteresis correlates with reduced J and/or reduced L, not just reduced loading.

Deliverables and milestones (falsifiable):
M1 (Node speciation): Quantified P:Al plateau and identified dominant Al–P proximity signatures (27Al{31P} correlation/RESPDOR) plus PDF evidence of preserved node order; defect index below pre-set threshold (e.g., medium-range PDF peak attenuation <30% relative to parent).
M2 (Porosity): BET retention ≥70% after grafting; ≥60–70% after diamine tethering depending on loading.
M3 (Covalent conversion): ≥70% handle conversion by digestion NMR and leaving-group mass balance (IC/HPLC).
M4 (Mechanism): Distance/mobility data show increased mean amine–amine spacing with dilution and/or reduced close-contact population with steric bulk; this correlates with reduced hysteresis and broader, TSA-aligned uptake.
M5 (Performance): Demonstrate increased Δn(TSA) at pCO2 0.10–0.15 bar relative to pristine MOF-520 and a reduced hysteresis metric versus a high-cooperativity diamine reference material under comparable conditions.
Feasibility:
1) Enabling chemistry is de-risked by explicit node speciation accounting and quantitative incorporation metrics. Rather than assuming ‘uniform’ grafting, the plan establishes a measurable saturation behavior (P:Al plateau) and validates Al–O–P formation using digestion NMR + ICP (for absolute stoichiometry), 27Al/31P proximity NMR (for bonding evidence), and PDF (for node restructuring/defects). This directly addresses uncertainty in mono-/bi-/bridging modes and whether grafting causes linker displacement.
2) Intrapore covalent tethering feasibility is improved by replacing primary alkyl chlorides with pore-reactive handles (OTs/OMs, epoxide, azide-click), each with established high-yield reactions under mild conditions. Conversion is quantified by digestion NMR and leaving-group mass balance (IC/HPLC), avoiding surface-biased XPS. Time-course kinetics explicitly determine whether confinement limits reaction rates.
3) Structural/porosity preservation is enforced via pre-registered gates (BET retention and crystallinity/PDF metrics). Mixed-graft dilution is built in as a primary design variable (not a contingency) to prevent pore blockage and to decouple node passivation from amine density.
4) The cooperativity/hysteresis claim is mechanistically anchored to measurable descriptors: amine–amine distance distributions (REDOR/DEER), mobility (VT ssNMR/EPR), and energetics (microcalorimetry Qst). These experimental observables parameterize a finite-cluster cooperative lattice model (ε, J, L, heterogeneity width), enabling quantitative linkage between steric/spacing design and isotherm/hysteresis outcomes.
5) MOF-520 is selected as a rigid, Al-carboxylate scaffold with high baseline porosity and known high working capacity for gases, providing a stable platform where incremental functionalization can be benchmarked against the parent. Phosphonate anchoring leverages strong Al–O bonding, while covalent diamine attachment mitigates volatility/migration and suppresses metal-site poisoning, supporting multi-cycle TSA in humid streams.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in experimental resolution: it pre-defines falsifiable gates, quantitation (digestion NMR+ICP), and orthogonal structural validation (27Al/31P NMR proximities, PDF defect index) rather than relying on surface methods. The mechanistic throughline—Al-site passivation + sterically/spacing-truncated ammonium–carbamate cooperativity to broaden steps and reduce hysteresis—is logically coherent and linked to measurable parameters (Qst, distance distributions, model J/L). However, several key risks are under-specified or internally optimistic: (i) Al–carboxylate MOFs can be vulnerable to competitive phosphonate binding; the plan assumes no linker displacement but does not define hard chemical boundaries (water activity, pH/base equivalents) that guarantee carboxylate retention beyond empirical gates. (ii) Sulfonate handles inside pores are prone to hydrolysis/solvolysis and can generate strong acids (TsOH/MsOH) that may accelerate node degradation or amine protonation; mitigation strategies (acid scavenging, real-time pH/anion tracking, post-reaction neutralization protocols) are not fully developed. (iii) Achieving ≥70% intrapore substitution on OTs/OMs without diffusion limitation and without quaternization/over-alkylation of diamines (or crosslinking between handles) is nontrivial; the proposal does not specify protecting-group logic, stoichiometry controls, or analytical separation of mono- vs bis-alkylated products. (iv) The finite-cluster cooperativity model is plausible, but connecting hysteresis quantitatively to equilibrium lattice parameters can be ill-posed because hysteresis often reflects kinetics/metastability; the plan would benefit from explicit kinetic measurements (rate-dependent isobars, zero-length column/breakthrough, intracrystalline diffusion proxies) to avoid over-interpreting equilibrium fits. Overall, the work is well grounded in the MOF-520/TSA/diamine concept chain and proposes a genuinely mechanistic (not purely empirical) route, but needs tighter control/diagnostics around framework stability during phosphonation and around competing side reactions during electrophile coupling.

Hypothesis: A chemically asymmetric, redox-inert 2D coordination polymer can be deliberately transformed during a two-step sequential MAPbI3 formation into an interfacial organometallic dipole lattice that deterministically shifts the perovskite Fermi level and amplifies the built-in potential. Specifically, a 2D Pb(II)–dicarboxylate/halopyridyl mixed-linker MOF nanosheet is first grown on the electron-transport oxide and then partially converted during PbI2 → CH3NH3PbI3 conversion. The asymmetric cleavage and ligand exchange of this MOF leaves behind an oriented array of fixed molecular dipoles and coordinatively saturated Pb–I motifs at the buried interface, producing a permanent electrostatic field that raises V_bi without relying on electronic charge transfer or ion immobilization.
Plan:
Step 1: Rational design and synthesis of a chemically asymmetric 2D Pb-based MOF precursor.
1.1 Design a 2D layered coordination polymer with Pb(II) nodes and two chemically inequivalent linkers: (i) a strongly binding, non-leaving linker (e.g., fluorinated terephthalate) and (ii) a weakly bound, polar halopyridyl-carboxylate linker bearing a large intrinsic dipole moment.
1.2 Grow this Pb-MOF as an oriented ultrathin film (3–10 nm) directly on TiO2 or SnO2 via interfacial layer-by-layer coordination chemistry, enforcing out-of-plane polarity by anchoring the non-leaving linker to the oxide surface.
1.3 Confirm long-range in-plane order and polar stacking by GIWAXS, polarized IR, and cross-sectional STEM.

Step 2: Two-step sequential MAPbI3 formation with controlled MOF-to-perovskite chemical transformation (methodological adaptation).
2.1 PbI2 exposure step: Treat the Pb-MOF film with a stoichiometrically limited PbI2 solution in a weakly coordinating solvent (GBL/IPA) to initiate partial ligand exchange only at the topmost coordination layer, preserving the bottom anchoring layer.
2.2 Conversion step: Expose the hybrid film to CH3NH3I vapor. During conversion, the weakly bound polar linker is selectively displaced and expelled, while the non-leaving linker remains anchored, producing MAPbI3 nucleation atop a residual Pb–O–aryl sublayer.
2.3 This asymmetric conversion generates an oriented interfacial dipole sheet arising from (i) fixed aryl–F groups pointing toward the oxide and (ii) MA+ alignment during crystallization, locking in an electrostatic potential gradient at the junction.

Step 3: Validation of mechanism and correlation to Fermi level and built-in potential.
3.1 Chemical transformation tracking: Use in situ XPS and solid-state NMR to quantify selective linker loss and residual Pb–O coordination after perovskite formation.
3.2 Dipole-induced energy shift: Measure vacuum level shifts by UPS/Kelvin probe before and after conversion; decouple dipole effects from doping via temperature-dependent Hall and capacitance measurements.
3.3 Built-in potential quantification: Extract V_bi from capacitance–voltage profiling and corroborate with surface photovoltage spectroscopy.
3.4 Device correlation: Fabricate control devices (bare oxide, symmetric Pb-MOF, conventional two-step MAPbI3) and correlate V_bi, Voc, and hysteresis with measured dipole density.
3.5 Causality mapping: Systematically vary linker dipole moment and cleavage energetics to establish a quantitative structure–dipole–V_bi relationship.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Pb(II) coordination polymers are chemically compatible with halide perovskite chemistry, and selective ligand exchange during perovskite conversion is thermodynamically favored. Oriented molecular dipoles at buried interfaces are known to shift vacuum levels and built-in potentials independently of free charge transfer.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): This approach exploits MOF chemistry as a *sacrificial, symmetry-breaking precursor* rather than an interlayer or electronic material. The innovation lies in molecular-level control of coordination asymmetry and programmed partial decomposition—core competencies of coordination polymer chemistry.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike electronic MOF interlayers or ion-binding strategies, this method creates a permanent, chemically locked electrostatic field that is immune to redox drift and ion migration. The built-in potential enhancement arises from fixed dipoles generated by controlled MOF-to-perovskite transformation, offering superior Voc stability and eliminating Fermi-level pinning by mobile species.
Critique: This is a highly sophisticated proposal that demonstrates strong command of coordination polymer chemistry, perovskite processing, and interfacial energetics. The engineering plan is detailed and largely actionable, particularly in the rational MOF design, oriented growth strategy, and multi-modal characterization suite. Logical consistency is generally strong: the idea of programmed asymmetric ligand cleavage to lock in interfacial dipoles is internally coherent and plausibly decoupled from mobile ions or charge transfer. However, several assumptions weaken full rigor: (i) the degree of dipole orientation retention after partial MOF decomposition is not quantitatively modeled; (ii) the selective survival of the non-leaving linker under PbI2/MAI exposure is asserted but not thermodynamically or kinetically bounded; and (iii) the contribution of MA+ alignment versus residual aryl–F dipoles to the net vacuum-level shift is not clearly separable, risking over-attribution to the MOF-derived lattice. Evidence grounding is strong and remains within chemistry/perovskite physics, though some validation techniques (e.g., Hall measurements in MAPbI3) may be experimentally marginal in thin interfacial regimes. The rationale is creative and addresses a real Voc stability bottleneck, but it would benefit from clearer falsifiability criteria and quantitative dipole–V_bi predictions.

Hypothesis:
Low-pressure CO2 uptake in hydroxyl-rich, alkali-stabilized frameworks such as CD-MOF-2 reflects at least two separable rate processes that are conflated in macroscopic isotherms and bulk uptake transients: (i) an intrinsic chemical fixation step in which CO2 is converted to carbonate/bicarbonate at free –OH sites stabilized by Rb+ (Asset 1), and (ii) one or more transport resistances (gas→film interfacial barrier, near-surface defect layer, intrafilm diffusion/percolation) that impose an apparent activation energy on uptake (Asset 3).
