We hypothesize that time-resolved PM-IRRAS on architecturally controlled CD-MOF-2 thin films, co-registered with QCM kinetics and supplemented by independent transport metrics, will uniquely identify the intrinsic chemical rate constant and its activation energy by exploiting model discrimination across thickness (50/150/500 nm), step magnitude (multiple CO2 partial-pressure jumps), and humidity (RH matrix with H2O/D2O and 13CO2).

Mechanistic rationale for overcoming reviewer-identified ambiguities: (1) Identifiability: a coupled reaction–diffusion–barrier model is structurally non-identifiable if fit to a single observable at one thickness/step; however, global fitting across multiple thicknesses and step sizes forces different parameter scalings (diffusion time ∝ L^2, interfacial resistance largely L-independent, chemical pseudo-first-order rate largely L-independent when normalized to site density), enabling separation of kchem, Deff, and interfacial mass-transfer coefficient (kint) with quantified confidence intervals. (2) Chemical specificity: PM-IRRAS directly tracks carbonate/bicarbonate vibrational birth/decay; isotopic shifts with 13CO2 and H/D substitution (H2O/D2O) discriminate carbonate vs bicarbonate/carbonic-acid-like species and explicitly parameterize water-assisted proton-transfer/speciation, preventing misassignment of water-dependent kinetics to “transport”. (3) Architectural causality: COF-5 is used only as a transport modulator if—and only if—quantitative structural/chemical controls verify it does not alter CD-MOF-2 nucleation/texture/porosity nor contribute independent carbonate-forming sites (Asset 4 used for defect/crystallinity tuning; reviewer concern addressed by explicit null tests). (4) Decisive falsification: if an ultrathin CD-MOF-2 regime (≤20–30 nm) eliminates diffusion limitations yet retains a high apparent Ea for carbonate band growth, the rate-limiting step is intrinsic chemistry; conversely, if Ea collapses with ultrathin films or with inert overlayers of known permeability, barriers dominate. Together these elements convert the original concept (decouple chemistry vs transport using PM-IRRAS + QCM) into a quantitatively identifiable and falsifiable mechanistic program.
Plan:
A. Film architecture: quantitative control, verification, and null chemistry tests
A1. Substrates and platforms (paired for IRRAS and QCM):
- PM-IRRAS: Au(100 nm)/Ti(5 nm) on Si wafers; RMS roughness < 2 nm verified by AFM to minimize uncontrolled EM-field variations.
- QCM: Au-coated AT-cut quartz crystals (standard 5 MHz) with identical Au surface finish.
- Flow cell: identical gas manifold geometry for both platforms; dead volume minimized (<1 mL) to ensure step times <1 s.

A2. COF-5 interlayer as transport-only modulator (and how we ensure it stays transport-only):
- Grow continuous COF-5 films (target thickness 20–80 nm) via solvothermal interfacial growth; tune crystallinity/defect density using dioxane/mesitylene ratios guided by the spinodal-vs-nucleation insight (Asset 4). Define two endpoints:
  (i) “high-defect/high-permeability” COF-5 (conditions favoring spinodal decomposition),
  (ii) “low-defect/low-permeability” COF-5 (conditions favoring slower nucleation/growth).
- Quantify COF-5: GIWAXS texture/orientation; cross-sectional SEM/TEM for continuity and thickness; ellipsometric porosimetry (EP) to measure accessible porosity/pore condensation behavior; AFM for roughness.
- Mandatory null tests (to prove no carbonate chemistry from COF-5): expose COF-5/Au films (no CD-MOF-2) to identical CO2/RH/temperature matrix and record PM-IRRAS; require absence of carbonate/bicarbonate bands in the diagnostic windows (validated with 13CO2 and H2O/D2O). If any band appears, COF-5 is disqualified as a “transport-only” modulator and replaced by an inert barrier set (see Section D).

A3. CD-MOF-2 film growth/immobilization with thickness series and ultrathin regime:
- Prepare three CD-MOF-2 thicknesses on both Au and COF-5/Au: 50 ± 10 nm, 150 ± 20 nm, 500 ± 50 nm; plus an ultrathin 20 ± 5 nm regime (aim: diffusion-limits vanish).
- Deposition route: seed-assisted growth or layer-by-layer immobilization from γ-cyclodextrin/RbOH solutions; enforce identical precursor concentrations and temperature; adjust growth time to hit target thickness.
- Quantify CD-MOF-2 loading and uniformity:
  - Cross-sectional SEM/TEM (film continuity, grain boundaries, interfacial voids).
  - Ellipsometry (thickness), AFM (roughness), profilometry (step-edge thickness if patterned).
  - GIWAXS/GIXRD to assess phase purity and texture; compare orientation distributions on Au vs COF-5/Au to test whether the interlayer changes nucleation.
  - Optional: scrape films (where feasible) for Kr/CO2 sorption or microbalance sorption to estimate accessible porosity; otherwise rely on EP + QCM-based capacity as proxy.
- Connectivity/percolation checks: (i) EP hysteresis metrics, (ii) inert-probe transient uptake (see Section C2) to diagnose pore blocking.

A4. Controlled surface/defect states in CD-MOF-2 (analogous to Asset 3 logic):
- For each architecture/thickness: prepare (i) pristine activated, (ii) mildly hydrated (controlled RH exposure, e.g., 60% RH for fixed time), (iii) ethanol-healed (ethanol soak, then thermal activation). Confirm chemical integrity by IR (–OH region) and TGA.

B. PM-IRRAS methodology: selection rules, probing depth, and quantitative band-to-site strategy
B1. PM-IRRAS configuration and optical considerations:
- Incidence angle 80–85°; p-polarized component emphasized; polarization modulation to suppress gas-phase CO2.
- Evaluate effective probing depth and field enhancement by measuring a calibration monolayer (e.g., alkanethiol) and by simulating reflectivity (transfer-matrix) using measured film thickness and refractive index (from ellipsometry). This constrains how much of the porous film contributes to signal and prevents over-interpreting band areas as bulk site density.
- Roughness correction: incorporate AFM-derived RMS roughness into optical model; reject films exceeding a roughness threshold (e.g., RMS > 20 nm for 150 nm films) to maintain quantitative comparability.

B2. Spectral assignments and isotopic/speciation discrimination:
- Record CO2-dose spectra with 12CO2 and 13CO2 to confirm carbonate-related shifts.
- Implement RH matrix with H2O vs D2O vapor (same water activity) to distinguish bicarbonate/carbonic-acid-like species involving proton transfer (H/D isotopic effects) from carbonate.
- Define diagnostic windows and fit strategy: multi-peak constrained fitting with isotopic-shift priors; extract time-dependent areas for carbonate-like and bicarbonate-like components separately.

C. Independent transport metrics (required for identifiability)
C1. COF-5-only permeation/tracer transport:
- Measure gas permeance through COF-5 films alone (high-defect vs low-defect) using a simple two-chamber permeation cell or QCM “backside dosing” configuration where feasible; alternatively, use EP-derived diffusional relaxation times as a proxy. This yields an independent constraint on COF-5 transport resistance.

C2. Inert-probe transient uptake on CD-MOF-2 films (separates transport from chemistry):
- Use a non-reactive probe under dry conditions (e.g., CH4 or Ar) and, optionally, a weakly adsorbing VOC like cyclohexane if compatible, to obtain uptake kinetics governed primarily by diffusion/interfacial barriers (Asset 3 precedent for uptake kinetics sensitivity to defects).
- Collect QCM transients for the inert probe across thicknesses and defect states; fit to diffusion/barrier model to estimate Deff and kint independently (or with tight priors) before fitting reactive CO2 datasets.

D. Decisive falsification controls: barrier vs intrinsic chemistry
D1. Inert, known-permeability overlayer (nonreactive diffusion barrier):
- Deposit a thin, nonreactive overlayer on CD-MOF-2 films with quantified permeability:
  - Option 1: ALD Al2O3 (e.g., 2–10 nm) with engineered nanopores via mild post-treatment, or
  - Option 2: inert polymer (e.g., crosslinked PDMS or parylene variant) with literature permeability and independently measured thickness.
- Requirement: overlayer must show no carbonate/bicarbonate IR bands and must not chemically modify –OH (confirmed by IR –OH region and unchanged equilibrium CO2 capacity at long times).
- Compare how this overlayer changes QCM uptake vs PM-IRRAS carbonate formation kinetics. A strong slowdown in QCM with minimal change in carbonate-band growth kinetics supports barrier-limited macroscopic uptake.

D2. Ultrathin CD-MOF-2 regime (diffusion-limits should vanish):
- For 20 nm films, diffusion times shrink dramatically; if carbonate band-growth still exhibits strong temperature dependence (high Ea) and is insensitive to added barrier layers, the chemical step is rate-limiting.

E. Kinetic/transport model, identifiability strategy, and global fitting
E1. Model structure (reaction–diffusion–barrier with speciation and water activity):
- State variables: CO2 concentration within film c(x,t); site fractions for carbonate θCO3 and bicarbonate θHCO3.
- Transport: ∂c/∂t = Deff ∂^2c/∂x^2 with boundary condition at gas/film interface including interfacial mass transfer kint.
- Chemistry (minimal identifiable form):
  - CO2 + S + H2O ⇌ HCO3–-S (rate constants k1, k-1; depends on water activity a_w)
  - CO2 + 2S ⇌ CO3–-S + SH (or alternative carbonate formation pathway), parameterized as effective pseudo-first-order k2 under given site and water conditions.
- Water enters via a_w (from RH) and via explicit speciation constraints gleaned from H/D substitution.

E2. Identifiability/discrimination plan (mandatory):
- Dataset design:
  - Thicknesses: 20/50/150/500 nm.
  - CO2 steps: at least 4 step magnitudes per temperature (e.g., 0→50 mbar, 0→200 mbar, 0→500 mbar, 0→1 bar) to vary driving force and saturation.
  - Temperatures: 278/298/318 K.
  - RH: 0/10/30% with H2O, and a matched subset with D2O.
- Observables:
  - PM-IRRAS: time series of band areas for carbonate and bicarbonate components.
  - QCM: time series of total mass uptake.
  - Independent transport priors: Deff and/or kint from inert-probe transients; COF-5 transport resistance from permeation/EP.
- Fitting approach:
  - Global nonlinear least squares or Bayesian inference across all conditions with shared parameters (Deff(L,architecture,defect state), kint(architecture,overlayer), kchem(T,RH), equilibrium constants/speciation parameters).
  - Report parameter confidence intervals and correlation matrices; demonstrate reduced correlation when including (i) multiple thicknesses, (ii) multiple step sizes, (iii) inert-probe priors.
  - Model selection: compare nested models (pure diffusion-limited, pure reaction-limited, mixed barrier+diffusion+reaction) using AIC/BIC and posterior predictive checks.

F. Thermodynamic consistency and chemical invariance checks
F1. Equilibria:
- Measure equilibrium CO2 isotherms on powders (benchmark) and on films (QCM equilibrium masses) to confirm CD-MOF-2 low-pressure affinity/selectivity remains consistent with literature (Asset 1) and that adding COF-5 or inert overlayers does not create new uptake plateaus or hysteresis inconsistent with CD-MOF-2 chemistry.
- CH4 controls to confirm selectivity and to serve as an inert-transport probe.

F2. Reactive-site perturbation controls:
- Partial –OH blocking (silylation/acetylation): predict strong suppression of carbonate/bicarbonate IR growth while inert-probe transport parameters remain similar; validates chemical assignment.
- Cation exchange Rb+→K+: predict systematic IR band position changes and altered kchem due to different carbonate stabilization (aligns with Asset 1 mechanism).

Deliverables and decision points:
- Go/no-go for COF-5 as transport-only modulator after null carbonate test and architecture invariance assessment (GIWAXS + SEM/TEM + EP).
- Quantified separation of kchem, Deff, kint with confidence intervals; Arrhenius Ea for kchem(T,RH) and for transport parameters; RH-dependent speciation map (carbonate vs bicarbonate fractions) tied to kinetics.
- Falsification outcome matrix (ultrathin films + inert overlayer + COF-5 variants) explicitly adjudicating barrier-dominant vs chemistry-dominant regimes.
Feasibility:
1. Quantitative identifiability is explicitly engineered into the design. The core reviewer concern—correlated diffusion/interfacial/chemical parameters—is addressed by (i) thickness scaling (20–500 nm), (ii) multiple CO2 step magnitudes, (iii) global fitting across temperatures, and (iv) independent transport constraints from inert-probe transients and COF-5-only permeation/EP. This combination is a standard remedy for reaction–diffusion identifiability and yields defensible confidence intervals rather than single best-fit values.

2. Architecture/composition effects are controlled and measured, not assumed. GIWAXS texture, cross-sectional SEM/TEM, ellipsometry/AFM, and EP collectively verify whether COF-5 alters CD-MOF-2 nucleation/orientation, film connectivity, or accessible porosity. The mandatory “COF-5-only under CO2/RH” PM-IRRAS null test prevents misattribution of carbonate signals to the interlayer. If COF-5 fails this criterion, the project remains viable using the inert overlayer barrier set.

3. Water/speciation is built into both experiments and model. A designed RH matrix with H2O/D2O and 13CO2 separates carbonate vs bicarbonate and explicitly parameterizes water activity in the microkinetic model, preventing water-assisted proton-transfer kinetics from being mis-labeled as transport activation energy. RH-dependent Ea trends become a mechanistic output rather than a confound.

4. Decisive falsification controls ensure mechanistic conclusiveness. The ultrathin CD-MOF-2 regime and the inert, known-permeability overlayer provide orthogonal tests that can force a clear interpretation: diffusion/barrier-limited behavior must collapse with reduced thickness but increase with added barrier; chemistry-limited behavior persists in ultrathin films and tracks speciation and cation/–OH perturbations.

5. The approach is grounded in validated precedents. CD-MOF-2’s reversible carbonate formation provides strong, assignable vibrational markers (Asset 1). Surface/near-surface defects creating uptake barriers—and their mitigation by solvent treatment—are established in MOFs (Asset 3), motivating explicit defect-state libraries and transport diagnostics. COF-5 offers a tunable crystallinity/defect platform to modulate transport (Asset 4), but is now treated with strict chemical-null and invariance gates to satisfy reviewer requirements.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong on identifiability and falsification for separating intrinsic carbonate-formation kinetics from transport resistances; the multi-thickness scaling, multi-step forcing, and independent transport priors directly address the classic reaction–diffusion non-identifiability problem. Chemical specificity is also well-treated via isotopic (13CO2) and H/D substitution to deconvolute carbonate vs bicarbonate pathways under humidity. The principal technical risks are (i) PM-IRRAS quantitation in porous, scattering MOF films: baseline drift, orientation/selection-rule sensitivity, and uncertain effective sampling depth may prevent direct conversion of band area to site fractions without additional calibration; (ii) the ultrathin (20 nm) regime may not preserve CD-MOF-2 crystallinity/porosity or may be dominated by interfacial dead layers, complicating the intended ‘diffusion-free’ limit; (iii) the overlayer controls (ALD Al2O3/polymer) are not guaranteed to be chemically inert toward hydroxyl-rich CD-MOF-2 or to preserve equilibrium capacity—small chemical passivation could masquerade as transport effects; and (iv) the microkinetic scheme (carbonate vs bicarbonate) is still somewhat underconstrained thermodynamically (site balance, water uptake/partitioning, and reversibility) unless water loading/activity inside the film is independently measured, not only imposed by RH.

Hypothesis:
A MOF-templated core/shell/shell PEC photoelectrode can achieve fg mL−1-class detection with ≤5% inter-electrode RSD only if three coupled design rules are satisfied and experimentally verified: (R1) a photostable semiconductor interface is maintained under the assay operating window (bias/pH/illumination) by a pinhole-free conformal protection layer thin enough to preserve tunneling/charge transfer yet robust enough to suppress CdS photocorrosion and Cd2+ leaching; (R2) the outer MOF “biogating” layer has a statistically uniform thickness and retained microporosity such that its effective permeability (Deff) and charge selectivity (Kpartition) dominate interfacial charge-transfer kinetics (kct) and thus photocurrent; and (R3) nanobody immobilization is truly site-specific (single-point attachment) so that receptor density (Γ) and active fraction (factive) are fixed across batches and become a controllable contributor to RSD.
Mechanistically, the conductive MOF-derived carbon core provides a low-resistance electron extraction network and suppresses local potential fluctuations (reduced series resistance, stabilized quasi-Fermi level under illumination), while the TiO2/CdS (or TiO2/ZnCdS) type-II cascade imposes directional photocarrier separation (electrons toward ITO/TiO2; holes to the electrolyte), increasing the achievable signal-to-noise at low analyte levels. The ultrathin ZIF-90 outer shell functions as a tunable diffusion/charge gate whose permeability to redox mediators and hole scavengers is quantitatively modulated by (i) antigen binding (local charge and steric crowding) and (ii) enzyme-generated precipitate (CN/HRP insoluble product) that reduces accessible pore volume. This converts binding into a measurable Δkct and ΔDeff that can be extracted by EIS/IMPS and directly linked to photocurrent attenuation. The proposal explicitly de-risks CdS instability by confining PEC operation to a pre-defined potential/pH window and by using ALD TiO2/Al2O3 (1–5 nm) as a conformal corrosion barrier that still permits ZIF-90 nucleation via surface hydroxyl chemistry, thereby closing the reviewers’ stability and standardization gaps.
Plan:
Step 0 — Pre-registered targets, decision points, and acceptance criteria (Go/No-Go)
0.1 Shell thickness targets (measured by TEM, n≥50 particles; report mean±SD and coefficient of variation, CV):
• Carbon core: hollow/porous polyhedron preserving ZIF-8 outline; wall thickness 20–60 nm.
• ZnS passivation interlayer: 1.0–2.5 nm (SILAR cycles calibrated by TEM).
• CdS (or Zn0.2Cd0.8S) photoactive shell: 8–20 nm.
• ALD protection layer (TiO2 or Al2O3): 1.5, 3.0, and 5.0 nm screening set.
• ZIF-90 gating shell: 5–15 nm (target 10 nm), CV(thickness) ≤15%.
0.2 Photophysics/transport Go/No-Go thresholds:
• TRPL: ≥1.5× lifetime increase vs CdS-only control; 
• IMPS: ≥30% increase in charge transfer rate constant (ktr) or ≥30% decrease in recombination parameter vs control;
• Dark EIS (before biofunctionalization): Rct within batch CV ≤10%.
0.3 Reproducibility decomposition targets (n≥10 electrodes/batch, ≥3 batches):
• Mass-loading RSD ≤3% (gravimetric/QCM control).
• Receptor surface coverage Γ RSD ≤5% (QCM-D or fluorescence calibration).
• Photocurrent baseline drift ≤5% over 1 h chopped illumination at operating bias.

Step 1 — Materials synthesis with stability-by-design
1.1 ZIF-8 template synthesis (morphology standardization)
• Prepare ZIF-8 rhombic dodecahedra (300–600 nm) by controlling Zn2+:2-methylimidazole ratio and mixing rate; tighten dispersity by seed-mediated growth if needed.
• QC: SEM (size distribution, n≥200); PXRD (phase purity); zeta potential (for later deposition consistency).

1.2 Conductive MOF-derived carbon core (preserve polyhedral geometry)
• Infiltrate ZIF-8 with dopamine (or furfuryl alcohol) to create an in situ polymer network; polymerize under mild conditions.
• Carbonize under N2 (optimize 700/800/900 °C) to obtain N-doped porous hollow carbon polyhedra.
• QC: Raman (ID/IG); XPS (N species); conductivity (four-point probe on films); TEM for hollow structure.

1.3 Semiconductor shell with engineered interfaces (ZnS → CdS/ZnCdS)
• Deposit ZnS interlayer by SILAR (Zn2+/S2−) to passivate carbon surface states and provide a chemically uniform sulfide surface.
• Grow CdS or ZnCdS shell by controlled ion exchange/sulfurization to form a conformal photoactive layer.
• QC: HAADF-STEM/EDS line scans to confirm continuous shell and composition; UV–Vis (band edge); XPS (Cd/Zn/S chemical states).

1.4 Mandatory CdS photocorrosion protection: conformal ALD barrier
• Apply ALD TiO2 or Al2O3 on the sulfide shell (screen 1.5, 3.0, 5.0 nm). Rationale: sub-5 nm layers can suppress oxidative photocorrosion while still enabling electron tunneling and preserving PEC response.
• Select oxide based on (i) best stability (least photocurrent decay), (ii) lowest Cd leaching (ICP-MS), and (iii) retained photocurrent.
• Acceptance criteria: ≤10% photocurrent loss after 2 h chronoamperometry (see Step 3.1) and Cd in electrolyte below method LOQ (or below pre-set ppb threshold) for the selected condition.

Step 2 — ZIF-90 “growth mode” defined by chemistry + uniformity metrics (not assumed epitaxy)
2.1 Replace unsupported “epitaxy” with a demonstrated nucleation strategy
• Use oxide ALD surface (TiO2/Al2O3) as the chemically justified anchor: surface –OH groups coordinate Zn2+ and promote heterogeneous nucleation of ZIF-90.
• Optional priming: brief exposure to Zn2+ to create a Zn–OH enriched surface; avoid PEI/thiol primers unless needed, because they can introduce variability and light attenuation.

2.2 ZIF-90 ultrathin shell growth (5–15 nm) with statistical acceptance criteria
• Perform room-temperature ZIF-90 growth (Zn2+ + imidazole-2-carboxaldehyde) under dilute conditions and short times to confine thickness.
• QC/acceptance:
  - TEM thickness statistics over n≥50 particles: mean 10±1.5 nm, CV ≤15%.
  - PXRD/FTIR: ZIF-90 fingerprint retained.
  - Porosity/biogating proxy: uptake/permeability of a size/charge probe series through the shell (see Step 4): e.g., [Fe(CN)6]3−/4− (anionic, ~0.9 nm hydrated), Ru(NH3)6]3+ (cationic), and ferrocene methanol (neutral), before/after ZIF-90 growth; require that transport is not fully blocked pre-assay.

Step 3 — Define operating window and stability protocol (mandatory)
3.1 Operating window pre-registration
• Buffer: near-neutral PBS (pH 7.4) as default for protein stability; also test pH 6.5–8.0 to map corrosion risk.
• Illumination: calibrated LED (e.g., 420–450 nm for CdS response) at fixed intensity (e.g., 50–100 mW cm−2) with temperature control.
• Bias: screen 0 to +0.2 V vs Ag/AgCl (or minimal anodic bias needed) to minimize sulfide oxidation; select bias giving maximal SNR with acceptable stability.

3.2 Stability assays and leaching (pass/fail)
• Chronoamperometry under chopped light for 2 h in assay buffer with hole scavenger (ascorbate or TEOA) and without (worst case).
• Measure Cd2+ leaching by ICP-MS from the electrolyte after 2 h and 8 h operation.
• Compare four conditions: (i) no ALD, (ii) 1.5 nm ALD, (iii) 3.0 nm ALD, (iv) 5.0 nm ALD; select the thinnest layer that meets stability and leaching criteria while preserving ≥70% of initial photocurrent.

Step 4 — Quantify “biogating” as a falsifiable transport model
4.1 Define the gating model and measurable parameters
• Treat ZIF-90 shell as a porous diffusion/partition layer. Effective permeability P = (Deff · Kpartition)/L, where L is shell thickness.
• Hypothesis to test: binding/precipitation decreases Deff and/or Kpartition, increasing Rct and decreasing photocurrent. Quantify ΔDeff and ΔRct and correlate with ΔIph.

4.2 Measure size/charge selectivity and extract Deff
• Use EIS with redox probes of different size/charge (anionic/cationic/neutral as above) to extract Rct changes and infer charge exclusion.
• Use IMPS to derive kinetic parameters under illumination (charge transfer vs recombination contributions) before/after (i) antigen binding and (ii) CN precipitation.
• Acceptance: demonstrate ≥3× larger ΔRct (or Δktr) upon immunorecognition for ZIF-90-gated electrodes vs non-gated passivation controls (SiO2 or polymer of similar thickness).

4.3 Geometric/steric framing tied to pore size
• ZIF-90 micropores (~sub-nm aperture typical of ZIFs) should exclude large proteins (CEA, ~5–10 nm scale) from entering, enforcing surface-near binding and making gating sensitive to surface blockage/charge.
• Precipitate amplification: enzymatic CN precipitate forms at/near the MOF outer surface and pore mouths, reducing accessible pathways for mediator/scavenger diffusion; quantify by comparing permeability before/after HRP reaction.

Step 5 — Site-specific nanobody immobilization (mandatory) + direct measurement of orientation/coverage
5.1 Replace non-specific aldehyde coupling with orthogonal single-point attachment
• Engineer nanobody with a single N-terminal cysteine tag (or ybbR/AviTag for enzymatic labeling) to enforce one attachment site.
• Convert ZIF-90 aldehydes to a selective handle: (option A) reductive amination to introduce a linker terminating in maleimide (for Nb–Cys); (option B) introduce azide/alkyne handle via aldehyde chemistry, then click to Nb bearing the orthogonal partner.
• Avoid Protein G as the primary strategy; use it only as a comparator control to quantify heterogeneity effects.

5.2 Quantify receptor density Γ and active fraction factive
• QCM-D (or ellipsometry on planar analogs) to quantify mass uptake and viscoelastic layer properties during Nb immobilization.
• Fluorescent labeling of Nb (single dye per Nb via site-specific tag) to calibrate surface density (molecules cm−2) and spatial uniformity.
• Binding capacity per area: measure captured antigen vs Γ to estimate factive; acceptance: factive ≥0.5 and Γ RSD ≤5% across batches.

Step 6 — Electrode fabrication with reproducibility controls separated by source
6.1 Standardized deposition/mass loading
• Electrophoretic deposition (EPD) of particles onto TiO2/ITO with controlled time/field; verify areal mass by QCM (planar witness) or gravimetry.
• Acceptance: mass loading RSD ≤3% (n≥10).

6.2 Decouple RSD contributors (mandatory)
• For each batch: (i) measure mass loading, (ii) measure Γ and factive, (iii) measure baseline photocurrent and Rct. Use variance partitioning to attribute inter-electrode RSD to deposition vs biofunctionalization vs intrinsic photoelectrode drift.

Step 7 — Immunoassay formats aligned to analyte class and amplification asset
7.1 Protein biomarker (CEA) sandwich PEC
• Capture: site-specifically immobilized anti-CEA Nb on ZIF-90.
• Detection: HRP@MAF-7 (Asset 1 logic: high enzyme payload) conjugated to secondary Nb/antibody.
• Readout: HRP catalyzes CN precipitation; quantify photocurrent decrease and correlate with ΔRct/ΔDeff.

7.2 Small molecule toxin (AFB1) competitive PEC
• Immobilize hapten on ZIF-90-gated electrode; competition with HRP@MOF–Nb probe (Asset 1) to form precipitate when bound.

Step 8 — Controls that directly test each mechanistic claim
• Stability controls: CdS with/without ALD; compare photocurrent decay and ICP-MS leaching.
• Growth-mode controls: ZIF-90 on ALD-oxide vs on bare sulfide; compare thickness CV and permeability.
• Biogating controls: replace ZIF-90 with dense SiO2 (similar thickness) and with nonporous polymer; compare probe permeability and ΔRct upon binding.
• Orientation controls: site-specific Nb vs random aldehyde coupling vs Protein G; compare Γ, factive, and electrode-to-electrode RSD.
• Photoarchitecture controls: no carbon core; no type-II cascade (single semiconductor); quantify TRPL/IMPS differences and LOD.

Step 9 — Performance endpoints (pre-registered)
• LOD: 3σ/slope; require ≥10× improvement over non-gated PEC control.
• Inter-electrode RSD: ≤5% at low/mid/high concentrations (n≥10, ≥3 batches).
• Mechanistic confirmation: (i) improved lifetimes/IMPS metrics (type-II + carbon), (ii) quantified ΔDeff/ΔRct gating (ZIF-90 + precipitate), (iii) stability/leaching compliance (ALD + operating window).
Feasibility:
1) Stability/compatibility risk (CdS photocorrosion) is converted into a tested operating envelope plus a defined barrier design. Instead of relying on TiO2 as a general mitigation, the plan mandates an ALD TiO2/Al2O3 conformal layer (1.5–5.0 nm screen), hour-scale chronoamperometry under calibrated illumination, explicit bias/pH screening, and Cd2+ leaching quantification by ICP-MS. This makes the “photostable under assay conditions” claim falsifiable.

2) The ZIF-90 shell is no longer assumed “epitaxial”; it is specified as a chemically justified heterogeneous nucleation on hydroxylated ALD oxide. Uniformity is enforced by acceptance criteria (TEM statistics over n≥50, thickness CV ≤15%) and by functional porosity tests using a size/charge redox probe series. This directly addresses variability risk and links shell quality to gating performance.

3) The central transduction mechanism (biogating → Δkct) is elevated from qualitative plausibility to a quantitative transport/kinetics model. By extracting effective permeability (via Deff/Kpartition) and correlating it with photocurrent modulation using EIS and IMPS before/after binding and precipitation, the proposal establishes a measurable causal chain from MOF gate physics to analytical sensitivity.

4) Orientation and receptor standardization are made truly site-specific by engineering a single-point attachment on the nanobody (e.g., N-terminal cysteine or orthogonal enzymatic tag) and coupling through orthogonal chemistry rather than relying on statistically random aldehyde reactivity or Protein G. Surface coverage and active fraction are directly measured (QCM-D/ellipsometry + site-specific fluorescence calibration + binding-capacity assay), enabling reproducibility claims to be tied to measured Γ and factive rather than asserted.

5) Reproducibility is decomposed into independent contributors (mass loading, biofunctionalization, photoelectrode drift) with pre-registered RSD targets and decision points. This, combined with MOF-derived morphology control (ZIF-8 templating) and standardized EPD mass loading, provides a concrete pathway to achieve ≤5% inter-electrode RSD across batches while maintaining the high-gain amplification logic demonstrated in MOF-encapsulated enzyme precipitation systems (Asset 1) and MOF-derived multi-shell photoactive architectures (Asset 2).
Critique: The proposal is unusually well-engineered for a PEC/MOF biosensor submission: it replaces several common hand-waves ("epitaxy", "stability", "uniformity") with measurable acceptance criteria and mechanistic readouts (TEM thickness statistics, ICP-MS leaching, chronoamperometry drift, EIS/IMPS gating signatures). The logic of the three design rules is coherent and, importantly, falsifiable. However, several high-risk couplings remain under-specified in a way that can undermine the claimed fg mL−1 performance and ≤5% inter-electrode RSD: (1) The ALD barrier is treated as simultaneously (a) pinhole-free corrosion protection and (b) sufficiently thin for tunneling/charge transfer, but there is no explicit plan to quantify pinhole density/continuity (beyond functional decay) or to deconvolute added series resistance vs true interfacial kinetics; 1.5–5 nm is plausible yet not guaranteed across high-surface-area polyhedra without conformality verification. (2) The ZIF-90 “biogating” model is framed as Deff·Kpartition/L control of kct, but the proposal lacks a clear parameter-identifiability strategy: EIS/IMPS changes can be fit by multiple equivalent circuits/assumptions, and without independent permeability measurements (or at least rigorous model selection), ΔRct may not uniquely map to ΔDeff or ΔKpartition. (3) The claim that ZIF-90 microporosity remains after aqueous biofunctionalization and HRP/CN precipitation is asserted with proxy probes, but the plan does not specify how to separate true micropore accessibility from crack/defect-mediated transport (a critical determinant of both sensitivity and RSD). (4) Reproducibility targets are strong, but the workflow still contains multiple batch-sensitive steps (SILAR ZnS, CdS/ZnCdS growth, ALD, MOF shell growth, EPD) whose cumulative variance may exceed the allocated RSD budget; the variance-partitioning is good, yet it is not tied to a quantitative error budget that shows feasibility of ≤5% total RSD under realistic compounding. Overall, the proposal is mechanically and logically strong but needs tighter metrology and identifiability to ensure the mechanistic claims are not underdetermined by the chosen electrochemical observables.

Hypothesis: A two-stage chemical-editing strategy—(i) statistically controlled NaOH defect/mesopore formation in an ethanol-rich medium followed by (ii) fluoride capping that is proven to be node-bound (terminal Zr–F/bridging Zr–F–Zr) rather than residual NaF—will yield a hierarchically porous Fe-porphyrin Zr-MOF whose peroxidase-like activity and alkaline durability improve simultaneously. Mechanistically, NaOH introduces a measurable density of missing-linker/terminal –OH(H2O) sites that increases transport and exposes a higher fraction of intact Fe–N4 porphyrins to substrates (effective site accessibility, not merely higher BET). Subsequent fluoride exchange replaces the most hydrolysis-prone terminal Zr–OH(H2O) with stronger Zr–F bonds, decreasing OH−-driven node dissolution and suppressing defect-propagation during pH 10–13 operation. Any apparent ‘redox tuning’ of the Fe(III)/Fe(II) couple will be treated as a testable (not assumed) secondary effect and will only be claimed if confirmed by node-independent, solution/operando spectroscopies and if rate enhancements persist after normalization to independently quantified active-site density. The core advance is a quantitatively validated decoupling: NaOH sets pore hierarchy and accessible-site fraction under explicit etch-stop criteria, while verified node fluorination locks in alkaline robustness without conflating physisorbed salt or amorphous fluoride phases with true Zr–F gating.
Plan:
Step 0 — Platform selection, baseline standards, and acceptance thresholds
0.1 Primary scaffold: PCN-222(Fe) (Zr6-oxo nodes + Fe-porphyrin linkers). Contingency: MOF-545(Fe) or PCN-224(Fe) if PCN-222(Fe) shows unacceptable Fe demetalation under the mildest etch conditions.
0.2 Baseline synthesis: modulator route (benzoic acid or acetic acid) targeting reproducible crystallinity and particle size; record baseline PXRD, BET, UV–vis (Soret/Q bands), ICP (Fe, Zr), and porphyrin content via digestion.
0.3 Predefine success criteria (used later in DOE):
- Structural retention: PXRD similarity index ≥ 0.85 vs pristine (Rietveld/Le Bail or correlation metric) after editing and after pH 13 soak.
- Leaching limits: Zr loss ≤ 5% and Fe loss ≤ 3% (relative to initial loading) after 24 h soak at pH 13.
- Fluoride incorporation: F:Zr within a targeted window consistent with partial terminal-site exchange (initial target 0.3–2.0; final window refined by EXAFS/XPS speciation).
- Catalysis: ≥ 2× improvement in Vmax or TOF_site at pH 10–11 vs pristine while maintaining ≥ 70% activity at pH 13 (relative to its own pH 7 rate).

Step 1 — Activation and salt-removal protocols (controls that prevent misassignment)
1.1 Activation: solvent exchange to ethanol (3× over 24 h), then mild vacuum/heat (e.g., 80–120 °C; temperature chosen to avoid porphyrin degradation) to standardize starting porosity.
1.2 Salt-removal SOP (applied to all NaF-treated samples and “NaF-adsorption controls”): repeated ethanol/water washes (e.g., 10 cycles), conductivity monitoring of supernatant to baseline, and final dialysis (if particle size permits) or Soxhlet extraction in ethanol for ≥ 12 h. Collect all washings for ion chromatography (F−) to mass-balance residual soluble fluoride.

Step 2 — Factorial DOE for NaOH etch (hierarchical porosity) with etch-stop criteria
2.1 DOE variables (initial 2-level factorial + center points; expand to response-surface if needed):
- [NaOH] = 5, 20, 50 mM
- Water fraction in EtOH/H2O = 5%, 20%, 40% v/v
- Etch time = 5 min, 30 min, 2 h
- Temperature = 25 °C (fixed initially; add 40 °C only if kinetics too slow)
(27 runs with center-point replication; reduce using fractional factorial if material throughput is limited.)
2.2 Etch procedure: disperse activated MOF at fixed solid loading (e.g., 1–2 mg/mL) in EtOH/H2O; add NaOH as pre-diluted aliquots with timed sampling. Quench at each time point by rapid separation and immediate ethanol washing.
2.3 Etch-stop criteria (measured as time-course; stop/flag conditions are quantitative):
- Leaching kinetics: ICP-OES/ICP-MS on supernatants for Zr and Fe at each time point; terminate etch condition if incremental Zr loss exceeds 1% per 10 min (or if Fe appears above background).
- Porphyrin integrity: UV–vis diffuse reflectance (or solution after digestion) tracking Soret band position/intensity; if Soret intensity drops > 10% (normalized to Zr), flag as porphyrin loss/demetalation.
- Missing-linker density: digest aliquots (acid digestion that fully dissolves framework) and quantify linker by 1H NMR vs Zr by ICP to estimate missing-linker fraction (linker:Zr deviation from pristine).
- Crystallinity: quick PXRD screen; discard conditions showing major peak loss/broadening beyond threshold.
2.4 Output of Step 2: a ranked subset (e.g., 3–5) of “safe etched states” spanning low/medium/high mesoporosity while meeting leaching + porphyrin integrity thresholds.

Step 3 — Fluoride capping DOE with node-resolved validation (distinguish Zr–F from NaF adsorption/amorphous phases)
3.1 Fluorination variables (applied to the selected etched states and pristine):
- [NaF] = 1, 10, 50, 100 mM
- Solvent = EtOH/H2O with minimal water required for F− mobility (e.g., 95/5 and 80/20)
- Time = 0.5 h, 4 h, 24 h
Maintain constant ionic strength controls where possible (e.g., NaCl at matched [Na+]) to identify non-specific electrolyte effects.
3.2 Speciation and quantification of fluoride incorporation (mandatory causal-link test #1):
- Bulk F:Zr ratio: digest MOF; quantify F− by ion chromatography and Zr by ICP-OES → report molar F:Zr with error bars.
- Quantitative XPS with depth profiling (gentle Ar cluster sputter if available): deconvolute F 1s and Zr 3d regions; compare surface vs subsurface F distribution.
- Zr K-edge EXAFS (preferred): fit Zr–F scattering path vs Zr–O; distinguish terminal Zr–F from bulk amorphous ZrF_x by coordination number/bond length and disorder parameters. If EXAFS access is limited, use combined quantitative XPS + 19F solid-state NMR (with reference compounds) and demonstrate persistence of F signal after aggressive salt-removal SOP.
- Salt adsorption controls: (i) pristine MOF exposed to NaF without etch; (ii) etched MOF exposed to NaCl; (iii) physical mixing of MOF with NaF followed by identical washing; all must show substantially lower retained F and/or different XPS/NMR signatures than true fluorinated samples.
3.3 Rule-out amorphous surface Zr–F phases: TEM/EDS mapping for F distribution; compare to PXRD amorphization signatures; ensure no new broad features consistent with amorphous ZrF_x dominate. If detected, adjust fluorination solvent (lower water), reduce NaF concentration/time, or introduce competitive ligands (acetate) to avoid precipitation.

Step 4 — Active-site density and integrity: move beyond BET as proxy (mandatory causal-link test #2 and #4)
4.1 Quantify intact Fe-porphyrin site density (Fe–N4 integrity):
- Fe and Zr by ICP (bulk).
- Porphyrin linker quantification by digestion + 1H NMR (linker per Zr) and compare to Fe content (Fe per linker). Deviations indicate demetalation or linker loss.
- Fe environment: Mössbauer (if available) and/or Fe K-edge XAS to verify Fe remains porphyrinic (vs μ-oxo Fe clusters or leached Fe redeposition). At minimum, compare UV–vis Q-band pattern + EPR signatures across treatments.
4.2 Define “accessible active-site fraction” independent of BET:
- Probe-molecule binding calibrated to porphyrin content where feasible: NO or CO binding (IR/UV–vis difference spectroscopy) to porphyrin Fe sites under controlled conditions, giving a measurable fraction of Fe capable of axial ligation.
- If gas binding is not feasible, use a competitive axial ligand titration (e.g., imidazole/pyrazine) with spectroscopic readout (Soret shift) to quantify accessible Fe sites.
4.3 Report catalytic metrics normalized three ways: per gram, per total Fe, and per accessible Fe site (TOF_site). Claims about “BET → accessibility → activity” are only accepted if TOF_site increases or remains constant while accessible-site fraction increases; a BET-only increase without preserved Fe–N4 integrity will be interpreted as non-productive porosity.

Step 5 — Peroxidase-like activity and ROS mechanism with artifact-free redox attribution (mandatory causal-link test #3)
5.1 Standard kinetics: TMB/ABTS + H2O2 over pH 7–13; extract Km, Vmax; measure initial rates in regimes avoiding mass-transfer limitation.
5.2 ROS assignment: EPR spin trapping (•OH/•OOH) + scavengers (isopropanol, SOD mimics, etc.) to differentiate radical vs heterolytic pathways.
5.3 Decouple electrochemical film artifacts:
- Run CV/DPV on identical films with matched mass loading and thickness; include EIS to quantify film resistance and separate conductivity changes from redox shifts.
- Node-independent Fe redox probing: (i) mediated redox titration in suspension with a series of soluble mediators spanning potentials; (ii) operando Fe K-edge XANES under H2O2 to observe Fe valence changes directly during catalysis. Only if these methods show systematic shifts correlating with verified Zr–F speciation will “F− tunes Fe redox microenvironment” be claimed.
- Control for electrolyte/adsorption effects: repeat kinetics with constant ionic strength and with fluoride-free sodium salts; assess H2O2 adsorption isotherms/uptake if needed.

Step 6 — Alkaline durability demonstration tied to node fluorination
6.1 Soak tests: pH 10, 12, 13 (NaOH) for 6 h, 24 h, 7 days in water and in EtOH/H2O matrices; quantify:
- PXRD retention, BET retention, pore size distribution evolution.
- Zr/Fe leaching (ICP) time-course.
- Persistence of node-bound F (digest + IC; XPS after soak).
6.2 Demonstrate causality: correlate stability improvements with node-bound F fraction (F:Zr and EXAFS/XPS speciation), not merely with total F added.

Step 7 — Application-relevant cascade demonstration (ethanol context preserved)
7.1 Cascade: alcohol oxidase (or alternative oxidase) generates H2O2 from ethanol; MOF nanozyme performs chromogenic readout at alkaline pH. Compare pristine vs etched vs etched+fluorinated under identical ethanol content and pH.
7.2 Show robustness: sustained response after repeated cycles and after alkaline pre-aging; quantify signal drift vs leaching and vs retained accessible-site fraction.

Deliverables and decision gates
- Gate A (after Step 2): identify etched conditions meeting stop criteria.
- Gate B (after Step 3): confirm node-bound fluoride via F:Zr + speciation (EXAFS or quantitative depth-profile XPS + NMR) with salt-removal mass balance.
- Gate C (after Step 4–6): accept or reject each causal link using predefined acceptance rules (below).

Acceptance rules (explicit falsification)
- If retained F is removed by salt-removal SOP and/or lacks node-bound signatures (EXAFS/XPS/NMR), “fluoride gating” is rejected; any stability/activity changes will be attributed to ionic strength or surface salt effects.
- If etching increases BET but decreases intact porphyrin density or accessible-site fraction, “BET→accessibility” is rejected for that condition; etch severity is reduced.
- If Fe redox shifts appear only in films (not in mediated titration/operando XANES) and track EIS resistance, “F− tunes Fe redox” is rejected as an artifact; mechanistic emphasis returns to transport + node stabilization.
Feasibility: The proposal is feasible because each contested causal link is converted into a quantitative, discriminating measurement with built-in controls. (1) Node fluorination is not inferred from a single spectroscopy: bulk F:Zr (digestion + ion chromatography/ICP) plus node-level speciation (Zr K-edge EXAFS or, at minimum, quantitative depth-profile XPS reinforced by 19F ssNMR) and rigorous salt-removal mass balance directly address the reviewer’s concern about residual NaF adsorption or amorphous fluoride phases. (2) NaOH etching risk is managed by an explicit factorial DOE with real-time stop criteria based on Zr/Fe leaching kinetics (ICP), porphyrin integrity (Soret band metrics), crystallinity (PXRD), and missing-linker quantification (digestion 1H NMR vs Zr). This converts ‘minutes–hours’ into statistically defensible windows tied to measurable damage thresholds. (3) The activity claim is protected against BET overinterpretation by independently quantifying intact porphyrin/Fe–N4 density and an accessible-site fraction (axial ligand/probe binding), then reporting TOF normalized per accessible Fe site. (4) Redox and ‘microenvironment’ effects are treated as conditional outcomes: electrochemical observations are cross-validated by solution-phase mediated redox titration and/or operando Fe XANES under H2O2 to eliminate film/conductivity artifacts. Together, these additions maintain the original concept chain (NaOH→hierarchical pores; NaF→base tolerance; porosity/accessibility→activity) while making each arrow testable and falsifiable with node- and site-resolved quantification.
Critique: Methodological execution is unusually well-resolved for a MOF nanozyme proposal: the NaOH etch is bounded by quantitative stop criteria (ICP leaching kinetics, Soret-band integrity, PXRD thresholds, missing-linker quantification), and the fluorination step is appropriately treated as a speciation problem (node-bound Zr–F vs physisorbed NaF or amorphous ZrF_x) with orthogonal measurements and stringent adsorption controls. Logical structure is strong: it explicitly separates transport/accessibility effects from intrinsic-site effects and requires TOF normalization to independently measured accessible Fe–N4 sites before claiming catalytic enhancement. Key score deductions arise from (i) residual ambiguity in the chemically realistic upper bound of F loading and binding motifs in Zr6 nodes under the proposed solvents/pH (the F:Zr target window 0.3–2.0 is plausible but not yet tied to a specific node stoichiometry model and charge-balance/defect chemistry for PCN-222), (ii) reliance on high-end instrumentation (Zr EXAFS, operando Fe XANES, Mössbauer) for decisive claims without a fully specified minimal-path alternative set that still conclusively distinguishes Zr–F from surface precipitates, and (iii) the NaOH etch regime may risk porphyrin demetalation/Fe migration in alkaline, partially aqueous alcohol mixtures; while you included safeguards, the proposal does not yet specify chelation/axial-ligation strategies (or metallation reconstitution checks) to prevent/diagnose subtle Fe site reconfiguration that could masquerade as activity gains.

Hypothesis: A permanently cationic Zn–azolate MOF can be engineered into an “ionic-lattice electret” only if its counterion is not freely mobile (DC conductor) nor rigidly pinned (mechanically inert), but instead resides in a metastable, bistable anion-binding pocket that allows Å-scale, reversible intra-pore relocation under small elastic strain (0.5–2%) while suppressing long-range diffusion. Under uniaxial compression, shear-enabled linker rotations and node distortions bias the occupancy of two nearby anion microstates (A/B) separated by ~1–3 Å, producing a measurable, fast (elastic-timescale) change in internal electrostatic potential ΔV at adsorption sites. This ΔV selectively stabilizes quadrupolar/polarizable adsorbates (CO2) over weakly interacting gases (N2/CH4) by increasing the electrostatic component of adsorption free energy, yielding a falsifiable, a priori predicted selectivity modulation (target ≥10% in IAST/breakthrough) that is temporally correlated with the fast electromechanical signal and decoupled from slow conductive artifacts. The design overcomes the reviewers’ concerns by (i) replacing ‘immobilized yet redistributable nitrate’ with a mechanically addressable but diffusion-suppressed NO3− in a defined pocket; (ii) establishing quantitative electromechanical and adsorption coupling predictions before synthesis (ΔxNO3− → ΔV → ΔΔGads → ΔSselectivity); (iii) using blocking-electrode, humidity-controlled, guard-electrode protocols to isolate true fast polarization from Maxwell–Wagner/electrode polarization and triboelectric effects; and (iv) employing a realistic synthetic fallback based on post-synthetic quaternization of a known Zn–azolate framework (phase-identified, porosity-gated) to ensure access to the targeted ionic topology.
Plan:
Step 0 — Quantitative, falsifiable pre-synthesis predictions (mandatory gates)
0.1 Define the mechanically accessible strain window and modulus targets
- Target elastic uniaxial strain: ε = 0.5%, 1.0%, 2.0% on pellet/monolith without fracture.
- Target framework compliance: effective Young’s modulus 0.5–5 GPa (tunable via mixed-linker ‘slip-plane’ fraction) so that ε is achievable under <50–200 MPa applied stress.

0.2 Build a coupled multiscale model: (mechanics → ion shift → electrostatics → adsorption)
- Periodic DFT (or DFTB if needed for screening) on a representative unit cell fragment containing: Zn–N node, tethered imidazolium, and anion-binding pocket.
- Compute two local minima for NO3− in pocket states A and B (Δx = 1–3 Å), with an energy offset ΔE0 ≤ 2–5 kJ·mol−1 to permit stress biasing but prevent thermal wandering.
- Apply cell deformation (ε = 0.5–2%) and compute the stress-dependent free-energy bias ΔE(ε) between A/B and the expected occupancy shift: pB/pA = exp[−ΔE(ε)/kT].
- Electrostatic mapping: calculate ΔV(ε) at identified adsorption hotspots (e.g., near pore-facing imidazolium/anion pair) using DFT-derived charge density or fitted point charges; output ΔV in mV–V.
- Adsorption energetics: compute ΔΔGads(ε) = ΔGads,CO2(ε) − ΔGads,CO2(0) and analogues for N2/CH4 via (i) DFT binding energies with quadrupole interaction decomposition and/or (ii) GCMC using stress-dependent electrostatic potential grids.
- Translate into selectivity prediction under IAST: predict ΔS = S(ε)/S(0) for CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4 at 298 K, 0.1–1 bar.

0.3 Set minimum detectable electromechanical benchmark from the model
- Convert predicted net polarization change to an expected charge density on pellet faces: ΔP (C·m−2) from dipole moment change per unit volume (DFT) and A/B occupancy shift.
- Define detection threshold: ΔQmin = 10 pC per cycle (instrument-limited, to be verified) implying ΔPmin ≈ ΔQmin/A where A is electrode area.
- Go/no-go Gate G0: proceed to synthesis only if model predicts (i) ΔΔGads,CO2 − ΔΔGads,N2/CH4 ≥ 0.25–0.5 kJ·mol−1 at ε ≤ 2% (sufficient for ~10% selectivity shift at 298 K), and (ii) ΔQcycle above ΔQmin with fast component τfast < 1 s.

Step 1 — Ion-pair motif redesign: diffusion-suppressed, mechanically addressable nitrate pocket
1.1 Replace ‘mobile nitrate in pores’ with a defined, bistable anion pocket
- Incorporate tethered H-bond donors adjacent to the pore-facing imidazolium: urea/thiourea or bis-amide motif (two N–H donors) positioned to bind NO3− in two geometrically nearby orientations.
- Architectural target: a “cationic cleft” comprising (imidazolium C2–H + urea/amide N–H donors) creating two metastable binding poses A/B separated by 1–3 Å along a shear direction.
- Design rule: NO3− binding enthalpy strong enough to suppress translational diffusion (activation barrier for hopping between pockets > 20–30 kJ·mol−1), but A/B interconversion barrier moderate (5–15 kJ·mol−1) to allow elastic-strain biasing without requiring humidity.

1.2 Linker specification (two-function linker: framework-forming + pocket-forming)
- Primary azolate for Zn–N framework: imidazolate/benzimidazolate core for ZIF-like stability.
- Pendant group: (i) quaternizable imidazole to form tethered imidazolium; (ii) appended urea/amide arm within 3–6 Å of the imidazolium to make the pocket.
- Mixed-linker compliance: 10–30% longer, rotatable azolate linker (e.g., benzimidazolate with flexible spacer) to create shearable sublattices (‘slip-plane’ concept) while maintaining connectivity.

Step 2 — Realistic synthetic route with explicit fallback and phase/porosity gates
2.1 Primary route (preferred): post-synthetic quaternization of a known Zn–azolate framework
- Rationale: avoids crystallization disruption from pre-installed permanent cations.
- Choose a Zn–azolate framework with pendant imidazole (neutral) groups pointing into pores (literature-known ‘functionalized ZIF’ families or mixed-linker ZIF analogues).
- Synthesize solvothermally from Zn(NO3)2·4H2O and the azolate linkers under standard ZIF conditions with careful base control.
- Post-synthetic quaternization: alkylate pendant imidazoles (e.g., MeI/MeOTf alternatives) to create tethered imidazolium sites without collapsing topology; immediately exchange to NO3− via controlled nitrate treatment (mild, aqueous-alcoholic) to set the counterion.

2.2 Secondary route (direct ionic synthesis): cationic-linker solvothermal assembly
- Conduct solvothermal assembly in DMF/MeOH with controlled water activity; minimize strong bases that promote anion exchange.
- Use Zn(NO3)2·4H2O as Zn source; maintain nitrate excess to suppress replacement by coordinating solvent anions.

2.3 Phase identification and porosity go/no-go gates
- Gate G1 (phase): PXRD match to targeted topology or reproducible new phase; reject dense nonporous phases.
- Gate G2 (porosity): N2(77 K) and CO2(195 K) uptake confirming permanent porosity; reject samples with collapsed uptake.
- Gate G3 (counterion placement): NO3− confirmed by IR (ν3), ion chromatography of digests, and elemental analysis; check for unintended anions.

Step 3 — Prove ‘metastable but not diffusive’: impedance + solid-state NMR metrics
3.1 Variable-T impedance spectroscopy with blocking electrodes
- Use sputtered Au (or Pt) blocking electrodes; implement guard-ring electrode geometry to suppress leakage currents.
- Measure ε′(ω), ε″(ω), and σ(ω) from 10−2 to 10^6 Hz at controlled RH (0%, 20%, 50%) and 298–343 K.
- Extract DC conductivity σDC and relaxation times. Success criteria: σDC low enough that electrode polarization dominates only at very low frequencies; fast polarization feature persists under dry conditions.

3.2 Solid-state NMR to quantify anion motion (diffusion vs local hopping)
- 15N (nitrate) and/or 2H (if deuterated urea/amide) relaxation to estimate motion timescales.
- If feasible, pulsed-field gradient NMR on digested/liquid analogs is not applicable; instead use T1/T2 and line-shape analysis for site exchange.
- Success criteria: evidence for local two-site exchange (A↔B) without signatures of long-range diffusion.

Step 4 — Tightened electromechanical protocol to isolate true fast polarization from artifacts
4.1 Pellet/monolith fabrication and electrode architecture
- Prepare dense porous monoliths/pellets with reproducible thickness; apply sputtered Au electrodes on both faces; use guard electrode and insulating collar to control fringe fields.
- Environmental control: sealed chamber with controlled RH (0–50%) and temperature (298 K).

4.2 Time-domain and frequency-domain separation of fast elastic vs slow conductive effects
- Quasi-static compression with defined stress ramp rates; record charge under open-circuit and short-circuit conditions.
- Apply dynamic mechanical excitation (0.1–100 Hz) and measure current phase relative to strain.
- Define ‘fast electret-like’ component as in-phase (or fixed phase) with strain at frequencies where ionic conduction cannot follow; define slow drift as conductive.

4.3 Artifact controls (mandatory)
- Inert pellet control: same pelletizing and electrodes but inert porous solid of similar modulus (e.g., neutral ZIF analogue) to quantify triboelectric/contact charging baseline.
- Electrode material reversal: Au vs carbon vs Pt to test electrode-dependent electrochemistry.
- Kelvin probe or surface potential mapping pre/post cycling to detect contact charging.
- Load under vacuum/inert gas to define baseline; then repeat under CO2/N2/CH4 to test adsorbate-coupled signal.

Step 5 — Stress-biased adsorption with explicit decoupling from pore-volume effects
5.1 Measure stress-dependent single-component adsorption isotherms
- CO2, N2, CH4 at 298 K under controlled applied uniaxial stress corresponding to ε = 0, 0.5, 1, 2% (calibrated mechanically).
- Correct for simple void-volume reduction by independent measurement of pellet thickness/porosity change under load and by using the rigid-lattice control.
- Extract Qst(ε) via multi-temperature isotherms or microcalorimetry if available.

5.2 Mixed-gas breakthrough with a piston-loaded fixed bed
- CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4 mixtures at 298 K under: (i) zero load, (ii) constant load, (iii) cyclic load.
- Compare measured selectivity shifts to IAST predictions generated from stress-dependent single-component fits.

5.3 Competitive adsorption under humid/polar interferents (NH3/H2O)
- Guided by NH3 competitive adsorption literature: test humid CO2/N2 with controlled RH and ppm–% NH3.
- Use DRIFTS to differentiate NH3 proton-transfer/H-bonding vs nitrate pocket interactions; quantify capacity loss and recovery when toggling stress.

Step 6 — Operando mechanistic verification: ion-pocket response under stress
6.1 Operando DRIFTS under compression
- Monitor nitrate ν3 band splitting/shift (pocket occupancy change), imidazolium/urea N–H shifts (anion H-bonding changes), and CO2 bands (electrostatic stabilization signature).
- Correlate spectral changes with the fast electromechanical component, not slow drift.

6.2 In situ PXRD under compression
- Track reversible lattice distortions and any peak broadening indicative of plastic deformation; verify elastic reversibility within ε ≤ 2%.

Step 7 — Controls that directly test causality (electrostatics vs mechanics)
7.1 Neutral analogue control
- Same topology/linker backbone but without quaternization (no tethered imidazolium; no NO3− pocket). Expect: minimal fast electromechanical signal and minimal stress-dependent selectivity.

7.2 Counterion polarizability/mobility control
- Replace NO3− with a less H-bond accepting, less coordinating anion (e.g., BF4−) only if it can be installed without framework collapse.
- Prediction: reduced ΔV and reduced stress-coupled selectivity modulation.

7.3 Rigid-lattice control
- Same ionic chemistry but 0% compliant linker fraction. Prediction: smaller ε-induced A/B bias, smaller ΔQfast, and smaller ΔS.

Step 8 — Quantitative success criteria (go/no-go)
- Electromechanical: reproducible fast component with ΔQcycle ≥ model-predicted threshold and stable over 10^4 cycles; σDC sufficiently low that response persists under dry conditions.
- Adsorption: ΔSselectivity ≥ 10% for CO2/N2 or CO2/CH4 at ε ≤ 2% with matching sign/magnitude to the pre-synthesis model.
- Mechanistic: correlated nitrate-pocket spectral signature (DRIFTS/NMR) with fast electromechanical response and adsorption modulation; absence of similar behavior in neutral/rigid controls.
- Stability: PXRD/porosity retention and nitrate retention post-cycling.
Feasibility:
Mechanistic plausibility with falsifiable predictions: The revised concept eliminates the internal contradiction of ‘immobilized yet redistributable nitrate’ by specifying a diffusion-suppressed, bistable anion pocket. This directly addresses reviewer concern (i) by targeting local A↔B hopping (Å-scale) rather than long-range NO3− migration that would produce DC conduction and humidity-driven drift. The mandatory pre-synthesis model translates realistic strains (0.5–2%) into quantitative ΔV at adsorption sites and ΔΔGads for CO2 vs N2/CH4, setting minimum detectable ΔQ and minimum selectivity modulation thresholds; the project can therefore fail fast (Gate G0) if the computed coupling is too small, addressing concern (iv).

Electromechanical signal discrimination: The protocol now uses blocking electrodes (Au/Pt), guard electrodes, controlled RH, and frequency/time-domain separation to distinguish a fast elastic polarization component from slow Maxwell–Wagner/electrode polarization and triboelectric/contact artifacts, addressing concern (ii). Artifact controls (inert pellets, electrode reversal, Kelvin probe mapping, vacuum baseline) are explicitly built in.

Synthetic realism and fallback: Recognizing that direct solvothermal crystallization of permanently cationic azolate frameworks can yield dense phases, the primary route is shifted to post-synthetic quaternization of a known porous Zn–azolate precursor, which is a common strategy to introduce permanent cations while preserving topology. Explicit PXRD/porosity/counterion gates (G1–G3) and a secondary direct-ionic route provide a realistic contingency plan, addressing concern (iii).

Relevance to competitive adsorption under polar interferents: The proposal retains the original chain (stress → electrostatics → competitive adsorption), but now anchors NH3/H2O competition in a framework where the anion pocket controls local fields and specific binding. This is consistent with literature showing that acid/base or strong H-bonding motifs dominate NH3 uptake and that adsorption behavior depends strongly on functional group arrangement and humidity; here, the pocket aims to modulate electrostatics without relying on uncontrolled water-mediated ion motion.

Overall, the revised plan is mechanistically tighter (bistable pocket rather than mobile ions), quantitatively pre-committed (ΔV/ΔΔGads/ΔQ thresholds), experimentally de-artifacted (blocking/guard protocols), and synthetically de-risked (post-synthetic ionic installation with phase/porosity gates).
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in pre-committing to falsifiable multiscale predictions (strain→anion microstate bias→ΔV→ΔΔGads→selectivity) and in explicitly engineering out the principal artifact pathways (Maxwell–Wagner/electrode polarization, humidity-driven conduction, triboelectric/contact charging). The main scientific risk is quantitative: (i) whether 0.5–2% elastic strain in a pellet/monolith can reproducibly bias an A/B nitrate occupancy enough to generate a ΔV at adsorption hotspots large enough to deliver ΔΔGads differences on the order of 0.25–0.5 kJ/mol at practical loadings, and (ii) whether a pocket can simultaneously enforce high long-range diffusion barriers (>20–30 kJ/mol) while maintaining a low local A↔B barrier (5–15 kJ/mol) without inadvertently creating additional ion-hopping pathways under compression, defects, or humidity. A second weakness is representativeness: periodic DFT on a ‘fragment/unit cell’ plus fitted charges may not faithfully capture disorder, defect populations, and field screening in real pellets, potentially overpredicting ΔV and underpredicting conductive relaxation. Finally, the adsorption-mechanics decoupling remains challenging experimentally: even with void-volume corrections and rigid controls, microstructural changes (grain rearrangement, contact area, pore accessibility) under stress can mimic selectivity shifts unless monolith architecture and in situ porosity metrics under load are tightly constrained.

Hypothesis: A helically scrolled MOF nanotube derived from a pre-registered, carboxylate-latticed 2D coordination nanosheet can sustain morphology-retentive conversion into a porous Zr6-cluster–stitched framework if (and only if) the precursor nanosheet is reticularly matched to the Zr6O4(OH)4 connectivity and the conversion proceeds via kinetically controlled, surface-confined cluster nucleation rather than bulk single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC–SC) exchange. In this architecture, directional ligand-to-metal/ligand-to-ligand charge-transfer (LMCT/LLCT) is not enforced by chirality alone but by a chemically encoded inner/outer surface redox asymmetry: asymmetric axial capping creates a permanent electrostatic potential gradient across the tube wall, while Zr6 stitching rigidifies registry and suppresses excimer-forming interlayer contacts. The result is (i) enhanced, tunable solid-state emission with reduced trap-mediated quenching and (ii) spatially vectorial charge separation that biases photogenerated electrons and holes toward chemically distinct inner versus outer surfaces, enabling measurable selectivity in CO2 photoreduction when catalytic sites are deliberately confined to one interface.
Plan:
Step 1 – Reticular precursor design with guaranteed Zr6 compatibility.
1.1 Ligand lattice pre-registration: Replace the generic salphen CP with a mixed-linker 2D coordination nanosheet built from (i) an atropisomeric, redox-active N2O2 chelating core (Ni(II) or Cu(II)) that defines in-plane conjugation and (ii) a co-planar, ditopic isophthalate-derived carboxylate linker whose O–O spacing (≈6.9–7.2 Å) and 120° geometry are matched to the equatorial edges of Zr6O4(OH)4 clusters. The carboxylates are positioned periodically (every ~1.5–2.0 nm) in the plane, forming a known (sql or kgm-type) 2D net that is crystallographically resolvable by GIWAXS/electron diffraction prior to scrolling.
1.2 Nanosheet formation: Grow 2–3 nm thick CP nanosheets by liquid–liquid interfacial coordination polymerization under modulator-free conditions to minimize defect density. Confirm in-plane order and lattice constants by GIWAXS and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED).

Step 2 – Deterministic helical scrolling with preserved lattice registry.
2.1 One-sided axial functionalization: Introduce 3–5% axial camphorsulfonate (or enantiopure menthoxyacetate) exclusively from the organic phase during interfacial growth to bind axial sites of Ni/Cu on only one face. This establishes a fixed dipolar and steric asymmetry without perturbing in-plane carboxylate registry.
2.2 Scrolling trigger: Apply a controlled solvent activity gradient (THF → MeCN/H2O, Δa_w quantified) to induce differential swelling. Helix pitch and diameter are tuned by sheet thickness and ionic strength, while in-plane diffraction is monitored to ensure lattice retention during scrolling.

Step 3 – Crystallographically defensible Zr6-cluster stitching (non-SC–SC).
3.1 Surface-confined Zr6 nucleation: Expose the helical CP scrolls to pre-formed Zr6O4(OH)4(modulator)x clusters (x = acetate/formate) in MeCN/H2O (≤10% H2O) at 50–70 °C. Use excess monocarboxylate modulator to slow ligand exchange, favoring stepwise substitution of modulators by pre-registered sheet carboxylates. This avoids uncontrolled Zr–O–Zr condensation.
3.2 Kinetic locking rather than bulk exchange: Zr6 clusters first bind within a single turn of the scroll, then progressively bridge adjacent turns only where lattice registry matches. Conversion is stopped at partial stitching densities (30–60%) to preserve porosity and avoid collapse.
3.3 Validation of registry: Compare in-plane GIWAXS/SAED before and after Zr6 incorporation; retention of peak positions (±2%) is required for pass. Loss of registry is a fail condition.

Step 4 – Proof of framework porosity vs. inter-scroll voids.
4.1 Gas sorption hierarchy: Measure N2 (77 K), Ar (87 K), CO2 (273/298 K), and Xe/Kr adsorption to extract pore-size distributions characteristic of Zr–carboxylate frameworks (≤2 nm). Contrast with collapsed-scroll controls.
4.2 Contrast-matched porosity tests: Perform positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) or Xe NMR to distinguish intrinsic framework pores from mesoscopic voids between scroll turns.

Step 5 – Quantification of cross-wall redox asymmetry and CT directionality.
5.1 Surface potential mapping: Use Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) on sectioned nanotubes to map inner vs outer surface potentials; a ≥50–100 mV difference is targeted.
5.2 Depth-resolved composition: Apply angle-resolved XPS and ToF-SIMS to confirm asymmetric axial capping and Zr6 distribution across the wall.
5.3 Directional charge separation tests: Perform transient absorption spectroscopy with selective inner- or outer-surface quenchers (e.g., tethered viologen vs TEMPO). Faster quenching on one interface constitutes pass/fail evidence of vectorial CT.

Step 6 – CO2 photoreduction with enforced interface asymmetry.
6.1 Catalyst localization: Confine molecular Re(I) or Mn(I) bipyridine carbonyl catalysts to the inner surface only (1–2% sites) via pre-installed docking ligands. Outer surface remains catalyst-free.
6.2 Photocatalysis and causality: Measure CO/ HCOO− production under 13CO2. Correlate rates and selectivity with KPFM-measured potential gradients and CT lifetimes. Compare to symmetric (two-sided capped) and unscrolled controls to isolate the role of geometry-induced redox asymmetry.
Feasibility: This revision removes the chemically fragile SC–SC claim and replaces it with a kinetically and crystallographically defensible pathway rooted in reticular chemistry. By pre-designing a carboxylate lattice whose spacing and geometry are explicitly matched to Zr6 cluster connectivity, the proposal satisfies the reviewer’s demand for registry rather than assuming it. Surface-confined cluster nucleation using pre-formed Zr6 units and strong modulators is a known strategy in UiO-type post-synthetic modification and minimizes amorphization risks. Importantly, porosity is proven by multiple orthogonal techniques that discriminate framework pores from inter-scroll voids. The charge-transfer mechanism is no longer inferred from chirality alone: it is quantified via surface-potential mapping, depth-resolved spectroscopy, and directional quenching experiments that directly test inner/outer redox asymmetry. Finally, CO2 reduction selectivity is mechanistically tied to enforced interface chemistry (catalyst localization + potential gradient), not to helicity as an abstract concept. Together, these changes convert the highest-risk steps into testable, pass/fail milestones and tightly couple helical morphology, electronic structure, and catalytic outcome.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in experimental resolution: it defines lattice-matching targets, specifies nucleation control via pre-formed Zr6 clusters and modulators, and sets clear structural validation criteria (GIWAXS/SAED retention ±2%). The biggest scientific risk is mechanistic over-determination: (i) the assumption that partial Zr6 “stitching densities” of 30–60% will both preserve helical morphology and generate an internally connected, intrinsically microporous Zr–carboxylate framework is not yet chemically justified—partial crosslinking may yield a mechanically locked composite with inter-turn voids rather than a true Zr6-node framework; (ii) cross-wall electrostatic potential gradients measured by KPFM on sectioned nanotubes can be dominated by contact potential/work-function artifacts, charging, or thickness variations, so the claimed ≥50–100 mV may not uniquely report “inner vs outer redox asymmetry”; (iii) catalyst localization to the inner surface at 1–2% while keeping the outer surface catalyst-free is nontrivial in a porous, defect-bearing, partially stitched wall—diffusion/redistribution and unintended binding to Zr6 carboxylate sites could erase interface specificity; and (iv) the link from chirality/scrolling to suppression of excimer-forming contacts and improved emission is plausible but under-specified—no quantitative structural handle (interchromophore distance/orientation distribution) is proposed to connect stitching to excitonic coupling and trap suppression. Overall, the logic is coherent and testable, but several causal claims (true framework porosity; unambiguous vectorial CT; enforced interface-only catalysis) remain insufficiently de-risked by controls that distinguish alternative explanations.

Hypothesis: A true single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC–SC) conversion can be made feasible inside a large-pore zeolite by replacing the speculative “volatile coordination-polymer + bulky S/N vapor linker + in-pore condensation” route with a literature-grounded, micropore-diffusible vapor-phase ligand-exchange pair and an explicit topotactic registry rule. Specifically, we hypothesize that (i) a zeolite single crystal (FAU-Y or *BEA) preloaded with a halide/amine-labile, low-molecular-volume metal–ligand precursor (Zn2+ or Co2+ with imidazole-derived ligands and charge-balancing halide/amine guests) will form an orientationally biased, pore-confined precursor lattice whose periodicity is commensurate with the zeolite supercage/channel repeat; (ii) exposure to a *small, zeolite-window-permeable* incoming linker vapor (imidazole derivatives ≤ ~6 Å kinetic diameter; e.g., imidazole, 2-methylimidazole, 2-mercaptoimidazole) will drive a topotactic anion/ligand exchange and node reconnection under solvent-free conditions, minimizing capillary/mechanical stress and therefore preserving the host single-crystal morphology; and (iii) “deterministic” missing-linker defects are programmed—not by generic mixed-linker lability—but by a falsifiable symmetry/stoichiometry rule imposed by periodic charge-compensation/anchoring sites in the zeolite (framework Al– sites with associated extra-framework cations and/or silanol nests) that enforce a commensurate mixed-linker superstructure and a predictable vacancy density at specific crystallographic sublattices. These defects create spatially repeating soft-donor pockets (–S/–N) where Hg2+ forms inner-sphere complexes (HSAB-driven), while the zeolite scaffold provides mechanical integrity and a parallel ion-transport network. The refined approach overcomes reviewer concerns by (a) using only linkers demonstrably small enough to traverse FAU (7.4 Å windows) or *BEA (6.6–7.7 Å) and avoiding in-pore multistep condensations, (b) defining an explicit epitaxial/topotactic relationship and diffraction-based pass/fail criteria for SC–SC vs re-nucleation, and (c) making defect periodicity an a priori structural model tied to zeolite Al/cation ordering that can be confirmed or rejected by SCXRD/EDT/PDF.
Plan:
Step 0 — System down-selection with pore/size constraints and topotaxy targets
0.1 Zeolite host choice and Al-pattern control: Use FAU-type zeolite Y single crystals (supercage ~13 Å; 12-ring windows ~7.4 Å) as the primary host; use dealuminated FAU and *BEA single crystals as controls for anchoring-site density. Prepare two FAU-Y variants: (A) high-Al (low Si/Al) for high periodic charge-compensation density, (B) dealuminated (steam/acid) for reduced Al-site density. Exchange extra-framework cations to Na+ (baseline) and separately to Ag+ or Cu+ (stronger π/soft interactions) to modulate precursor anchoring.
0.2 Incoming linker size gate: Restrict to single heteroaromatic linkers that can diffuse through 12-ring windows and do not require in-pore condensation: imidazole (HIm), 2-methylimidazole (2-MeIm), and 2-mercaptoimidazole (2-MIm-SH). These provide N-donor connectivity (ZIF-type formation) and introduce S-donor sites directly without post-condensation chemistry.
0.3 Precursor/MOF pair selection (vapor-processable and exchangeable): Use a halide/amine-labile Zn2+ (or Co2+) precursor phase capable of ligand exchange to imidazolates under vapor/low-solvent conditions. Concretely, target a pore-confined “ZnX2·(Im)2” (X = Cl−/Br−) coordination network or cluster-like precursor assembled inside the zeolite from ZnX2 and imidazole/amine guests. The exchange step will replace labile X−/neutral donors with imidazolate/mercaptoimidazolate to form a ZIF-like node connectivity (Zn(Im)2 topology family) under mild heating.

Step 1 — Build an ordered, pore-confined, SCXRD-trackable precursor inside zeolite single crystals
1.1 Zeolite activation without defecting the host: Dehydrate zeolite single crystals under dynamic vacuum (10−5–10−6 mbar) with a staged temperature ramp (120 °C → 250 °C) to remove water while minimizing dealumination.
1.2 Vapor-assisted infiltration (demonstrably feasible reagents): In a sealed glass/metal ampoule, co-load activated zeolite single crystals with (i) ZnCl2 (or CoCl2) and (ii) imidazole (or a small amine such as NH3 or ethylenediamine in sub-stoichiometric amounts) as a transient, volatile base/ligand. Heat to 120–180 °C to promote vapor transport and uptake. Rationale: ZnCl2 and imidazole have sufficient vapor pressure/transport under heated sealed conditions and are widely used in solvent-free/ionothermal-like regimes (Asset 1 logic: non-aqueous templating/structure control).
1.3 Enforce orientational bias via charge-compensation sites: Use the FAU-Y(A) (higher Al) sample to promote periodic anchoring of Zn-containing species near Al–O− sites (via electrostatics and cation mediation). This creates a testable prediction: higher Al content increases the degree of guest lattice orientation and the intensity of satellite/commensurate reflections.
1.4 Verify “ordered precursor” *before* attempting conversion:
  - Single-crystal XRD: retain zeolite host reflections; search for additional, weaker guest-derived reflections and/or diffuse features consistent with a commensurate superstructure.
  - Synchrotron SCXRD mapping in reciprocal space: collect full reciprocal-space volumes to detect (hkl)host ± q satellites; quantify mosaicity broadening.
  - Complementary: Pair distribution function (PDF) to confirm local Zn–N/Cl coordination environments inside the host.
Pass/fail criterion: If only amorphous guest loading occurs (no commensurate order, only diffuse scattering), pivot to increased anchoring (Ag+-exchanged FAU) and/or lower loading to reduce disorder.

Step 2 — Vapor-phase ligand exchange to a ZIF-like framework with S/N functionality (no in-pore multistep chemistry)
2.1 Incoming linker delivery: Expose precursor-loaded zeolite single crystals to controlled vapor of 2-MeIm and/or 2-mercaptoimidazole (2-MIm-SH) in a second sealed ampoule under inert atmosphere. Temperature window: 120–160 °C (below zeolite stability limits; above diffusion threshold for the linker).
2.2 Exchange/conversion mechanism: Drive halide/neutral-donor displacement by imidazolate/mercaptoimidazolate formation (deprotonation assisted by residual basic guests/extra-framework cations). The conversion is designed as a single-step ligand exchange/reconnection rather than a condensation sequence.
2.3 Control of mixed-linker incorporation (defect programming handle): Use a *commensurate composition rule* tied to periodic charge-compensation:
  - Model: Each framework Al– site (negative charge) is associated with an extra-framework cation. During conversion, these sites preferentially stabilize mercaptoimidazolate (more polarizable, stronger interactions), biasing its placement at positions proximal to Al-rich supercages.
  - Therefore, by tuning Si/Al and cation type, we predefine a superlattice of “S-rich” linker positions. Where steric/electrostatic mismatch occurs, a predictable fraction of nodes must remain undercoordinated (missing-linker/vacancy) to satisfy local charge/geometry—yielding a non-random vacancy pattern.
2.4 Make “determinism” falsifiable a priori: Construct three structural models prior to experiments:
  - M0 (random defects): mercaptoimidazolate and imidazolate randomly distributed; vacancies statistically distributed.
