0.1 Target structure: UiO-66/UiO-67 family (Zr6O4(OH)4 nodes; fcu topology) with mixed linkers.
0.2 Target peptide incorporation: 5, 10, 20 mol% functional linker (rest: BDC or BPDC).
0.3 Go/no-go crystallography: (i) PXRD indexable to fcu with <1% lattice mismatch vs simulated mixed-linker model; (ii) total scattering/PDF showing preserved Zr–O (~2.1 Å) and Zr–Zr (~3.5 Å) correlations; (iii) no amorphous fraction >10% by Rietveld + internal standard; (iv) porosity retained: N2 BET > 800 m2/g at 10 mol% peptide-linker.
0.4 Target performance benchmarks (membrane, 2–10 µm active layer):
• CO2/N2 (dry, 1 bar, 25–50 °C): CO2 permeance ≥ 500 GPU and selectivity ≥ 30 (or CO2/CH4 selectivity ≥ 20).
• Li-ion separator (1 M LiPF6 EC/DEC or EMC, 25 °C): ionic conductivity σ ≥ 0.5 mS/cm; Li+ transference number t+ ≥ 0.6 (target ≥ 0.7); area-specific resistance stable within ±20% over 72 h soak.
• Drug release (PBS, 37 °C): sustained release over 24–120 h with <30% burst (first 2 h) for a cationic model drug; cytocompatibility ≥ 80% viability (MC3T3-E1 or fibroblasts) in extract test.

Step 1 — Reticularly constrained peptidomimetic linker design (single binding mode)
1.1 Replace flexible 6–9mer peptides with *short, constrained peptidomimetics* that present two terminal carboxylates at fixed distance/angle compatible with UiO fcu edges.
Design set A (β-strand-mimetic): dipeptide/tri-peptide capped with aromatic ‘strut’ to control geometry, e.g., HOOC–Ph–(CONH–X–CONH)–Ph–COOH, where X carries a side-chain charge (Asp/Glu for fixed anion; Lys-like cation avoided initially to reduce protonation variability).
Design set B (stapled turn): cyclic/bridged scaffold (e.g., diketopiperazine-based) functionalized with two para-carboxyphenyl arms to enforce near-linear dicarboxylate presentation.
1.2 Charge placement: prioritize *anionic* groups (Asp/Glu mimics, sulfonate as optional second generation) to create Li+-affine sites while enabling Donnan exclusion of anions in partially wetted pores.
1.3 Mixed-linker dominance: structural linker = BDC (UiO-66) for smaller pores (better anion exclusion) or BPDC (UiO-67) if porosity loss is excessive; decision based on BET and ion transport.
1.4 Binding-mode control: avoid phosphonates in Gen1 (too strong/multidentate with Zr, high amorphization risk); use dicarboxylates exclusively with monotopic modulators.

Step 2 — Chemically constraining synthesis variables (modulator + water activity), with low-dimensional ML
2.1 Reaction platform: microwave solvothermal in DMF with controlled water activity; temperature 120–150 °C; 15–60 min.
2.2 Modulators (reticular control): acetic acid and/or formic acid as monotopic competitors to suppress uncontrolled oligomerization; modulator equivalents screened narrowly (e.g., 20, 40, 80 equiv vs total dicarboxylate).
2.3 Water activity/ionic strength: water equivalents (e.g., 2, 5, 10, 20 equiv vs Zr) and optional LiOAc (0–50 mM) to probe ionic strength effects on nucleation without exploding search space.
2.4 ML constraint: Bayesian optimization over a 3–4D space only: {modulator type, modulator eq, water eq, temperature/time}. Objective function is *structure-tied*, not generic crystallinity:
Objective = w1*(Rietveld fcu-fit score) + w2*(PDF similarity to UiO reference) + w3*(peptidomimetic incorporation verified by digestion NMR) + w4*(BET retention).
Stopping rules: stop when posterior probability of meeting go/no-go criteria exceeds 0.8 or after N=25 experiments.

Step 3 — Operando validation of ‘coordination-selected conformer’ incorporation (replaces overstated solvent-locking)
3.1 In situ synchrotron PXRD during microwave/solvothermal growth (or capillary reactor analog): track nucleation onset, phase purity, and lattice parameter shifts vs peptide-linker fraction.
3.2 In situ total scattering/PDF (time-resolved) on selected conditions to detect whether Zr6 cluster formation precedes linker ordering and whether peptide-linker changes local order.
3.3 Isotope labeling: 13C at linker carboxylates and 15N at amide(s) of peptidomimetic.
3.4 SSNMR constraints: 13C CPMAS line shapes for carboxylate coordination; 15N chemical shift anisotropy/2D 15N–13C correlation to distinguish incorporated conformers and H-bonding environment.
3.5 Solvent-history test (critical falsification): synthesize under two water activities giving similar PXRD; compare SSNMR and pair distribution signatures. If conformation/coordination environment is invariant, we conclude solvent does not encode conformation; we then reframe solvent as a kinetic selector only and proceed with the best-performing structural condition.

Step 4 — Membrane engineering with explicit support chemistry, oriented growth, and thickness/grain-boundary control
4.1 Support selection:
• Gas separation: α-alumina or ZrO2 tubular/flat supports with 100–200 nm top layer.
• Battery separator: porous polyimide (PI) or PVDF-HFP scaffold pre-coated with an inorganic ALD ZrOx (5–20 nm) to promote nucleation and chemical robustness.
4.2 Surface functionalization for seeding: polydopamine (PDA) primer (5–20 nm) on polymer supports (Asset 2 logic: universal adhesion, conformal coating); carboxylate-terminated silane (e.g., CPTES-derived) on ceramic supports to anchor Zr clusters.
4.3 Seeding/oriented intergrowth:
• Apply UiO seed layer (50–200 nm nanoparticles) by dip-coating; fix with mild thermal treatment.
• Secondary growth under optimized Step 2 conditions to form continuous layer; thickness controlled by growth cycles (1–3 cycles) and precursor concentration.
4.4 Grain-boundary selectivity control: modulator-rich secondary growth to heal intercrystalline voids; verify by permporometry (He, SF6) and dye infiltration tests.
4.5 Mechanical/chemical stability tests (predefined):
• Adhesion: tape test + scratch test; target no delamination.
• Hydration/electrolyte soak: 72 h in water and 1 M LiPF6 EC/DEC; PXRD retention and permeance/σ within ±20%.
• Swelling/wetting: sorption isotherms with water vapor; contact angle and QCM-D on model films to quantify wetting transitions.

Step 5 — Application-specific validation with explicit failure-mode probes
5.1 CO2 capture/separation (dry):
• Pure-gas and mixed-gas permeation; calculate permeance and selectivity.
• Correlate CO2 affinity with isosteric heat (Qst) from adsorption isotherms; test competitive adsorption with trace water (0–50% RH) to quantify performance loss.
Failure mode checks: peptide site protonation or residual modulator blocking pores; diagnose by IR (carboxylate stretches), TGA-MS, and BET.
5.2 Li-ion transport (carbonate):
• Measure σ by EIS; t+ by Bruce–Vincent method; Li plating/stripping in symmetric Li||Li cells to assess dendrite suppression.
• Anion mobility control: quantify PF6−/TFSI− uptake by ICP (P, F, S) after soak; evaluate Donnan exclusion by comparing conductivity with LiTFSI vs LiPF6.
Failure modes: excessive anion uptake (low t+), pore flooding causing loss of selectivity, framework degradation; diagnose via 19F NMR of extracts + PXRD/PDF.
5.3 Drug delivery/tissue interface (narrowed, proof-of-concept only):
• Use one model cationic drug (e.g., rhodamine B or lidocaine·HCl) and one neutral (e.g., dexamethasone) to map charge effects.
• Release in PBS at 37 °C; fit to Korsmeyer–Peppas to distinguish diffusion vs gate effects.
• Cell tests limited to extract cytotoxicity + adhesion on membrane surface; optional incorporation of a minimal RGD motif as a *second-generation pore-external tag* only if base membrane is cytocompatible (Asset 1 logic, but kept out of Gen1 to avoid crystallization disruption).

Step 6 — Composition verification (addresses polymorphism/heterogeneity directly)
6.1 Digestion 1H/13C NMR to quantify linker ratios and confirm peptidomimetic integrity.
6.2 ICP-OES for Zr content; calculate node/linker stoichiometry.
6.3 Elemental analysis/XPS depth profiling on membranes to confirm uniform incorporation vs surface enrichment.

Decision gates (explicit):
Gate A (powder): if fcu topology + incorporation verified at ≥10 mol% and BET ≥800 m2/g → proceed to membranes.
Gate B (membrane): if defect-free by permporometry and stable after water + electrolyte soak → proceed to CO2 + Li metrics.
Gate C (function): if CO2 targets met but Li targets fail (or vice versa), adjust pore size (UiO-66 vs UiO-67), peptide fraction (5–20%), and anionic site density; no expansion of solvent space beyond Step 2 variables.
Feasibility:
1) Structural feasibility is de-risked by reticular dominance and conformational constraint. The major linker (BDC/BPDC) enforces the UiO fcu net, while the peptidomimetic is intentionally a *minor functional dopant* with (i) dicarboxylate-only coordination and (ii) reduced conformational degrees of freedom, directly addressing the reviewer concern that flexible 6–9mers generate multiple binding modes and amorphous Zr–peptide polymers. Modulator control (AcOH/HCOOH equivalents) is an established route to suppress polymorphism and regulate defect chemistry in Zr-MOFs.
2) The ‘solvent-encoded conformation’ claim is replaced with a falsifiable operando framework. In situ synchrotron PXRD and total scattering/PDF during crystallization explicitly test whether different water activities/modulator loads change the incorporated coordination environment and growth pathway. Isotope-labeled SSNMR provides direct constraints on incorporated amide/carboxylate environments, enabling a causal link (or refutation) between synthesis history and coordinated conformer.
3) Membrane intergrowth is engineered (not asserted): support choice, surface chemistry (including PDA as a universal primer on polymers), seeding, secondary growth, thickness control by growth cycles, and defect-healing via modulator-rich conditions are specified. Stability is quantified under the two harsh environments central to the proposal—water and carbonate electrolyte—using predefined retention criteria (PXRD/PDF + performance drift limits).
4) Cross-domain performance is made realistic by explicit benchmarks and failure-mode assays. The decoupling mechanism (dry CO2 vs wetted Li+) is treated as a design hypothesis to be stress-tested with controlled humidity/wetting experiments, anion uptake quantification, and electrolyte-dependent transport comparisons. If trade-offs emerge (e.g., high CO2 selectivity but low t+ due to anion mobility), the response variables are limited to pore size (UiO-66 vs -67), peptide fraction, and anionic site density—maintaining coherence while avoiding uncontrolled scope.
5) ML is constrained to a low-dimensional, physically motivated space (modulator identity/eq, water activity, temperature/time) with uncertainty-aware stopping and structure-tied objectives (Rietveld + PDF + incorporation + BET). This prevents ‘optimization veneer’ and ensures that data acquisition maximally informs chemically meaningful decisions.
Critique:
The proposal is unusually strong in execution specificity for Zr-MOF synthesis validation and membrane fabrication: clear go/no-go crystallography/PDF thresholds, incorporation quantification, defect diagnostics, and stability windows in both water and carbonate electrolytes. The key logical improvement versus the prior ‘solvent-locking’ claim—replacing it with a falsifiable coordination-selected conformer framework—is scientifically coherent and appropriately instrumented.

Primary deductions come from (i) an under-justified transport mechanism for achieving simultaneously high CO2 permeance/selectivity in a 2–10 µm UiO layer while also adding polar/charged sites that typically increase water sensitivity and can depress gas diffusivity; the humidity tolerance is acknowledged but not built into the success criteria beyond testing. (ii) The Li+ transference argument relies on Donnan exclusion/anion immobilization inside UiO pores, but UiO-66/67 apertures and defect-mediated mesoporosity/grain boundaries often dominate ion transport; without a quantitative defect-density/charge-density model (or a plan to decouple pore vs grain-boundary conduction), the mechanistic attribution risks being post hoc. (iii) The “aqueous biocompatibility for drug release/cell interfacing” leg is operationally feasible but scientifically thin relative to the rest: it is not clearly shown that the same membrane chemistry/state used for battery electrolyte exposure is compatible with cell-contact (residual modulators, leachables, and Zr/ligand release), nor is there a plan to resolve conflicting design constraints (hydrophilicity/charge for Li+ vs protein adsorption/fouling for tissue interface).

Overall, the proposal is well-engineered and logically tighter than typical multi-domain MOF membranes, but the cross-domain coupling claims (one platform serving gas separation + battery + biointerface) remain only partially mechanistically unified.

Hypothesis: Embedding a **specifically defined, electropolymerized sulfonated conjugated polymer network**—derived from redox-active aniline/phenazine-type monomers—as a thin, percolating interphase within aligned mesochannels of a hierarchically porous Ni–Fe MOF monolith will *intrinsically* lower the OER Tafel slope at reconstructed Ni(Fe)OOH sites by accelerating the rate-determining proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) step, rather than merely improving mass transport or reducing ohmic losses. Mechanistically, the hypothesis rests on three coupled effects: (i) **field-directed confined electropolymerization** produces a wall-bound, electronically conjugated polymer network that maintains continuous electronic wiring during MOF-to-oxyhydroxide reconstruction; (ii) **immobilized sulfonate groups (–SO3−)** form nanoconfined hydration shells that act as a local proton/anion relay, stabilizing *OH/*OOH intermediates and reducing the activation barrier for O–O bond formation at Ni(Fe)OOH; and (iii) spatial co-localization of polymer and reconstructed oxyhydroxide ensures that these effects occur at the same catalytic length scale. By explicitly deconvoluting electronic resistance, ionic transport, and intrinsic kinetics, the proposal posits that a genuine change in intrinsic Tafel slope (reaction order–consistent with PCET acceleration) can be demonstrated without sacrificing micropore-accessible surface area required for high-current-density water oxidation.
Plan:
Step 1: **MOF monolith and pore architecture definition**.
1.1 Select a NiFe-BTC–type MOF (Ni:Fe = 3:1 to 4:1) known to reconstruct to Ni(Fe)OOH under anodic bias. Synthesize ~50–200 µm thick monolith films on Ni foam or carbon paper via evaporation-induced self-assembly (EISA) using MOF nanoparticles and Pluronic F127 as a soft template.
1.2 Target pore metrics *a priori*: micropores <2 nm preserved; mesochannels 10–25 nm diameter, >70% connectivity (SAXS + tomography). Acceptance criterion: ≤20% loss in BET surface area and ≤15% loss in micropore volume after all processing.

Step 2: **Locking down the electropolymerizable COP chemistry**.
2.1 Monomer set (pre-validated ex situ): (i) **2-aminobenzenesulfonic acid (ABS)** as the sulfonated, redox-active unit; (ii) **5,10-dihydrophenazine (DHP)** as a bifunctional conjugation extender; (iii) optional 1–5 mol% tris(4-aminophenyl)amine (TAPA) to introduce controlled crosslinking. All monomers exhibit reversible oxidation between +0.6 and +0.9 V vs Ag/AgCl in alkaline media.
2.2 Coupling mechanism: oxidative C–N/C–C coupling via radical cations generated under potentiostatic control (+0.85 V vs Ag/AgCl), yielding a **crosslinked but π-conjugated sulfonated network** (classified as a COP-like network rather than a linear polyaniline). Crosslink density is governed by TAPA fraction and total passed charge.
2.3 Confined electropolymerization protocol: infiltrate monomers into mesochannels by capillary wetting; perform potentiostatic polymerization with charge densities of 5–30 mC cm−2. Growth kinetics will be pre-calibrated on model mesoporous ITO electrodes to establish thickness–charge relationships and confirm wall-coating (not pore filling).

Step 3: **Quantitative pore-blocking control and spatial registration**.
3.1 After each polymerization increment, measure N2 sorption and electrochemical double-layer capacitance. Hard stop if BET loss exceeds 20% or mesopore diameter shifts below 8 nm.
3.2 Verify spatial registration using cross-sectional STEM-EELS and ToF-SIMS mapping of S (from –SO3−) versus Ni/Fe–OOH (O K-edge, Fe L-edge) before and after anodic reconstruction. Acceptance metric: ≥70% spatial overlap coefficient within ±5 nm of channel walls.

Step 4: **Electrochemical reconstruction and kinetic discrimination**.
4.1 Reconstruct MOF nodes via stepped anodic activation in 1.0 M KOH (1.35–1.55 V vs RHE). The confined sCOP remains electronically percolating during transformation.
4.2 Full kinetic deconvolution: apply 100% iR compensation; perform thickness-dependent studies (vary monolith thickness 20–200 µm); conduct operando EIS under OER bias with DRT and porous-electrode modeling to separate charge-transfer resistance from ionic diffusion.
4.3 Demonstrate intrinsic Tafel change: compare Tafel slopes after correcting for film resistance and local pH; perform OH− reaction-order analysis and H/D isotope experiments (KOH vs KOD). A true kinetic effect is defined as a ≥10 mV dec−1 Tafel slope reduction persisting after resistance correction and showing a measurable kinetic isotope effect.

Step 5: **Benchmarking and durability**.
5.1 Extract TOFs normalized to electrochemically addressable Ni/Fe redox charge; benchmark at 10, 100, and 500 mA cm−2.
5.2 Long-term chronopotentiometry (≥100 h at 200 mA cm−2), post-mortem TEM/XPS/ICP, and Faradaic efficiency for O2 (GC).
Feasibility:
1. **Chemical realism of the COP**: Aniline- and phenazine-based oxidative electropolymerization is well established; introducing ABS ensures permanent sulfonation without post-functionalization. The proposed network is explicitly defined as a *crosslinked conjugated polymer* (COP-like), avoiding ambiguity around COF crystallinity.
2. **Controlled growth and pore preservation**: Charge-limited electropolymerization and pre-calibration on mesoporous electrodes provide a quantitative handle on film thickness, directly addressing pore-blocking risk with explicit acceptance thresholds.
3. **Mechanistic discrimination**: By combining full iR compensation, thickness scaling, operando EIS/DRT, reaction-order analysis, and isotope effects, the plan rigorously separates intrinsic kinetic changes from transport artifacts—directly answering the reviewer’s concern about Tafel slope interpretation.
4. **Spatial co-localization proof**: Cross-sectional STEM-EELS and ToF-SIMS mapping provide operational metrics for ‘registration’ between sulfonated polymer and reconstructed Ni(Fe)OOH, rather than an asserted alignment.
5. **Literature grounding**: Prior demonstrations of low Tafel slopes in MOF-derived heterostructures (Asset 1), enhanced Ni–Fe MOF OER kinetics (Asset 2), and sulfonated conjugated polymers as conductive, hydrated networks (Asset 5) collectively support the proposed coupling of confined conductivity and PCET modulation.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in execution specificity (quantified pore metrics, charge-density windows, hard acceptance criteria for pore blocking, and spatial-overlap metrics from STEM-EELS/ToF-SIMS). The mechanistic claim—intrinsic Tafel slope reduction via PCET acceleration from immobilized sulfonate hydration shells co-localized with reconstructed Ni(Fe)OOH—is plausible but not yet logically closed: in 1.0 M KOH, interfacial proton activity is tightly constrained and OER on NiFeOOH is often discussed in terms of OH−-coupled steps rather than free-proton relays; thus, the sulfonate effect could manifest primarily as altered local ionic strength/water activity, double-layer structure, or buffering rather than a true PCET mediator. The plan partially mitigates this with reaction-order and KIE tests, but it still risks over-interpreting Tafel slope changes because (i) Tafel slopes in porous, reconstructing films can remain sensitive to distributed ohmic/ionic resistances and evolving active-site density even after nominal iR compensation, and (ii) TOF normalization to Ni/Fe redox charge can be distorted by polymer redox capacitance and by changes in NiOOH/Ni(OH)2 redox accessibility induced by sulfonate/Donnan effects. Finally, the polymer chemistry is described as COP-like and ‘π-conjugated’, but without direct in-pore verification of conjugation length, doping state, and conductivity under OER potentials; if the polymer becomes over-oxidized, de-doped in strong base, or insulating after long bias, the key ‘wiring during reconstruction’ premise weakens.

Hypothesis: A single Zr6-based, mixed-linker MOF platform can be engineered to deliver three *mechanistically distinct* and therefore defensible selectivity modes—(1) equilibrium multigas selectivity predicted by IAST in rigid, accessible pores; (2) aqueous heavy-metal capture governed by speciation-coupled inner-sphere complexation at thiol sites; and (3) stimuli-responsive dye/drug uptake–release governed by transport gating/kinetics—provided that each regime is modeled and validated with the appropriate framework and with explicit go/no-go metrics. Mechanistically, we hypothesize that: (i) CO2/N2/CH4 separation will be dominated by quadrupole–field interactions and confinement in a water-tolerant Zr6 MOF with controlled missing-linker defects that generate polar adsorption sites while maintaining pore rigidity; under these conditions, multicomponent adsorption will be quantitatively captured by IAST using uncertainty-propagated fits to single-component isotherms (DSL/Langmuir-Freundlich), including controlled humidity as a competitive adsorbate. (ii) In water, soft heavy-metal selectivity (Hg2+ ≫ Pb2+ > Cd2+ ≫ Ca2+/Mg2+) will arise from thiol/thiolate inner-sphere binding (Hg–S) on pendant –SH groups, with uptake limited by metal speciation (chloride/hydroxide complexes), thiol pKa/oxidation state (–SH/–S−/–S–S–), and Zr-node hydrolytic stability; therefore, predictive capability requires surface-complexation/speciation modeling rather than IAST. (iii) For dyes/drugs, azobenzene units will not be claimed to change equilibrium adsorption thermodynamics directly; instead, measurable differences will arise from light/pH-modulated *transport accessibility* (effective pore-limiting diameter and diffusion coefficient), so a gated-access kinetic model (non-equilibrium diffusion–reaction) will be used to link switching extent to uptake/release rates and deliverable dose. This refined structure overcomes the reviewer’s concern about conceptual overreach by restricting IAST to its validated domain (multigas physisorption in rigid pores) while using mechanistically appropriate, experimentally constrained models for aqueous ion capture and gated molecular delivery, all mapped onto a single, tunable MOF architecture (linker ratio, defect density, thiol oxidation state, azobenzene loading) with clear quantitative success criteria.
Plan:
Step 1 — Platform selection, linker identities, and topology/pore targets (design freeze before synthesis).
1.1 Base framework choice: Use a UiO-type Zr6O4(OH)4 node platform to maximize hydrolytic stability (Zr–carboxylate bonds), targeting an fcu topology for synthetic robustness and scalable defect control.
1.2 Mixed-linker set (explicit candidates; final selection by solubility/compatibility screening):
  • L1 (thiol linker): 2,5-dimercaptoterephthalic acid (DMTPA) *or* 2-mercapto-terephthalic acid (MTPA) as a pendant thiol/carboxylate heterofunctional dicarboxylate for soft-metal binding.
  • L2 (inert pore-shaping linker): terephthalic acid (BDC) as a diluent to tune thiol-site density and preserve crystallinity.
  • L3 (azobenzene linker): azobenzene-4,4′-dicarboxylic acid (AzoBDC) to introduce photoswitchable moieties within the pore wall (not assumed to create large, flexible “mesocages”; instead targeted to modulate pore-limiting diameter/transport).
1.3 Structural descriptor targets:
  • Pore limiting diameter (PLD) target: 5–9 Å for strong CO2 confinement while allowing N2/CH4 access; PLD to be extracted from Ar(87 K) or N2(77 K) sorption + pore size analysis.
  • Defect (missing-linker) density target: 0–10% of linker sites to introduce polar sites while maintaining water stability; quantified by TGA/solution NMR of digested samples and complemented by positron annihilation or adsorption-based defect proxies.

Step 2 — Synthesis with engineering resolution (linker ratio, modulator, thiol protection/oxidation control).
2.1 Solvothermal synthesis matrix (DoE): Prepare a compositional library UiO-66-(BDC)x(MTPA/DMTPA)y(AzoBDC)z with x+y+z=1.
  • Initial molar grids: (y=0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20), (z=0, 0.05, 0.10), balance BDC.
  • Modulator control (defects): acetic acid or formic acid (0–100 equiv vs. Zr) to tune missing-linker defects; water content in DMF controlled (0–5 vol%).
2.2 Thiol integrity plan:
  • Handle thiol linkers under inert atmosphere when feasible; include antioxidant (e.g., trace BHT) during linker storage.
  • Quantify thiol vs disulfide: Raman (S–S band), XPS S 2p (thiol/disulfide/thiolate), and Ellman’s assay after digestion to determine accessible –SH.
  • If thiol oxidation is unavoidable during synthesis, implement post-synthetic reduction (mild, framework-compatible reductant) and re-quantify –SH; set acceptance criterion (≥70% thiol in –SH/–S− form).
2.3 Node protection/water stability:
  • Avoid high defect levels in thiol-rich compositions; set preliminary ceiling defect density at which PXRD crystallinity and water stability remain acceptable (defined in Step 4).
  • Post-synthetic solvent exchange (MeOH) + activation under controlled temperature to avoid thiol oxidation and collapse.

Step 3 — Structural and chemical descriptor mapping (inputs → descriptors → performance).
3.1 Quantify descriptors for each library member:
  • Linker incorporation: digested 1H NMR/LC-MS for BDC:MTPA/AzoBDC ratios.
  • Defect density/open site proxies: TGA, acid uptake titration, CO adsorption IR (for Lewis acidity), and water sorption hysteresis.
  • Porosity: N2 (77 K) and CO2 (273 K) isotherms; PLD and surface area.
  • Switching extent: in situ UV–Vis diffuse reflectance or solid-state NMR to quantify trans/cis fraction under irradiation; define “switching amplitude” as Δ(trans→cis) under application-relevant irradiation in hydrated and dry states.

Step 4 — Regime A (valid IAST domain): CO2/N2/CH4 multigas separation under dry and controlled humidity.
4.1 Single-component isotherms: CO2, N2, CH4 at 273/298/313 K up to 1 bar (and optionally to 10 bar if equipment permits). Fit isotherms using dual-site Langmuir (DSL) and Langmuir–Freundlich; select model by AIC/BIC and residual analysis.
4.2 Uncertainty propagation: Use bootstrap resampling of isotherm fits to generate confidence intervals on IAST-predicted selectivities and working capacities.
4.3 Humidity as competitive adsorbate:
  • Measure H2O vapor isotherms (298 K) and repeat CO2 isotherms at fixed relative humidity (e.g., 20% and 50% RH) using a humidified gas stream or pre-equilibration.
  • Treat H2O explicitly as a competing component where equilibrium is reached; report CO2/N2 selectivity retention under RH.
4.4 Mixture validation beyond IAST:
  • Breakthrough experiments for CO2/N2 (15/85) and CO2/CH4 (e.g., 10/90) at 298 K; include dry and 20% RH conditions.
  • Go/no-go metrics (Regime A):
    – IAST CO2/N2 selectivity ≥ 30 at 298 K, 1 bar for 15/85 feed (benchmarking Asset 1 logic), with ≥70% selectivity retained at 20% RH.
    – Dynamic CO2 working capacity ≥ 1.5 mmol g−1 between adsorption (0.15 bar CO2) and desorption (0.01 bar) at 298 K.
    – ≥50 cycles with <10% loss in breakthrough capacity.

Step 5 — Regime B (aqueous heavy metals): speciation-coupled surface complexation + stability/leaching tests.
5.1 Water stability and leaching gate before adsorption claims:
  • Immerse MOF in DI water and synthetic wastewater (pH 5–8, 10 mM ionic strength) for 1, 7, 30 days; monitor PXRD, BET retention, Zr leaching (ICP-MS), and linker loss (TOC/LC-MS).
  • Go/no-go stability: Zr leaching < 1% of total Zr over 7 days; PXRD crystallinity retained; thiol content loss < 20%.
5.2 Speciation-aware adsorption design:
  • Target ions: Hg2+, Pb2+, Cd2+ as soft/borderline; competitors Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+; anions Cl−/SO42−/HCO3−.
  • Conduct batch isotherms and kinetics at controlled pH (5.5, 7.0, 8.0) and ionic strengths (1–100 mM NaCl). Include NOM proxy (humic acid) to assess fouling.
  • Model metal speciation in solution (e.g., hydroxo/chloro complexes) and fit uptake to a surface complexation model where binding sites are quantified from thiol assays (site density) and pH-dependent thiol deprotonation is included.
5.3 Mechanistic validation:
  • XPS S 2p shifts (S–Hg), Hg LIII-edge EXAFS where available to confirm inner-sphere Hg–S coordination; compare to Pb/Cd to quantify selectivity origin.
  • Regeneration: thiol-compatible elution (e.g., thiourea or mild chelator) vs pH swing; track thiol oxidation after cycles.
  • Go/no-go metrics (Regime B):
    – Distribution coefficient Kd(Hg) ≥ 10^5 mL g−1 at pH 7, 10 mM NaCl, with Ca/Mg present (1–5 mM).
    – Selectivity factor Hg/Ca ≥ 10^3 under the above conditions.
    – Capacity ≥ 200 mg Hg g−1 (or justified by site density) with ≥80% capacity retained after 5 adsorption/desorption cycles.

Step 6 — Regime C (dye/drug): transport gating and non-equilibrium uptake/release (not IAST).
6.1 Guest selection and conditions:
  • Dye: methylene blue (cationic) and methyl orange (anionic) to decouple electrostatics from size.
  • Drug: doxorubicin as a canonical cationic, π-stacking-capable payload.
  • Media: buffered aqueous solutions (pH 5.5 and 7.4) with physiologically relevant ionic strength.
6.2 Demonstrate that azobenzene switching changes *transport*:
  • Quantify uptake/release kinetics under dark vs irradiation (365–450 nm as appropriate), and at pH values that modulate framework/guest charge.
  • Fit to a gated diffusion model (effective diffusivity D_eff and/or permeability P as a function of switching state) rather than equilibrium-only models.
  • Measure pore accessibility changes by time-resolved uptake (stopped-flow UV–Vis) and, where possible, pulsed-field gradient NMR (guest diffusion) or QCM on thin films.
6.3 Go/no-go metrics (Regime C):
  • Demonstrate ≥3× change in apparent uptake rate constant (k_app) or D_eff between switched states at constant concentration.
  • Demonstrate reversible modulation over ≥10 light on/off cycles with <15% drift in kinetic response.
  • Maintain framework crystallinity and <1% Zr leaching in the delivery buffer over 72 h.

Step 7 — Integration logic (single platform, separate validation frameworks).
7.1 Use the same material library to identify compositions that satisfy Regime A metrics first (IAST-valid gas separation), then filter by Regime B stability/leaching gates, then test Regime C gating.
7.2 Explicitly avoid “orthogonal selectivity” claims unless the same composition passes the quantitative metrics in all three regimes; otherwise report a Pareto front (gas vs water stability vs gating amplitude) and identify best-in-class compositions for each application.

Step 8 — Risk controls and contingencies.
8.1 If azobenzene switching amplitude is too small in rigid UiO pores: move AzoBDC to a lower fraction (≤5%) and use it as a surface/defect-adjacent gate (more free volume), or fabricate a thin-film/particle-shell architecture where switching modulates entrance rather than internal cavities.
8.2 If thiol causes instability or excessive defectivity: reduce y, use BDC dilution, or switch to thioether (less oxidation-prone) while accepting lower Hg affinity; alternatively, confine thiols to post-synthetically modified defect sites to decouple them from the primary lattice.
8.3 If humidity collapses CO2 selectivity: decrease defect density (fewer strong H2O sites) and/or add hydrophobic linker fraction (e.g., methylated BDC) while tracking CO2 capacity/selectivity trade-offs.
Feasibility:
1) IAST scope is narrowed to where it is defensible and testable: multicomponent physisorption of CO2/N2/CH4 in rigid pores at equilibrium. This directly leverages the precedent that open/polar sites in robust MOFs yield high CO2 selectivity and that IAST can predict mixture behavior from high-quality single-component isotherms (Asset 1). By adding explicit isotherm models (DSL/Langmuir-Freundlich), model selection criteria, and uncertainty propagation, the proposal converts IAST from a rhetorical “unifier” into a quantified, falsifiable design-and-validation loop.

2) Heavy-metal capture is treated with correct controlling chemistry: aqueous uptake depends on speciation, hydration, thiol pKa/oxidation, and node stability—factors not parameterized by IAST. The revised plan therefore uses speciation-coupled surface complexation modeling, competitive-ion matrices, and direct coordination probes (XPS/EXAFS), aligning with established mechanisms for MOF-based toxic ion removal where defects/functional groups control selectivity and kinetics (Asset 2). The inclusion of stringent hydrolytic stability and leaching gates prevents over-interpretation of adsorption data from partially degraded solids.

3) Dye/drug behavior is recast as gated transport (kinetics), not equilibrium selectivity: photoswitching and pH-triggered gating inherently introduce accessibility limits and time dependence that violate IAST assumptions. The plan explicitly measures switching extent and demonstrates functional gating by quantifying changes in uptake/release kinetics (≥3×), thereby meeting the reviewer requirement to show transport modulation “not just spectroscopy.” The use of composite/thin-film contingencies is consistent with established MOF-composite strategies for functional deployment and stability (Asset 3).

4) Engineering-resolution mapping connects synthesis knobs to structure to performance: linker ratios, modulator-controlled defects, thiol oxidation state, and azobenzene fraction are treated as independent variables; measurable descriptors (site density, defect density, PLD, switching amplitude, leaching) serve as intermediates; and each application has quantitative go/no-go metrics under defined operating conditions (RH, partial pressures, pH, ionic strength, competitors). This directly addresses the critique about missing topology/pore targets, unclear open-site generation without sacrificing water stability, and lack of success criteria.

5) The proposal remains coherent with the original concept chain (dual-function mixed-linker Zr6 MOF; thiol sites; azobenzene switching; competitive adsorption modeling) while preventing conceptual overreach by using the right physical chemistry model for each regime and by requiring experimental validation that matches each model’s assumptions.
Critique: Methodologically, the plan is unusually well-engineered for a mixed-linker UiO platform: it specifies a synthesis DoE, quantifies key descriptors (linker incorporation, defects, thiol state, switching extent), and aligns each application with a model whose assumptions are appropriate (IAST only for equilibrium multigas; surface complexation for ions; gated transport for delivery). Score deductions arise from several depth/feasibility gaps that remain: (1) Mixed-linker co-incorporation of thiol dicarboxylates plus AzoBDC in fcu UiO-66 at the proposed fractions is nontrivial; the proposal does not define a quantitative compositional “phase map” (single-phase window vs segregation) nor a crystallographic/total-scattering plan (e.g., PDF) to confirm defect chemistry and linker distribution beyond digestion NMR. (2) Defect engineering is treated as a scalar “0–10%” target, but missing-linker vs missing-cluster defects have qualitatively different impacts on PLD, water uptake, acidity, and stability; current proxies (TGA, water hysteresis, acid titration) may not resolve defect type, risking mechanistic ambiguity in both humidity-affected CO2 adsorption and metal binding. (3) The heavy-metal model is directionally correct, but it under-specifies the surface complexation formalism (e.g., site types, charge balance, electrostatics term) and how parameters will be identifiable given simultaneous variables (speciation, pH, ionic strength, NOM, thiol oxidation, and possible Zr–OH binding). (4) The azobenzene gating claim is plausible but precarious in UiO pores: cis/trans changes may be sterically suppressed and/or dominated by surface/defect-localized AzoBDC; the plan includes contingencies, but the primary pathway lacks an a priori geometric feasibility check (e.g., linker conformer/rotamer accessibility within fcu cages, predicted PLD modulation magnitude) to justify the ≥3× kinetic modulation metric. Overall, the logic is coherent and the concept-chain integration is strong, but several key mechanistic discriminants (defect type, linker spatial distribution, switching feasibility in-cage) are not yet pinned down at the level needed to fully de-risk interpretation.

Hypothesis: Embedding L-proline as a chiral, monodentate/bidentate secondary coordinating modulator inside a tetraphenylethylene (TPE)-based single-walled metal-organic nanotube will enforce weak, yet directionally biased pi-stacking among TPE panels, producing a synergistic effect between (i) stabilized single-walled tube formation (defect-suppressed, uniform channels) and (ii) increased local concentration/activation of epoxide and CO2 at Ni open sites via proline’s H-bonding and Lewis base functionality. This dual stabilization + microenvironment tuning will raise intrinsic turnover frequency (TOF per accessible Ni site) while enabling hierarchical assembly (bundles/flowers) that improves mass transport without collapsing the single-walled tube topology. Methodological adaptation: replace conventional monotopic modulators (e.g., acetate/benzoate) with L-proline (and N-protected derivatives) as a stereochemically programmed modulator/guest that simultaneously (a) coordinates transiently to Ni during solvothermal growth to bias tube topology and (b) remains in the channel as a removable/partially retained co-catalytic lining to tune substrate diffusion and transition-state stabilization.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a Ni-based TPE-derived multitopic ligand system that is known to form single-walled nanotubes (benchmark against Ni–TCPE-type chemistry) and define two synthetic baselines: (A) no modulator and (B) standard monotopic modulator (acetate or benzoate) to reproduce tube vs non-tube outcomes.
1.2 Prepare a modulator library: L-proline, D-proline (stereochemical control), N-Boc-L-proline (reduced metal binding; preserves H-bond donor/acceptor pattern differently), and proline methyl ester (suppresses carboxylate coordination). These enable separating coordination effects from purely supramolecular effects.
1.3 Define a catalytic probe reaction identical to Asset 1 (CO2 cycloaddition to epoxides) with standardized epoxide set (epichlorohydrin + one bulky epoxide) to diagnose diffusion vs intrinsic-site effects.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Proline-programmed solvothermal assembly: conduct solvothermal syntheses where proline is introduced as (i) a coordination modulator (0–50 mol% vs metal), and (ii) a post-synthetic channel guest via solvent exchange to decouple growth effects from microenvironment effects.
2.2 Topology steering via weak pi-stacking control: tune solvent polarity (DMF/MeCN/EtOH ratios) and ionic strength to favor offset TPE pi-stacking. Hypothesis-driven control variable: proline enforces a specific offset/rotation between TPE panels through stereochemically biased H-bonding to linker substituents, yielding uniform tube circumference and suppressing inter-tube fusion.
2.3 Hierarchical structuring without pyrolysis: induce controlled nanotube bundling into flower-like superstructures (analogy to Asset 2’s hierarchical benefit but kept as coordination polymer) by slow antisolvent vapor diffusion (e.g., Et2O into DMF) in the presence of low equivalents of proline zwitterions as inter-tube “soft glue” (electrostatic + H-bond) while maintaining weak pi-stacking between adjacent tubes. Implement a two-stage protocol: (Stage I) grow discrete single-walled nanotubes; (Stage II) assemble hierarchically via antisolvent and proline-mediated bridging.
2.4 Active-site accessibility engineering: partially remove proline by thermal/vacuum activation to create a mixed lining state (fraction retained) and quantify retained proline via elemental analysis and ssNMR; target an optimum where proline enhances CO2/epoxide preorganization but does not block Ni sites.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structure confirmation: use single-crystal XRD when possible; otherwise combine PXRD/Rietveld refinement with PDF analysis to confirm single-walled tube metrics (outer/inner diameters) and to distinguish from alternative topologies (e.g., thicker-walled or interpenetrated structures). Use TEM/cryo-TEM for direct tube diameter and wall count; AFM for bundle thickness.
3.2 Mechanism of weak pi-stacking modulation: quantify TPE stacking geometry using solid-state UV–vis/fluorescence (aggregation-induced emission changes), variable-temperature PXRD (stacking sensitivity), and ssNMR (chemical shift anisotropy changes). Compare L- vs D-proline to prove stereochemically biased packing. Complement with periodic DFT/MD to compute stacking energies and proline-mediated H-bond networks.
3.3 Catalytic metrics with site normalization: measure TOF normalized to accessible Ni sites using CO chemisorption or in situ IR probe binding (and/or acid titration where appropriate). Perform kinetic isotope/competition tests (small vs bulky epoxide) to separate diffusion limitation from intrinsic activation.
3.4 Synergy quantification: establish a factorial design with variables (tube topology: yes/no), (proline present: yes/no; retained fraction), (hierarchical assembly: discrete/bundled). Synergistic effect is validated if TOF increase exceeds the additive contributions of (i) topology-only improvement and (ii) proline-only microenvironment effects. Use Thiele modulus/Weisz–Prater analysis to verify reduced internal diffusion resistance in hierarchical samples.
3.5 Stability and recyclability: perform 20-cycle tests (as in Asset 1) and leaching analysis (ICP-MS). Track single-walled integrity post-catalysis by PXRD/TEM and monitor single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) or quasi-SCSC behavior during activation/guest exchange by in situ PXRD.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 demonstrates that single-walled metal-organic nanotube channel architecture and site distribution can deliver very high TON/TOF for CO2–epoxide cycloaddition, implying that further control of channel microenvironment and defect density is a direct lever on TOF. L-proline is a well-characterized chiral, bifunctional molecule (carboxylate + secondary amine) capable of transient metal coordination, H-bonding, and zwitterionic electrostatics—features that can bias supramolecular packing and stabilize specific assemblies.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Coordination modulation is an established MOF method to control crystal growth and topology, but the adaptation here is using an amino acid modulator to simultaneously (a) program weak pi-stacking among aromatic panels (TPE) and (b) act as a removable/partially retained channel lining that provides cooperative activation (Lewis base/H-bond) near Ni Lewis acidic sites. This is a molecule-level, rationally designed intervention rather than a generic additive.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with standard monotopic modulators, proline introduces stereochemically defined, multipoint interactions that can reduce polydispersity and suppress tube-wall thickening/fusion, yielding more uniform single-walled nanotubes with higher accessible site density. Compared with simply making hierarchical structures (Asset 2), the proposal preserves the intact coordination polymer (no pyrolysis), enabling true site-defined catalysis while still leveraging hierarchical assembly to reduce transport limitations—thereby improving intrinsic TOF and apparent rates simultaneously, with mechanistic separability via L/D and protected-derivative controls.
Critique: This is a technically ambitious and unusually well-articulated proposal with strong command of MOF/nanotube chemistry, catalysis normalization, and hierarchical transport analysis. The engineering plan is detailed, multi-pronged, and largely executable with current techniques (PXRD/PDF, ssNMR, cryo-TEM, site-normalized kinetics). The central hypothesis—that proline can weakly bias TPE pi-stacking while acting as a bifunctional microenvironmental co-catalyst—is logically coherent and supported by appropriate controls (L/D, Boc, ester). However, some deductions are warranted. First, the causal link between stereochemical bias of proline and long-range, uniform pi-stacking among TPE panels remains speculative and may be overdetermined relative to the weak interaction energies involved. Second, the proposal risks conflating growth modulation effects with post-synthetic guest effects despite the stated decoupling strategy; in practice, disentangling these may be experimentally nontrivial. Third, while hierarchical assembly is carefully positioned as non-destructive, the structural integrity of single-walled tubes under antisolvent-driven bundling is not fully de-risked. These issues do not undermine feasibility but temper confidence in the universality of the claimed synergistic effect.

Hypothesis: Deliverable gas capacity in MOFs is governed by the pressure-dependent accessibility and depopulation of *ensembles of adsorption microstates*, rather than by total pore volume or static pore geometry alone. Specifically, we posit that deliverable capacity emerges from the topological organization of energetically heterogeneous binding sites under equilibrium thermodynamics, where many-body packing constraints and framework flexibility modulate which subsets of sites are populated at storage pressure and reversibly depopulated at delivery pressure. We hypothesize that a binding-site–centric graph representation—constructed from adsorption free-energy landscapes generated with a single, validated interaction model and evaluated across multiple framework conformational states—will capture this microstate accessibility more faithfully than geometry-only or rigid-structure descriptors. In this formulation, graph edges do not primarily encode kinetic diffusion barriers, but instead encode *equilibrium cooperativity and exclusion effects* (e.g., steric crowding, overlap of adsorption basins, pressure-induced site merging) that determine the density of accessible adsorption states. A physics-regularized graph neural network (GNN), trained to predict pressure-dependent site occupancy distributions across framework states, will therefore outperform existing ML approaches in predicting deliverable capacity and enable chemically interpretable design rules that remain valid beyond a single MOF family.
Plan:
Step 1: Unified physical model and system selection.
1.1 Interaction model unification: Adopt a single, transferable force-field framework for both adsorption potential mapping and GCMC labeling (e.g., TraPPE for CH4/N2 with UFF-derived framework parameters, validated against experimental Henry constants and isosteric heats for benchmark MOFs). To quantify model uncertainty, generate an ensemble of interaction parameterizations (±5–10% ε, σ scaling) and propagate uncertainty into site energies and labels.
1.2 MOF set spanning rigidity and flexibility: Include (i) rigid isoreticular UiO-family MOFs (UiO-66/67/68 with –NH2, –NO2, –CF3, –CN linkers) as a controlled baseline, and (ii) canonical flexible/breathing MOFs (e.g., MIL-53(Al), DUT-49, ZIF-8) where pressure-induced pore deformation or gating is experimentally established (cf. Asset 1). This explicitly tests when topology-only descriptions fail.

Step 2: Adsorption microstate and graph construction.
2.1 Adsorption free-energy landscapes: Compute 3D adsorption free-energy maps for CH4 and N2 via Widom insertion and biased sampling using the unified force field on each framework state. Identify local minima (binding basins), saddle regions, and basin overlaps.
2.2 Binding-site graph definition: Nodes correspond to binding basins annotated with free energy (ΔG_site), basin volume, site type (metal-cluster, linker, window), and local curvature. Edges do not represent diffusion rates; instead, they encode equilibrium coupling metrics: (i) basin overlap volume, (ii) mutual exclusion penalties derived from overlap of adsorption probability densities, and (iii) pressure-induced basin coalescence. These features quantify many-body packing constraints rather than kinetics.

Step 3: Explicit treatment of framework flexibility.
3.1 Multi-state representation: For flexible MOFs, generate an ensemble of framework conformations via MD under osmotic ensemble conditions or pressure-biased simulations. Construct a state-graph where each node represents a framework state with its own binding-site graph; edges between states encode free-energy penalties for structural transitions.
3.2 Label generation: Perform GCMC on each framework state to obtain pressure-dependent occupancies; compute deliverable capacity by Boltzmann-weighted averaging over states at P_high and P_low, ensuring thermodynamic consistency.

Step 4: GNN architecture and learning objectives.
4.1 Architecture: Implement a hierarchical GNN where (i) intra-state message passing learns site occupancy distributions under many-body constraints, and (ii) inter-state aggregation learns framework-state population shifts with pressure.
4.2 Physics-regularized loss: Replace hard monotonic constraints with site-type-conditioned priors. Regularize node embeddings against independently computed Henry constants and isosteric heats, and penalize violations of thermodynamic consistency (e.g., nonphysical occupancy ordering with pressure).
4.3 Training and generalization tests: Pre-register leave-one-functional-group-out, leave-one-MOF-family-out, and leave-one-flexible-system-out cross-validation. Track uncertainty-aware prediction intervals from the force-field ensemble.

Step 5: Validation, benchmarking, and inverse design.
5.1 Experimental validation: Synthesize top-ranked candidates from both rigid and flexible classes. Measure CH4/N2 isotherms, deliverable capacities, and variable-temperature sorption to separate enthalpic vs entropic contributions.
5.2 Ablation and benchmarking: Systematically remove edge (cooperativity) features, flexibility/state information, and site-type annotations to demonstrate when binding-site connectivity and framework breathing control performance. Benchmark against pore-volume descriptors and persistent-homology-based ML models (cf. Asset 2).
5.3 Inverse design with constraints: Limit inverse design to regions of latent space supported by training uncertainty bounds; propose chemically realizable linker modifications or window expansions and validate at least one out-of-family MOF experimentally.
Feasibility: This revised framework directly addresses reviewer concerns by enforcing strict physics–model alignment and explicitly distinguishing equilibrium thermodynamics from kinetics. Using a single validated interaction model for both site identification and GCMC labeling eliminates circularity. Reframing graph edges as equilibrium cooperativity and exclusion metrics, rather than diffusion barriers, aligns the representation with the fact that deliverable capacity is typically governed by thermodynamic site accessibility. Flexibility is no longer implicit: multiple framework states are explicitly sampled, labeled, and learned, with validation on canonical breathing MOFs supported by prior high-pressure and sorption studies (Asset 1). Hard monotonic chemistry constraints are replaced with site-type-conditioned priors and thermodynamic regularization tied to Henry constants and heats of adsorption, avoiding nonphysical bias. Finally, pre-registered generalization tests and uncertainty-aware inverse design ensure that claimed predictive and design advantages extend beyond a single MOF family, strengthening the case for both mechanistic insight and practical impact.
Critique: The proposal is technically ambitious and generally well-structured, with a coherent mechanistic thesis: deliverable capacity emerges from pressure-dependent population/depopulation of heterogeneous site ensembles under many-body constraints and flexibility. The strongest elements are (i) explicit separation of equilibrium thermodynamics from kinetics, (ii) multi-state treatment for flexible MOFs with Boltzmann weighting, and (iii) pre-registered generalization tests/ablations. However, several core constructs are under-specified in ways that risk irreproducibility and confounding: (1) the mapping from 3D free-energy fields to discrete “basins” (minima/saddles) lacks a defined algorithm, resolution criteria, and stability across conformations; basin identification is notoriously sensitive to grid spacing, sampling noise, and choice of collective variables. (2) The proposed edge features (overlap volume, mutual exclusion penalties, basin coalescence) are not rigorously derived from a stated statistical-mechanical model; without a clear correspondence to an approximate occupancy model (e.g., lattice gas, cluster expansion, Mayer-f function graph), the GNN may learn dataset-specific correlations rather than the claimed transferable physics. (3) The force-field “unification” (TraPPE + UFF-derived framework) is plausible for CH4/N2 but is not reliably transferable across open-metal sites, polar functional groups, and flexible frameworks; ±5–10% scaling is a weak uncertainty model that may not capture systematic errors (electrostatics, polarization, framework partial charges, flexibility-induced parameter breakdown). (4) For flexible MOFs, the plan to generate osmotic-ensemble states and then perform per-state GCMC with Boltzmann weighting is directionally correct, but the thermodynamic stitching is delicate; the proposal does not specify how the adsorption-induced stress and host free energies are computed consistently (risk of double counting or missing host-guest coupling), especially for strongly breathing materials (DUT-49, MIL-53). Overall, the logic is strong but would benefit from a tighter derivation linking graph quantities to equilibrium occupancy and deliverable capacity, and a more defensible uncertainty/validation strategy for the interaction model across diverse chemistries.

Hypothesis: Embedding X60(TFSI)2 as a confined ion-pair dopant inside the mesochannels of metallated PCN-224 will generate a verifiable mixed electronic/ionic conductor only if (a) the X60/X60•+ redox couple is thermodynamically capable of oxidizing the porphyrin π-manifold in the MOF (rather than being quenched at the Fe/Co center or at the Zr6 node), and (b) TFSI− exhibits measurable anion mobility under a controlled, explicitly defined level of solvent/electrolyte uptake without dopant leaching or pore collapse. Mechanistically, we posit a two-network transport model: (1) Electronic network: partial outer-sphere electron transfer from PCN-224(M)-porphyrin to X60(TFSI)2 produces a population of porphyrin π-radical cations (Por•+) that can hop between proximate porphyrins (through-space/through-bond via the rigid TCPP arrangement), while X60 remains as a counter-cationic redox buffer that stabilizes Por•+ and suppresses back-electron transfer. The intended charge-compensation locus is the porphyrin π-system (Por → Por•+), not the axial metal center; Fe(III) and Co(III) are used only after pre-validating that their redox states do not serve as dominant electron sinks (go/no-go: Por•+ yield per dopant ≥ 0.2 by spin quantification). (2) Ionic network: confined TFSI− anions provide local electroneutrality and enable ionic polarization/charge screening, but only when a small, quantified amount of sorbed solvent/electrolyte raises the effective dielectric constant and reduces ion-pair binding energy. We therefore hypothesize an optimum ‘wet-but-not-swollen’ state (defined by gravimetric sorption and in situ lattice parameter tracking) where anion mobility increases (measurable ionic transference number) while mesoporosity retention and dopant immobilization remain high. Under these validated transport conditions, oxidation catalysis rates will increase because (i) higher steady-state Por•+ (or metal–oxo equivalent) density lowers the charge-transfer resistance and (ii) faster anion rearrangement reduces local charge buildup at catalytic sites, improving Faradaic efficiency. We will test this in one stability-validated catalytic window: electrocatalytic oxygen evolution (OER) in near-neutral buffered electrolyte where porphyrinic frameworks and Zr6 nodes are substantially more stable than in strongly alkaline media, allowing operando correlation of carrier density (EPR/UV–vis–NIR/XAS), transport (Hebb–Wagner/EIS), and activity without confounding demetallation/oxidative linker destruction.
Plan:
Step 0 (Front-loaded pre-validation): Redox alignment + explicit spectroscopic predictions (mandatory).
0.1 Build a redox-level alignment table (all potentials reported vs Fc/Fc+ and converted to NHE where needed):
  - Measure oxidation potentials of (i) H2TCPP linker, (ii) PCN-224 (free-base), and (iii) PCN-224(M) (M = Fe, Co) as thin films on FTO/GC using non-aqueous electrolyte (e.g., 0.1 M TBAPF6 in MeCN) by CV/DPV. Extract E1/2(Por/Por•+) and (if present) metal-centered couples.
  - Measure X60/X60•+ (and/or X60•+/X60•2+ if accessible) under identical conditions (same solvent/electrolyte, same reference) to avoid systematic offsets.
  - Define a doping driving force ΔE = Eox(Por/Por•+) − Ered(X60/X60•+) and set a quantitative criterion for viable p-doping: ΔE ≥ +0.10–0.20 V.
0.2 Define charge-compensation locus and expected signatures (pre-registered predictions):
  - If porphyrin-centered doping occurs: UV–vis–NIR should show attenuated Soret band plus emergent NIR polaron/Por•+ absorption; EPR should show an organic radical signal (g ~ 2.002–2.004) with intensity scaling with dopant loading; for Fe/Co variants, deconvolute metal signals using frequency/temperature dependence.
  - If metal-centered trapping dominates: expect changes in XPS/XAS at Fe/Co edges and weaker/absent Por•+ NIR features; treat this as a failure mode.
0.3 Quantify radical yield per dopant (go/no-go metric):
  - Perform spin counting by quantitative EPR (calibrated standard) on a loading series (0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.50 X60 per porphyrin). Require ≥0.2 spins per X60 at the optimum loading window to proceed to catalysis.

Step 1: Host framework construction with stability and redox control.
1.1 Synthesize PCN-224 with high crystallinity; activate via solvent exchange (DMF → acetone/MeOH) and vacuum activation. Confirm structure by PXRD and porosity by N2 sorption.
1.2 Post-synthetic metallation (two-track to manage redox traps):
  - Track A (primary): Co(II) insertion followed by controlled oxidation to Co(III) only after doping validation; Co offers cleaner porphyrin-centered spectroscopy relative to Fe in many cases.
  - Track B (secondary): Fe insertion for comparison; employ Mössbauer/XAS to monitor Fe valence/spin-state and identify electron-trapping.
1.3 Establish a degradation/demetallation diagnostic baseline (before doping): soak PCN-224(M) in the intended buffered electrolyte for 24–72 h; check PXRD, UV–vis diffuse reflectance, ICP of supernatant, and porosity.

Step 2: Architected X60(TFSI)2 confinement with explicit anti-leaching design criteria.
2.1 Infiltration solvent design (dielectric + swelling control):
  - Use a binary solvent system that dissolves X60(TFSI)2 yet minimizes framework swelling: chlorobenzene:acetonitrile (v/v tuned via preliminary swelling screening). Target minimal PXRD peak shift (<0.2% d-spacing change) during solvent exposure.
2.2 Doping protocol (incipient wetness with loading ceiling):
  - Load X60(TFSI)2 at 0.02–0.20 equivalents per porphyrin as the primary window; avoid >0.20 unless porosity and diffusion metrics remain acceptable.
  - Anneal 60–80 °C under mild vacuum to remove free solvent while retaining confined ion pairs.
2.3 Two spatial architectures (to separate transport vs blocking):
  - Uniform loading: slow diffusion infiltration (hours) followed by solvent removal.
  - Shell-enriched gradient: short infiltration (minutes) + rapid solvent stripping; intended to create an electronically conductive shell while preserving internal pore volume.
2.4 Confinement verification and quantitative failure checks:
  - N2 sorption: go/no-go BET/mesopore retention ≥70% of undoped PCN-224(M).
  - TGA + elemental analysis to quantify X60/TFSI content.
  - Solid-state NMR (19F) and XPS (F 1s/S 2p) to confirm TFSI presence.
  - TOF-SIMS depth profiling to validate spatial distribution and post-test migration.

Step 3 (Mandatory): Separate and quantify ionic vs electronic transport, tied to controlled uptake.
3.1 Define “operating uptake states” by sorption isotherms:
  - Measure gravimetric uptake of (i) water vapor and (ii) buffered electrolyte vapor/aerosol surrogate if feasible; define three states: dry (≤0.5 wt%), intermediate (1–5 wt%), and wet (5–15 wt%).
  - Monitor structural response with in situ PXRD during uptake to flag swelling thresholds.
3.2 Electronic conductivity (σe) under each uptake state:
  - Four-probe on pressed pellets and thin films (to avoid grain-boundary artifacts). Target: ≥10× increase vs undoped PCN-224(M) at intermediate uptake.
3.3 Ionic conductivity and transference (σion, tion) using blocking-electrode methods:
  - AC impedance with ion-blocking electrodes (e.g., Au) to extract σion; complement with DC polarization / Hebb–Wagner (ion-blocking/electron-blocking configurations) to obtain tion and te.
  - Correlate σion with uptake and with dopant loading; confirm that σion rises at intermediate uptake without concurrent dopant loss (ICP of soak solutions; F/S quantification in electrolyte).
3.4 Leaching/migration stress test (explicit failure mode control):
  - Soak doped samples in the buffered electrolyte at open circuit and under bias; quantify leached X60/TFSI and metal by LC/UV (X60), ion chromatography (TFSI−), and ICP-MS (Fe/Co/Zr). Go/no-go: ≤5% dopant loss and ≤1% metal loss over 24 h.

Step 4: Single, stability-validated catalytic test-bed + operando correlation (mandatory).
4.1 Primary reaction: OER in near-neutral buffer (e.g., borate or phosphate, pH ~7–9) using immobilized MOF films on conductive substrates.
  - Rationale: avoids harsh alkaline conditions that accelerate porphyrin oxidation/demetallation; enables clearer linkage between carrier density and catalytic current.
4.2 Film architecture and mass-transport control:
  - Prepare reproducible MOF films (doctor blade/electrophoretic deposition) with identical mass loading; confirm electrochemically active surface area proxies and film thickness.
4.3 Operando/near-operando mechanistic readouts synchronized to rate:
  - Operando UV–vis–NIR (reflectance mode) during potential steps to track Por•+ population vs applied bias.
  - Operando EPR (if feasible) or quasi-operando freeze-quench EPR to quantify radical density under turnover.
  - XAS (Co/Fe K-edge) pre/post and at selected potentials to confirm whether the metal center changes valence (and whether this correlates with activity).
  - EIS under catalytic potentials to extract charge-transfer resistance (Rct); require that Rct decreases in proportion to σe and Por•+ density.
4.4 Performance metrics and attribution logic:
  - Compare: undoped PCN-224(M), doped PCN-224(M) uniform, doped gradient, physical mixture with free X60(TFSI)2, and polypyrrole-in-PCN-224 benchmark.
  - Report: onset potential (defined current), Tafel slope, Faradaic efficiency (O2 quantification), stability (chronoamperometry), and turnover frequency normalized per metalloporphyrin.
  - Attribution criterion: activity enhancement must track (i) increased σe and/or Por•+ density and (ii) decreased Rct, while leaching remains below thresholds; otherwise classify as surface/hydrophobicity effect and pivot.

Go/No-Go Criteria (explicit):
G1 Porosity retention after doping: ≥70% BET and preserved mesopore signature.
G2 Electronic conductivity gain: ≥1 order of magnitude at intermediate uptake state.
G3 Mixed conduction proof: tion between 0.05–0.5 under intermediate uptake (non-zero ionic contribution) with stable σe.
G4 Chemical stability: ≤5% X60/TFSI loss and ≤1% Fe/Co loss after 24 h soak + ≤5% loss after electrolysis.
G5 Mechanistic correlation: operando spectroscopy shows Por•+ (or defined carrier) density correlates with current and Rct across loading series.

Contingency pivots (pre-defined):
- If ΔE is insufficient for porphyrin oxidation or Por•+ yield is low: switch to a more oxidizing confined dopant (same confinement strategy) or reduce metallation redox traps by using free-base PCN-224 for transport validation first.
- If σion is negligible without excessive uptake/swelling: operate under controlled humidity/solvent co-adsorption to reach intermediate uptake, or redesign to introduce localized polar sites (minimal linker functionalization) while maintaining hydrophobicity.
- If Fe/Co act as dominant traps: prioritize metal-free or Co-only systems and re-introduce metal catalysis only after transport is validated.
Feasibility:
This revision directly addresses the reviewers’ two main uncertainties by making the mixed-conduction mechanism conditional on quantifiable thermodynamics and transport metrics prior to catalysis.

1) Electronic transport feasibility (thermodynamic and locus-validated): The plan explicitly measures, on the same reference scale and in the same medium, (i) Por/Por•+ oxidation potentials in the MOF film and (ii) the X60 redox couple, producing a redox alignment table that determines whether p-doping is thermodynamically allowed (ΔE threshold). The charge-compensation locus is explicitly defined as porphyrin-centered; competing metal-centered redox trapping is treated as a measurable failure mode using EPR spin counting, UV–vis–NIR polaron bands, and Fe/Co XAS/XPS. The required dopant-to-radical yield (≥0.2) and ≥10× σe improvement provide pre-catalysis evidence of a percolative electronic network rather than localized, quenched charge.

2) Ionic transport feasibility (anion mobility under controlled uptake, not hand-waving): Rather than assuming TFSI− mobility in a low-dielectric mesochannel, the proposal defines discrete uptake states via sorption and tests ionic transference directly with blocking-electrode EIS and Hebb–Wagner polarization. This design explicitly anticipates that some solvent/electrolyte uptake is necessary to reduce ion-pair binding, while simultaneously guarding against swelling and leaching with in situ PXRD thresholds and strict dopant/metal loss limits. The result is a falsifiable claim: measurable tion in an intermediate uptake window without structural compromise.

3) Sharpened catalytic test-bed and stability window: The proposal narrows to a single primary reaction—OER in near-neutral buffered electrolyte—to reduce confounding degradation pathways associated with strongly alkaline OER. A dedicated diagnostic plan (ICP leaching, PXRD/porosity retention, metal-edge XAS) is integrated to distinguish true mixed-conduction-driven rate enhancement from dopant migration, surface deposition, or hydrophobicity-only effects.

4) Mechanism-to-performance causality: By synchronizing operando (or quasi-operando) carrier-density readouts (EPR/UV–vis–NIR) with EIS-derived Rct and catalytic current across a dopant loading series and architecture variants (uniform vs gradient), the proposal can attribute improved activity to increased charge-carrier density and reduced charge-transfer resistance, or else reject the mechanism. This is reinforced by direct comparisons to physical mixtures and polymer-filled PCN-224, aligning with literature that polymer infiltration boosts conductivity but risks pore blocking—here tested against explicit porosity and diffusion preservation criteria.
Critique: Methodologically, the program is unusually well-resolved for a MOF-doping proposal: it pre-registers spectroscopic signatures, defines quantitative go/no-go thresholds (spin yield, porosity retention, σe gain, tion window, leaching limits), and includes appropriate controls (physical mixture, polymer benchmark, gradient vs uniform loading). The main scientific risk is the central, unproven assumption that a confined dicationic redox couple (X60(TFSI)2) will (i) remain sufficiently immobilized yet (ii) still enable outer-sphere oxidation of the porphyrin π-manifold at meaningful yield inside PCN-224 mesochannels; ion pairing and local dielectric in a mostly hydrophobic channel can strongly suppress effective redox activity and apparent ΔE relative to solution CV. The proposal partially mitigates this by defining uptake states, but it does not yet specify how the redox alignment measured in MeCN/TBAPF6 translates to the intended near-neutral aqueous-buffer operating environment (interfacial potential drops, junction potentials, and solvent-dependent reorganization energies could decouple ΔE from in-framework ET). Second, the transport model treats TFSI− mobility as beneficial for screening, yet TFSI− is typically weakly coordinating but can be kinetically sluggish in confined, low-polarity pores; demonstrating a stable tion in 0.05–0.5 while also meeting ≤5% dopant loss under bias is ambitious. Finally, the catalytic attribution remains vulnerable to an alternative explanation: X60(TFSI)2 could alter wettability/film microstructure and apparent OER kinetics without genuine bulk mixed conduction; the current control set helps, but a stricter decoupling of surface vs bulk effects is needed (e.g., thickness dependence, through-plane vs in-plane conductivity under operando hydration).

Hypothesis: Humidity-induced water pore filling in flexible/open-metal-site MOFs can be converted from a performance liability into a controllable “hydric gate” for gas separation and storage if the framework is methodologically adapted to include (i) spatially diluted water-nucleation sites and (ii) hydrophobic constrictions that delay percolating H-bond networks. Specifically, we hypothesize that engineering a mixed-node NU-1500-type topology with partial capping of Cr3+ open sites (to suppress early chain formation) plus perfluoro-aryl ‘pore-lining’ at the channel–pore junction will shift the water adsorption step to higher RH, prevent continuous water wires that cause pore filling, and preserve dry-gas uptake/selectivity under humid feeds. Mechanistically, dilution/capping reduces the density of strong primary adsorption enthalpy sites that seed 1D water chains; hydrophobic constrictions raise the free-energy barrier for hydrogen-bond network propagation into larger pores, thereby preventing capillary-like filling. In situ diffuse-reflectance IR (DRIFTS) with isotopic H2O/D2O will directly resolve the transition from metal-bound OH to chain-like water to liquid-like pore filling, enabling a quantitative structure–hydration–separation relationship.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select NU-1500-Cr as the mechanistic baseline (known RH-dependent sequence: metal-site saturation → chain growth → hexagonal pore filling) and define target gas pairs relevant to humid separations/storage (CO2/N2, CO2/CH4; optional H2/CO2) at 298–323 K.
1.2 Design two adapted variants (same topology, different water-network propensity):
  A) Site-diluted/capped NU-1500: post-synthetic partial capping of Cr3+ open sites with weakly coordinating, sterically small ligands (e.g., formate/acetate or neutral pyridine-N-oxide) to reduce water nucleation density without collapsing porosity.
  B) Junction-hydrophobized NU-1500: covalent linker modification introducing perfluoro-aryl substituents positioned at channel–pore junctions (synthetic linker swap or post-synthetic electrophilic aromatic substitution where compatible) to create hydrophobic constrictions.
1.3 Prepare controls: pristine NU-1500-Cr; a fully capped analogue (upper bound for water suppression); and a hydrophilic analogue (e.g., hydroxylated linker) to validate directionality.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Synthesis/functionalization:
  - Grow NU-1500-Cr (or closely isoreticular analogue) under solvothermal conditions; activate via solvent exchange and supercritical CO2 or carefully programmed thermal vacuum activation.
  - Implement controlled partial capping: expose activated MOF to dilute solutions/vapors of capping agents under anhydrous conditions; tune extent by time/activity; quantify via ICP/OES (metal), 1H/19F NMR of digested samples, and IR marker bands.
  - Implement hydrophobic constrictions: incorporate fluorinated linker (isoreticular design to preserve pore size distribution) or perform post-synthetic modification to install –C6F5/–CF3 groups oriented into the pore.
2.2 Humidity-programmed sorption + spectroscopy coupling (methodological adaptation):
  - Build a humidity-stepped gas dosing manifold coupled to in situ DRIFTS and a microbalance (gravimetric vapor sorption). Execute RH ramps (0–90% RH) at fixed T with simultaneous IR acquisition.
  - Use H2O/D2O isotopic substitution to separate framework OH/OD, metal-bound water, and H-bonded network signatures; deconvolute ν(OH)/ν(OD) envelopes to track chain formation vs liquid-like filling.
  - Add co-adsorption experiments: at each RH plateau, dose CO2 (and CH4/N2) while maintaining RH; record competitive uptake (dual-component gravimetry or volumetry) and IR bands (e.g., ν3(CO2), carbonate/bicarbonate signatures if formed).
2.3 Mechanistic modelling tightly coupled to experiments:
  - Parameterize water–framework interactions using DFT cluster models (Cr3+ site with/without cap; local fluorinated environment) to obtain binding energies and vibrational assignments.
  - Run MD/GCMC in a humidity-dependent grand canonical framework to predict percolation thresholds (water network connectivity) and pore filling onset; compute spatial distribution functions and H-bond network metrics that map onto IR observables.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Quantify the “hydric gate” shift: compare RH at which IR indicates chain formation (emergence of strongly H-bonded OH red-shifted band) and RH at which pore-filling (liquid-like broad band) occurs; correlate to gravimetric step positions.
3.2 Evaluate gas separation/storage performance under humidity:
  - Measure single-component and mixture breakthrough (packed-bed) for CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4 at controlled RH (e.g., 0, 20, 40, 60%); determine dynamic selectivity and working capacity.
  - Assess cyclic stability: RH swing + pressure swing cycles; monitor crystallinity (PXRD), porosity (N2 77 K), and IR fingerprints of functional groups.
3.3 Establish causality: link capping degree and fluorination density to (i) suppression of early metal-site hydration signatures, (ii) delayed water-network percolation, and (iii) retention of CO2 adsorption enthalpy/uptake under humid conditions. Use multivariate regression between IR-derived hydration-state fractions and separation metrics to produce a predictive descriptor set.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Prior NU-1500-Cr studies show a sequential RH mechanism where open Cr3+ sites nucleate water chains that propagate and culminate in pore filling, with IR capable of distinguishing hydration states; water-stable MOFs (e.g., DMOF-TM) still undergo reversible water-loading structural responses affecting separations. These directly support targeting the nucleation/percolation steps rather than only “water stability.”
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Open-metal-site dilution/capping is a chemically precise, MOF-native knob to reduce primary water binding enthalpy density; pore-lining fluorination is a rational supramolecular strategy to raise the free-energy barrier for H-bond network propagation without destroying crystallinity. The combined adaptation explicitly targets the mechanistic pathway (site saturation → chain growth → pore filling) rather than empirically screening MOFs.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to pristine NU-1500-Cr, the adapted materials are expected to (i) shift the water adsorption step to higher RH (delaying pore filling), (ii) maintain accessible pore volume for CO2/CH4 under humid feeds, and (iii) enable an IR-quantified hydration-state “gate function” that can be engineered. Compared to purely hydrophobic MOFs that lose CO2 affinity, site dilution preserves strong CO2 binding motifs while selectively weakening water’s percolation pathway. Compared to flexible MOFs where hysteresis complicates process design, controlling water-network formation reduces humidity-driven variability and improves predictability in pressure/temperature swing operation.
Critique: Mechanistic framing is strong and appropriately targets the known NU-1500-Cr sequence (metal hydration → chain growth → pore filling), with DRIFTS isotopic labeling well matched to disentangling hydration motifs. Engineering detail is generally high (controls, quantification methods, RH-programmed co-adsorption, breakthrough), but several key execution risks are under-specified: (i) “mixed-node NU-1500-type” and partial capping at Cr3+ sites could introduce heterogeneity, charge-balance changes, or ligand redistribution that alters CO2 affinity and/or framework flexibility; there is no explicit plan to map spatial distribution of capped vs uncapped sites or to verify that capping does not create new strong water nucleation sites or block transport. (ii) The fluorinated ‘junction’ placement is chemically plausible but not yet synthetically resolved—EAS/PSM feasibility on the NU-1500 linker chemistry, positional selectivity, and orientation into the pore are not demonstrated; fluorination may also reduce CO2 uptake via decreased quadrupole interactions or by reducing pore polarity more broadly than intended. (iii) The proposed MD/GCMC “humidity-dependent grand canonical framework” and percolation-threshold prediction are conceptually correct but need clearer, validated protocols (force-field transferability for Cr3+ OMS with partial capping; treatment of polarization/chemisorption; coupling to IR observables) to avoid post hoc fitting. Overall, the proposal is well grounded and creative, but would benefit from tighter structure–property causality tools and explicit go/no-go criteria to manage synthetic and modeling uncertainty.

Hypothesis: Orientationally programmed electrophoretic deposition (OP‑EPD) of high–aspect-ratio NU‑1000-type MOF platelets onto 3D carbon paper can be made quantitatively reliable by using a shear-dominant alignment regime (with optional magnetic assist only after susceptibility is measured) to achieve a target out-of-plane texture (Herman’s orientation factor f ≥ 0.6).
