This alignment will primarily create through-plane electronic percolation pathways ("c-axis highways") for Marcus-type redox hopping in oxidatively doped NU‑1000 films, lowering the through-plane film resistance (Rfilm,⊥) measured by EIS/4‑probe geometries. The proposal explicitly decouples electronic benefits from ionic transport: platelet alignment will be engineered to preserve (or improve) ionic access by enforcing inter-platelet mesoporosity via spacer/glue selection and wetting control; if ionic tortuosity increases, the mechanistic claim is constrained to electronic transport only. After conversion, ‘orientation retention’ is defined as (i) morphological texture retention (lamellae/platelet-stack alignment across thickness) and (ii) catalytic phase texture (any statistically significant preferred orientation of Ni2P nanocrystallites relative to the electrode normal). The conversion sequence (confined metal loading + shrinkage-managed carbonization + low-temperature phosphidation) is designed to preserve (i) even if (ii) is partial; the go/no-go criterion is that aligned-MOF electrodes yield measurably lower through-plane electronic resistivity and/or lower charge-transfer resistance (Rct) after conversion versus randomly oriented controls at identical loading and porosity. Mixed-linker ‘hopping enhancer’ chemistry is retained only if topology/habit and reversible oxidative doping are experimentally verified (PXRD + digestion NMR + GIWAXS texture + EIS-derived Dhopping); otherwise, the redox-hopping claim is restricted to a MOF-stage mechanistic validation rather than a required driver of final Ni2P@C kinetics.
Plan:
Step 0 — De-risking overview (explicit go/no-go gates)
G0.1 Alignment gate: demonstrate f ≥ 0.6 (GIWAXS/SAXS azimuthal integration) at film thickness 2–10 μm on carbon paper without cracking/delamination.
G0.2 Transport gate: show that alignment decreases through-plane electronic resistivity (ρ⊥) by ≥10× vs random, while ionic permeability (electrolyte uptake and symmetric-cell ionic resistance) is not degraded by >2×; otherwise constrain claims to electronic transport only.
G0.3 Texture inheritance gate: after conversion, demonstrate preserved morphological texture (cross-sectional SEM/TEM + tomography) and a statistically significant anisotropy difference (aligned-derived vs random-derived) in either electronic transport (ρ⊥/ρ∥) or EIS-extracted Rct at identical catalyst mass and porosity.

Step 1 — MOF platelet synthesis, charge programming, and mixed-linker verification
1.1 Platelet NU‑1000 analogue synthesis (baseline, no mixed-linker): synthesize Zr6O4(OH)4-based NU‑1000-type platelets using pyrene tetracarboxylate (H4TBAPy) under modulated solvothermal conditions tuned for high aspect ratio (e.g., benzoic/acetic acid modulator; low water activity; targeted lateral size 1–5 μm, thickness 50–200 nm). Quantify habit by SEM/TEM and AFM (thickness distribution).
1.2 Surface charge/adhesion: post-synthetically install phosphonate anchoring at node-termini using phenylphosphonic acid (PPA) or 4-carboxyphenylphosphonic acid under conditions that cap terminal –OH/H2O without collapsing pores. Quantify incorporation via P 2p XPS, ICP (P:Zr), and FTIR (P–O stretches). Target zeta potential ≤ −30 mV in chosen EPD solvent.
1.3 Optional mixed-linker ‘hopping enhancer’ (only if topology/habit survives): introduce 5–15 mol% electron-donating pyrene-derived tetratopic analogue (e.g., alkoxy/alkyl substituted) during synthesis.
   • Go/no-go: (i) PXRD matches NU‑1000 topology within peak shifts/broadening limits; (ii) digestion 1H NMR gives linker ratio within ±2 mol% of feed; (iii) platelet habit retained (aspect ratio within 20% of baseline).

Step 2 — Quantified alignment physics and OP‑EPD cell design
2.1 Alignment strategy selection (shear-first, magnetic optional):
   A) Shear-dominant alignment (primary): use a Couette or parallel-plate shear cell integrated with EPD electrodes.
      • Geometry: electrode gap 2–5 mm; working electrode = carbon paper (Toray-type) mounted as stationary plate; counter electrode = Pt mesh; shear imposed by a rotating inner cylinder (Couette) or oscillating plate.
      • Shear rates: start 200–2000 s−1 (viscosity-adjusted with 1–5 wt% PVP or PMMA-free viscosity modifiers that do not adsorb strongly), guided by rotational Peclet number Pe_r = (γ̇/Dr). For platelets with Dr ~ 0.1–10 s−1 (to be measured by DLS/rotational diffusion estimates), target Pe_r ≥ 10 for deterministic alignment.
      • Quantitative check: measure viscosity η and compute hydrodynamic aligning torque scaling τhydro ~ η γ̇ V (V = platelet volume). Confirm alignment kinetics by time-resolved SAXS (if available) or ex situ GIWAXS after defined shear times (e.g., 10, 30, 60 s).
   B) Magnetic alignment (optional assist, not assumed): only pursued after measuring magnetic susceptibility anisotropy Δχ of Co-doped platelets (SQUID/VSM). Required condition for feasibility is that magnetic energy Umag = (Δχ V B^2)/(2μ0) exceeds thermal energy by factor ≥5 (Umag ≥ 5kBT). If unmet at B ≤ 1 T (practical lab magnets), magnetic alignment is dropped.
2.2 OP‑EPD parameters (pulsed field to reduce polarization/cracking):
   • Solvent: MeCN or EtOH/MeCN mixtures with controlled ionic strength; add 0.1–0.5 mM TBAPF6 (or analogous) to stabilize current without collapsing double layer.
   • Field: 20–150 V cm−1 square-wave; duty cycle 20–40%; frequency 10–200 Hz; deposition time 30–300 s to reach 2–10 μm.
   • Temperature control: 20–25 °C to keep η constant (affects alignment).
   • Target: uniform mass loading (e.g., 0.3–1.0 mg cm−2) quantified gravimetrically and by ICP (Zr).
2.3 Orientation lock-in without pore occlusion:
   • Replace speculative “nanoglue” with two screened options and a rejection criterion:
     (i) Vapor-phase diacid crosslinking (e.g., oxalic/succinic vapor) targeting node-node bridging at sub-monolayer coverage.
     (ii) <3 wt% silica from TEOS vapor infiltration followed by low-temp (≤120 °C) condensation.
   • Go/no-go: N2 sorption (powder analogues) shows ≤15% BET loss; electrolyte uptake (Step 3) not reduced >20%.

Step 3 — Orientation metrics (in situ/ex situ) with explicit targets
3.1 GIWAXS/GIWAXS-azimuthal analysis on films: collect 2D patterns and compute Herman’s orientation factor f from azimuthal intensity of (00l) (MOF) or equivalent reflections.
   • Target: f ≥ 0.6 for aligned; f ≤ 0.2 for random.
3.2 2D SAXS (or USAXS) for mesoscale lamellae alignment: quantify anisotropy of scattering to confirm platelet-stack alignment (morphological texture), not only crystallographic.
3.3 Cross-sectional electron diffraction mapping: prepare FIB cross-sections; collect nano-beam electron diffraction (NBED) / SAED along thickness to map local orientation distribution and identify misorientation gradients.

Step 4 — Transport mechanism decoupling (electronic vs ionic)
4.1 Through-plane electronic conductivity/resistivity:
   • Build a through-plane test stack: Au-coated flat punch contacts on top of MOF film on carbon paper; apply defined pressure; measure I–V and extract ρ⊥. Compare to in-plane interdigitated electrode measurements (ρ∥) on insulating substrates with transferred films.
4.2 Redox-hopping validation (MOF-stage mechanistic test, not assumed to drive final catalyst):
   • Perform oxidative doping in TBAPF6/MeCN; quantify mixed-valency via CV and in situ UV–vis–NIR (polaron band).
   • EIS under controlled potentials to extract apparent Dhopping and compare aligned vs random (expect Dhopping,⊥ >> Dhopping,∥ if c-axis oriented, consistent with NU‑1000 anisotropy literature).
   • Deliverable: correlation between f and Rfilm,⊥ (and/or Dhopping,⊥).
4.3 Ionic permeability/wetting and tortuosity:
   • Electrolyte uptake: gravimetric uptake and contact-angle measurements in target aqueous electrolyte (e.g., 1 M KOH).
   • Symmetric-cell ionic resistance: assemble two identical MOF-coated carbon papers facing each other with separator and electrolyte; EIS to estimate effective ionic resistance/tortuosity independent of faradaic kinetics.
   • Decision rule: if ionic resistance increases >2× with alignment at same thickness/loading, claims are narrowed to electronic benefits and mitigation is pursued (increase inter-platelet mesoporosity via sacrificial spacer in Step 2.3).

Step 5 — Controlled conversion to Ni2P@C with shrinkage/sintering suppression and defined ‘retention’ metrics
5.1 Confined metal loading to avoid sintering:
   • Prefer incipient wetness infiltration using Ni(NO3)2 (±Co(NO3)2) in minimal solvent, targeting 5–15 wt% Ni relative to MOF-derived carbon yield.
   • Optionally pre-anchor Ni2+ via phosphonate sites (chelation) to reduce migration.
   • Verify spatial distribution pre-pyrolysis by STEM-EDS on microtomed sections.
5.2 Shrinkage-managed carbonization:
   • Two-step pyrolysis under Ar: 300–350 °C (1–2 h, slow ramp 1 °C min−1) to carbonize organics while preserving morphology; then 650–750 °C (0.5–1 h) to improve conductivity but limit platelet collapse. Only pursue 800–900 °C if morphology retention is verified at 750 °C.
   • Add sacrificial spacer option (screened): co-infiltrate a removable salt (e.g., NaCl nanoparticles) or polymer microspheres to template mesopores; remove post-carbonization by water wash. Go/no-go by SEM/TEM showing preserved inter-platelet voids.
5.3 Low-temperature phosphidation:
   • NaH2PO2 upstream in tube furnace; 300–350 °C for 1–2 h under Ar/H2 to form Ni2P while minimizing sintering.
5.4 Define and measure orientation retention:
   (i) Morphological retention: quantify lamellae alignment from cross-sectional SEM/TEM + 3D FIB-SEM tomography (orientation distribution of platelet-like features; target: aligned-derived maintains ≥70% of pre-pyrolysis texture parameter).
   (ii) Crystallographic texture (if present): 2D GI-XRD of Ni2P; compute texture coefficient differences vs random-derived. Not required for success if (i) and transport anisotropy persist.

Step 6 — Electrocatalysis with causality controls
6.1 Electrocatalytic testing (choose primary reaction to match catalyst):
   • HER/OER in 1 M KOH (consistent with Ni2P literature). Report η10, Tafel slope, TOF proxies, ECSA-normalized activity, and 50–100 h stability.
6.2 Operando-relevant EIS:
   • EIS at catalytic potentials to extract Rct and mass-transport elements; correlate Rct with (a) post-conversion ρ⊥ and (b) morphological texture parameter.
6.3 Mandatory control matrix (aligned vs random at each stage):
   • MOF films: aligned OP‑EPD vs random EPD vs solvothermal film (if feasible).
   • Converted catalysts: aligned-derived Ni2P@C vs random-derived Ni2P@C at identical Ni loading and carbon mass.
   • Spacer/glue control: with vs without spacer/glue at fixed f.
   • Mixed-linker control: only if Step 1.3 passes, otherwise omitted.

Deliverables and timelines (high-level)
D1 (Months 1–3): Achieve reproducible alignment (f targets) and quantify torque feasibility (Pe_r and/or Umag criterion).
D2 (Months 3–6): Electronic/ionic decoupling dataset (ρ⊥, ρ∥, uptake, symmetric-cell EIS) establishing what alignment improves.
D3 (Months 6–12): Post-conversion texture retention proof (tomography + GI-XRD) and aligned vs random performance delta in HER/OER with operando EIS linkage.
Feasibility:
1) Alignment physics is de-risked by making shear the primary alignment mechanism with explicit, measurable control parameters (cell geometry, γ̇ range) and a quantitative criterion (Pe_r ≥ 10) rather than assuming magnetic alignment. Magnetic alignment is treated as optional and gated by a SQUID/VSM-derived Δχ and an Umag/kBT threshold at practical B fields.

2) The electron-vs-ion transport critique is addressed by explicitly separating claims and measurements: (i) through-plane electronic resistivity/conductivity (ρ⊥) using dedicated geometries and (ii) ionic permeability/tortuosity using electrolyte uptake + symmetric-cell EIS. The project only asserts reduced “ionic blocking” if ionic metrics improve or remain comparable; otherwise, the mechanistic statement is constrained to electronic percolation improvements, preventing conflation.

3) Texture inheritance is redefined from a vague “crystallographic registry” to two measurable constructs: morphological texture retention (platelet/lamellae alignment across thickness) and any Ni2P crystallographic texture (2D GI-XRD). Because high-temperature steps can erase crystallographic texture, the conversion protocol is intentionally shrinkage-managed (≤750 °C unless proven safe) and sintering-suppressed (confined loading + low-T phosphidation + optional sacrificial spacers). Success is judged by a statistically significant aligned-derived vs random-derived anisotropy in transport/EIS and/or performance, not by peak ratios alone.

4) Mixed-linker doping and redox-hopping are retained but no longer a weak causal leap: topology/habit preservation is required by PXRD + digestion NMR + morphology metrics, and redox-hopping measurements are framed as a MOF-stage mechanistic validation (consistent with NU‑1000 anisotropic Dhopping literature) rather than an assumed determinant of the final Ni2P@C catalyst unless a clear empirical correlation is observed.

5) Overall, each weak link has a go/no-go experiment and a fallback path (drop magnetic alignment; constrain ionic claims; accept morphological—rather than crystallographic—retention; drop mixed-linker doping) that preserves the proposal’s core chain (OP‑EPD → quantified texture → transport/EIS → controlled conversion → electrocatalysis) while aligning with known behavior of NU‑1000 films and MOF-derived phosphide@carbon electrodes.
Critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-engineered: it specifies measurable alignment targets (Herman’s f), a physically grounded alignment regime (shear with Pe_r gating), and a control matrix that directly tests causality (aligned vs random at identical loading/porosity). The strongest feature is the explicit decoupling of electronic vs ionic transport using dedicated through-plane resistivity geometries and symmetric-cell ionic resistance—this addresses a frequent conflation in textured-electrode claims. Deductions are primarily due to (i) incomplete risk accounting for carbon-paper heterogeneity: local pore architecture and roughness can dominate apparent texture/ρ⊥ and complicate GIWAXS interpretation unless spatially resolved mapping/replicates are built in; (ii) potential ambiguity in the central transport mechanism: “c-axis highways” and Marcus hopping in oxidatively doped NU-1000 films is plausible but may be difficult to isolate from contact resistance, grain-boundary effects, and percolation via carbonized binder/glue after conversion; (iii) conversion-stage texture inheritance may be dominated by shrinkage, capillary collapse, and Ni2P nucleation kinetics, making the link between pre-conversion crystallographic texture and post-conversion Rct tenuous unless rigorous normalization (true porosity, Ni2P particle size distribution, carbon conductivity, wettability) is enforced; and (iv) some metrology is ambitious for the timeline (time-resolved SAXS under shear, 3D FIB-SEM tomography with statistically meaningful ODF extraction) and may become the rate-limiting deliverable.

Hypothesis: A topologically reprogrammed, single-phase MOF-derived intraframework heterojunction—created by hydrothermal cation-exchange to generate spatially segregated bimetallic nodes (n-type Ti-rich oxo nodes juxtaposed with p-type Cu-rich redox nodes) inside a robust Zr-fumarate framework—will maximize pervaporation fresh water productivity at an optimal Cu:Ti:MOF mass ratio because (i) node-to-node band-offset within the same continuous pore network forms a built-in field that biases proton/water-wire transport (Grotthuss-type hopping) while electrostatically penalizing hydrated ion entry, and (ii) topology-preserving linker “rewiring” (mixed-linker fumurate/sulfonated-fumarate) creates a percolating hydrophilic sublattice that maintains crystallinity yet increases water uptake and connectivity without introducing nonselective voids. The productivity maximum occurs when Cu/Ti node domains percolate (maximizing internal junction density) but remain below the threshold where excessive redox/oxo clustering collapses micropore continuity or increases salt leakage.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a hydrolytically robust parent MOF topology: start from UiO-66-family Zr-fumarate (fumarate as short linker to maximize pore wall polarity and stability). Target: fcu net with high water stability.
1.2 Define the topological modification goal as “mixed-linker rewiring” rather than defect creation: synthesize Zr6O4(OH)4 nodes with a controlled fraction (0, 10, 20, 30 mol%) of sulfonated fumarate (fumarate-SO3H) co-linker to create a hydrophilic, ion-repelling sublattice while preserving fcu connectivity.
1.3 Define intraframework heterojunction components as node-localized redox/oxo centers: Cu(II) (electron-accepting/redox-active, can create hole-rich sites under hydration) and Ti(IV) (oxo/hydroxyl-rich, electron-donating n-type character when partially hydrolyzed). The junction is internal (node-domain juxtaposition), not MOF@oxide.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Topology-preserving mixed-linker MOF synthesis (baseline):
- Solvothermal formation of Zr-fumarate / fumarate-SO3H mixed-linker MOFs using ZrCl4, fumaric acid, and sodium sulfofumarate (or sulfonated fumarate precursor) with acetic acid as crystallization modulator. Optimize to obtain phase-pure fcu crystals (PXRD) with controlled linker ratios (digest NMR).
2.2 Methodological adaptation (structurally novel): hydrothermal, spatially programmed cation-exchange to create intraframework bimetallic-node domains and internal heterojunctions.
- First exchange: Hydrothermal Ti installation. Suspend activated mixed-linker MOF in aqueous Ti precursor that favors node-binding (e.g., Ti(IV) lactate or Ti(IV) citrate complex, mildly acidic pH 3–4) in a Teflon-lined autoclave at 80–120 °C. Aim: partial substitution/coordination at node –OH/H2O sites forming Ti–O–Zr bridging/hydroxo grafts without nucleating TiO2.
- Second exchange: Hydrothermal Cu installation with spatial bias. Re-suspend Ti-modified MOF in aqueous Cu(II) acetate with chloride-free conditions; use a short hydrothermal pulse (60–100 °C) and exploit sulfonate-rich regions (from fumarate-SO3H) to preferentially coordinate Cu(II) near those linkers (electrostatic/chelation bias), generating Cu-rich nano-domains juxtaposed to Ti-rich domains within one crystal.
- Mass ratio programming: prepare a composition library by varying (a) Ti loading (0–15 wt% as Ti), (b) Cu loading (0–15 wt% as Cu), and (c) sulfonated-linker fraction (0–30 mol%). Determine actual mass ratios by ICP-OES (Zr/Ti/Cu) plus digest 1H NMR for linker ratio.
2.3 Membrane construction emphasizing junction utilization (not filler blending artifacts):
- Grow an oriented, sub-micron MOF thin film directly on a porous polymer support (e.g., PAN or PES) via seeded secondary growth to avoid polymer-filler interfacial voids.
- Post-synthetic hydrothermal exchanges (Ti then Cu) are performed on the already-grown MOF film to ensure junctions reside inside the selective layer.
- Optionally apply a nanometric PVA “gutter” layer only on the feed side to enhance mechanical integrity while keeping the MOF film as the primary selective pathway.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Confirm topology retention and mixed-linker rewiring:
- PXRD + Rietveld/Le Bail to confirm fcu net retention after exchanges.
- Digest 1H NMR to quantify fumarate vs fumarate-SO3H incorporation.
- Pair distribution function (PDF) or EXAFS (Zr K-edge, Ti K-edge, Cu K-edge) to verify Ti–O–(Zr) grafting and Cu coordination environments without oxide nanoparticle formation.
3.2 Prove intraframework heterojunction formation (spatially segregated node domains):
- STEM-EDS/EELS mapping across single crystals/film cross-sections to visualize Ti- and Cu-enriched nanodomains.
- Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) on films under controlled humidity to detect internal potential gradients consistent with built-in fields.
- Water-vapor sorption + in situ IR/Raman to quantify hydrogen-bond network strengthening and sulfonate hydration.
3.3 Mechanistic linkage to selective water transport and salt exclusion:
- Measure water self-diffusion in films by PFG-NMR (or QENS) vs composition; correlate with KPFM-derived potential gradients.
- Measure salt uptake (NaCl, MgCl2) by ion chromatography after equilibration; expect minimized uptake at optimized Cu/Ti and sulfonate fraction.
- Streaming potential/zeta potential of films in saline to quantify Donnan exclusion enhancement from sulfonate sublattice plus junction field.
3.4 Desalination performance and productivity maximum:
- Pervaporation of synthetic seawater (3.5 wt% NaCl) and high-salinity brine (10–20 wt% NaCl) at controlled temperature; record flux, salt rejection, and compute fresh water productivity.
- Identify the optimum in productivity vs Cu:Ti:MOF mass ratio and sulfonated-linker fraction.
- Controls: (i) parent Zr-fumarate film, (ii) mixed-linker only (no metals), (iii) Ti-only, (iv) Cu-only, (v) same total metal loading but reversed exchange order to test spatial programming, (vi) films deliberately forced to form TiO2/CuO nanoparticles (alkaline hydrothermal) to show that nanoparticle formation degrades selectivity relative to intraframework junctions.
3.5 Stability testing:
- 200 h continuous pervaporation with periodic saline cycling; track PXRD, ICP leaching (Ti/Cu), and performance retention.
- Chloride tolerance and anti-fouling tests (humic acid, SDS) to evaluate robustness of junction chemistry under realistic feeds.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: (a) Mixed-linker strategies are established to tune MOF pore polarity and charge while preserving topology, enabling rational transport control. (b) Hydrothermal/post-synthetic metalation and cation exchange at node –OH sites is a known route to install new functionalities in robust Zr-MOFs without collapse, and internal charge separation (built-in fields) is a validated mechanism in heterojunction-enabled transport/catalysis. (c) Mass-ratio optima are empirically common in heterojunction systems because interfacial density and percolation compete with blockage/aggregation; here the analogous parameter is internal junction density vs pore continuity.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal is MOF-native: it uses topological modification via mixed-linker “rewiring” of the coordination network and node-specific post-synthetic hydrothermal exchange to create an intraframework heterojunction. The junction is not an external oxide coating or physical mixture; it is encoded at the coordination-polymer node/linker level, aligning with coordination chemistry design principles.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to conventional MOF/oxide heterocomposites or defect-rich fillers, the single-phase intraframework heterojunction (i) eliminates nonselective interfacial voids (selective layer is a continuous MOF film), (ii) maximizes junction density per unit transport path because junctions reside inside pores, (iii) provides a tunable electrostatic/field-driven selectivity lever (Cu/Ti distribution + sulfonate sublattice), and (iv) offers a clean mass-ratio optimization axis (Cu:Ti loadings) directly tied to a mechanistic proxy (KPFM potential gradients, PFG-NMR diffusion), enabling a defensible productivity maximum rather than empirical trial-and-error.
Critique: This is a highly sophisticated and largely well-constructed proposal that demonstrates deep familiarity with Zr-MOF chemistry, mixed-linker topology control, and post-synthetic node modification. The strongest aspects are (i) the insistence on single-phase intraframework heterojunctions rather than composites, (ii) explicit mass-ratio programming tied to a mechanistic proxy (junction density vs pore continuity), and (iii) an unusually rigorous validation suite (EXAFS/PDF, KPFM, PFG-NMR). Score deductions arise from two areas. First, the electronic-structure argument (n-type Ti vs p-type Cu nodes, band offsets, built-in fields) is conceptually appealing but only semi-quantitative; no explicit discussion of Fermi-level alignment, defect states, or hydration-induced redox equilibria is provided, leaving ambiguity as to whether the field strength is sufficient to measurably bias proton/water-wire transport over nanometer scales. Second, the hydrothermal cation-exchange selectivity and spatial segregation (Cu-rich vs Ti-rich domains) relies heavily on sulfonate bias and kinetic control, but lacks a clear thermodynamic or kinetic model to demonstrate that domain formation, rather than statistical node decoration, will dominate across a film. These gaps do not invalidate feasibility but slightly weaken logical closure.

Hypothesis: A coprecipitation-derived, spatially segregated Fe3O4@Zr-MOF core–shell sorbent will enable high-capacity phosphate capture and low-chemical regeneration by enforcing a reversible inner-sphere binding mechanism: phosphate will bind predominantly to Zr6-oxo node defect sites as Zr–O–P bridges during uptake, while a redox-triggered, local pH/ligand microenvironment generated at the Fe3O4 core under mild stimuli (low-voltage electro-Fenton/H2O2 or weak chelator wash) will selectively weaken Zr–O–P linkages without collapsing the framework, enabling phosphorus recovery as concentrated phosphate and sustaining performance over many cycles. Mechanistically, (i) high-affinity Zr(IV)–phosphate coordination at engineered missing-linker sites provides selectivity and capacity, (ii) the coprecipitated magnetite core provides rapid separability and a controllable interfacial chemical potential that accelerates desorption, and (iii) the core–shell architecture prevents Fe leaching and preserves MOF crystallinity by isolating redox chemistry from Zr–carboxylate bonds. FT-IR spectroscopy will be used operando/ex situ to track formation and removal of P–O–Zr/Fe bands and to quantify regeneration completeness via band deconvolution.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a water-stable Zr-MOF platform with accessible Zr6 nodes and known phosphate affinity (UiO-66 family or MOF-808). Prepare a mixed-linker formulation to introduce controlled defect density: use terephthalate (BDC) plus a monocarboxylate modulator (formate/acetate) to create missing-linker sites while retaining topology.
1.2 Define phosphate speciation conditions relevant to remediation/regeneration (pH 6–8 for adsorption; regeneration screens at pH 9–11 carbonate or 10–50 mM citrate/EDTA alternatives). Prepare competitive anion matrices (SO4^2−, HCO3−, Cl−, NO3−, SiO3^2−) and natural organic matter (humic acid) challenge solutions.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—coprecipitation to enforce core–shell segregation and interfacial anchoring:
  a) Coprecipitate Fe3O4 nanoparticles (10–30 nm) from Fe(II)/Fe(III) salts (1:2) under N2 at 70–80 °C by base addition, but perform coprecipitation in the presence of a thin polydopamine (PDA) priming layer (dopamine self-polymerization at pH ~8.5) to supply catechol/amine anchors.
  b) Grow a Zr-MOF shell directly on Fe3O4@PDA via solvothermal synthesis: ZrCl4 (or ZrOCl2·8H2O) + BDC (and defect-inducing modulator) in DMF/H2O with controlled water content to favor nucleation on PDA rather than in bulk. Target 20–80 nm shell thickness by varying precursor concentration and time.
  c) Post-synthetic node activation to maximize phosphate-accessible sites while maintaining robustness: solvent exchange (EtOH/H2O), then mild thermal activation (120–150 °C) to open Zr–OH/H2O sites; optionally introduce a small fraction of phosphonate-free, basic pendant groups (e.g., amino-BDC) to promote electrostatic preconcentration without competing with Zr sites.
2.2 Phosphate capture testing:
  a) Measure kinetics and isotherms at pH 6–8; quantify capacity and selectivity under competing ions.
  b) Use magnetic separation to demonstrate process intensification (fast solid–liquid separation without filtration).
2.3 Regeneration adaptation—stimulus-assisted desorption while preserving the Zr framework:
  a) Baseline regeneration: carbonate wash (Na2CO3/NaHCO3, pH 10–11) vs. mild chelator wash (citrate 10–50 mM, pH 7–9) to identify lowest chemical demand.
  b) Redox-assisted regeneration (core-enabled): apply low H2O2 dose (0.5–5 mM) with brief low-voltage electrostimulation (or aeration) to activate Fe3O4 surface cycling; the goal is to generate transient interfacial OH−/reactive species that disrupt Zr–O–P bridging locally, accelerating desorption at lower bulk pH/chemical concentration.
  c) Capture recovered phosphorus: precipitate eluate as struvite (MgNH4PO4·6H2O) or Ca-phosphate by controlled addition of Mg2+/NH4+ or Ca2+; evaluate purity and mass balance.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural integrity and phase analysis across cycles: PXRD (MOF crystallinity), TEM/EDX mapping (core–shell retention; P distribution), BET/porosity, and ICP-OES (Zr/Fe leaching).
3.2 Mechanistic verification using FT-IR spectroscopy as the primary chain-end tool:
  a) Identify adsorption signatures: growth of ν(P–O) bands (1000–1100 cm−1) and emergence/shift consistent with inner-sphere Zr–O–P; monitor changes in Zr–OH/μ3-OH region and carboxylate symmetric/asymmetric stretches to detect unwanted linker displacement.
  b) Regeneration tracking: quantify reduction of phosphate bands after regeneration; apply peak deconvolution to separate free/outer-sphere phosphate vs. bridged phosphate; correlate with desorbed phosphate concentration.
  c) Complementary: XPS (P 2p chemical state; Zr 3d shifts), zeta potential vs pH to link electrostatics, and optional in situ ATR-FTIR during adsorption/desorption to capture reversible binding kinetics.
3.3 Performance metrics: capacity retention over ≥20 cycles, regeneration efficiency (% desorbed), chemical consumption per gram P recovered, and selectivity coefficients in complex matrices; compare to non-magnetic Zr-MOF and to Fe3O4–ZIF-8 analogs to isolate the effect of Zr-node binding + core-enabled regeneration.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr(IV)-oxo clusters form strong inner-sphere complexes with phosphate (Zr–O–P), underpinning high selectivity (supported by Zr-MOF phosphate binding literature). Magnetic MOF composites show high recyclability and fast separation, and prior work demonstrates coprecipitation as a robust route to embed Fe3O4 for regeneration-ready adsorbents. FT-IR is well-established for diagnosing phosphate binding modes through ν(P–O) evolution and metal–oxygen–phosphorus bridging signatures.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal leverages MOF node chemistry (defect-engineered Zr6 clusters) as the primary binding motif while using a coprecipitated magnetic core purely as a physical handle and controllable interfacial stimulus source. The core–shell design is a supramolecular/architectural adaptation that preserves coordination-polymer integrity by spatially separating redox-active iron from Zr–carboxylate nodes.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with Fe3O4–ZIF-8 phosphate sorbents, Zr-node binding offers higher thermodynamic selectivity for phosphate and improved hydrolytic stability; compared with plain Zr-MOF powders, the magnetic core enables rapid separation and, critically, a lower-chemical-demand regeneration via interfacial stimulus-assisted desorption. Operando/ex situ FT-IR provides a direct, cycle-by-cycle mechanistic readout of P-binding and removal, enabling rational optimization of defect density and regeneration conditions rather than empirical trial-and-error.
Critique: This is a technically sophisticated and well-articulated proposal with strong command of Zr-MOF chemistry, phosphate coordination mechanisms, and composite material design. Engineering resolution is high: synthesis, defect control, shell thickness tuning, regeneration chemistries, and analytical validation are all specified at an actionable level. Logical consistency is strong but not flawless—the central assumption that mild Fe3O4-mediated redox or electro-Fenton conditions can selectively weaken Zr–O–P bonds without perturbing Zr–carboxylate coordination is plausible but under-justified thermodynamically and kinetically. Evidence grounding is solid and stays within the chemistry/MOF domain, though the reliance on FT-IR deconvolution as a primary quantitative regeneration metric risks overinterpretation without stronger corroboration from P mass balances and operando controls. The rationale is compelling and non-trivial, addressing the genuine bottleneck of chemical-intensive regeneration in Zr-based phosphate sorbents via an architectural rather than compositional innovation.

Hypothesis: A humidity–CO2-gated, spatially segregated dual-domain MOF composite can improve *competitive selectivity* for soft heavy metals (Pb(II), Cd(II), Cu(II)) **without relying on net bulk acidification**, by operating in a narrowly defined speciation window where (i) amine sites reversibly bind CO2/H2O as ammonium bicarbonate to modulate surface charge and ion-pairing, and (ii) thiol/oxo capture sites retain sufficient deprotonation to enable inner-sphere complexation. The key mechanistic refinement is that CO2 does not universally enhance adsorption: instead, selectivity gains are predicted only when bicarbonate formation increases local ionic strength and electrostatic screening at the amine-rich shell—thereby suppressing outer-sphere uptake of hard background cations—*while carbonate complexation of Pb/Cd/Cu remains subdominant* and thiol pKa shifts do not fully quench soft-donor binding. By explicitly modeling and measuring carbonate speciation, thiol protonation, and transport across a defined amine-shell thickness, the system is designed to function as a true two-stage adsorptive architecture rather than a mixed bed. Regeneration is hypothesized to be feasible because binding at thiol sites is dominated by reversible inner-sphere coordination (ΔGads moderated by protonation state and competition), not irreversible precipitation or oxidation-driven trapping, and because CO2 removal collapses ammonium bicarbonate, reducing electrostatic stabilization of metal–surface complexes under low-ionic-strength wash.
Plan:
1. **Pre-registered speciation and surface-complexation modeling (boundary conditions first):**
1.1 Develop a PHREEQC-based aqueous speciation model including Pb(II)/Cd(II)/Cu(II) carbonate complexes, background Na+/Ca2+/Mg2+ (10–50 mM), and humic acid complexation.
1.2 Couple this to a surface complexation model with explicit equilibria for (a) amine ↔ ammonium ↔ ammonium bicarbonate, (b) thiol ↔ thiolate (including pKa shifts under electrostatic fields), and (c) metal–thiolate and metal–Zr–oxo complexes. Parameterize with literature constants and refine using titration data (see 3.2).
1.3 Use the model to map a design space (pH 5–7.5, pCO2 0–0.2 atm, ionic strength 1–50 mM) identifying regions where CO2 is predicted to enhance vs diminish Pb/Ca and Cd/Mg selectivity. This map pre-defines all experimental operating points.

2. **MOF synthesis with quantified site densities:**
2.1 Amine-gated shell: UiO-66 mixed-linker MOF (terephthalate/2,5-diaminoterephthalate) synthesized to a target amine density of 2–3 mmol –NH2 g−1 MOF, verified by acid–base titration and elemental analysis.
2.2 Thiol capture domain: UiO-66 post-synthetically thiolated via diazotization–thiolation, targeting 1–1.5 mmol –SH g−1 MOF. Thiol accessibility quantified by Ellman’s reagent and XPS S 2p fitting.

3. **Architectural assembly and validation (core–shell, not mixed):**
3.1 Sequential dip-coating/ultrasonication deposition on melamine sponge or ceramic monolith: inner thiol-MOF first, followed by outer amine-MOF shell.
3.2 Define shell thickness (5–50 µm) by controlling coating cycles; verify spatial segregation via FIB-SEM/EDS cross-sections, ToF-SIMS depth profiling, and micro-CT for connectivity.
3.3 Quantify transport: measure effective diffusivity of Pb(II) and Ca2+ through the amine shell using time-lag experiments; calculate Damköhler numbers to demonstrate staged capture rather than equilibrium mixing.

4. **Operando verification of CO2 gating under aqueous flow:**
4.1 Use 13CO2-labeled humid gas to condition the sorbent; perform operando ATR-FTIR in flow to track bicarbonate/carbonate bands on amine sites during water exposure.
4.2 Quantify bicarbonate loading (mmol g−1) and amine protonation via combined FTIR integration and ex situ 13C ssNMR.
4.3 Measure zeta potential and local pH (fluorescent probes) as a function of gating state; compare against model predictions.

5. **Adsorption, selectivity, and controls:**
5.1 Conduct single and competitive isotherms (Pb/Cd/Cu vs Ca/Mg/Na) under CO2-gated, N2-gated (matched ionic strength), and carbonate-free conditions.
5.2 Include hard controls: amine-only MOF, thiol-only MOF, physically mixed amine+thiol MOFs, and spatially segregated composites.
5.3 Report capacities normalized strictly to *active MOF mass* (excluding support), with independent mass balance by digestion/ICP-OES.

6. **Regeneration and reversibility tests:**
6.1 Measure isosteric heats of adsorption (temperature-dependent isotherms) for Pb(II) under gated vs ungated states.
6.2 Perform competitive elution with CO2-off switching (dry N2) and ≤0.05 M benign electrolyte; track desorption kinetics and mass balances.
6.3 Monitor thiol oxidation and reversibility over ≥20 cycles using S K-edge XANES and XPS; correlate any oxidation with capacity loss.

7. **Fixed-bed demonstration:**
7.1 Run continuous-flow columns using operating points validated by modeling; generate breakthrough curves and fit with Thomas/Yoon–Nelson models incorporating effective diffusivity.
7.2 Compare performance against ZIF-coated sponges and single-function MOFs under identical matrices.
Feasibility: This revised plan directly addresses reviewer concerns by constraining claims to a quantitatively defined speciation regime rather than assuming universal CO2 benefit. Carbonate competition is explicitly incorporated and tested via carbonate-free and matched-ionic-strength controls, ensuring that observed selectivity changes arise from gating chemistry rather than pH or salinity artifacts. The core–shell architecture is no longer inferred but validated through cross-sectional imaging and transport analysis, with shell thickness and diffusivity linked to Damköhler numbers to prove staged capture. Thiol chemistry risks are mitigated by (i) direct measurement of thiol pKa and oxidation state, (ii) thermodynamic validation of reversible binding via isosteric heats, and (iii) regeneration protocols grounded in competitive desorption rather than assumed lability. Capacity targets are reframed as conditional outcomes tied to measured site densities and accessibility, with strict normalization to active MOF mass to avoid inflation. Collectively, the proposal closes the speciation–transport–thermodynamics loop demanded by the reviewers, transforming the CO2–humidity concept from mechanistic overreach into a falsifiable, model-driven adsorptive separation strategy.
Critique:
The proposal is unusually strong in mechanistic falsifiability: it pre-registers a speciation/surface-complexation design map, anticipates failure modes (carbonate complexation dominance; thiol quenching/oxidation), and builds matched-ionic-strength and carbonate-free controls to isolate the CO2 effect from salinity/pH artifacts. The engineering plan is detailed (site-density quantification, cross-sectional validation, time-lag diffusivity, operando 13CO2 ATR-FTIR/ssNMR, multicycle XANES/XPS) and directly addresses the key bottleneck in prior “CO2 helps adsorption” narratives by limiting claims to a narrow speciation window.

Key score deductions are driven by remaining physical/chemical ambiguities that could undermine interpretability. (i) The stated mechanism attributes selectivity gains to bicarbonate-induced ionic strength/electrostatic screening at the amine shell, but this is difficult to disentangle from Donnan exclusion and from local pH shifts within a porous, buffering, carbonate-containing shell; zeta potential and fluorescent pH probes may not resolve intrapore conditions at relevant length scales. (ii) The surface complexation model includes multiple coupled equilibria (amine protonation/bicarbonate, thiol pKa shifts, metal–thiolate, metal–oxo, humics) with many parameters; without a clear identifiability strategy and independent constraints (e.g., potentiometric titration across ionic strengths, spectroscopic speciation of bound metals), fits may be non-unique. (iii) The regeneration premise (“reversible inner-sphere coordination”) is plausible for some complexes but not assured for Pb/Cu with thiolates in oxidizing, carbonate-bearing waters; even mild oxidation/crosslinking or multinuclear surface complexes can introduce hysteresis not captured by isosteric heats alone. (iv) UiO-66 diazotization–thiolation can compromise crystallinity/porosity and introduce heterogeneous binding environments; the plan measures accessibility but does not specify acceptance criteria linking structural integrity to performance.

Overall: high merit, strong rigor, but needs tighter experimental discriminants for the proposed electrostatic-screening mechanism and stronger parameter-identification discipline to prevent “model-supported” but non-diagnostic conclusions.

Hypothesis: Embedding the hemilabile sulfonated linker PSBA into defect-engineered UiO-66-(OH)2 will create a *chemically addressable defect microenvironment* in which reversible guest uptake induces a cooperative, two-state rearrangement ("gate-closed" ↔ "gate-open") localized at missing-linker Zr6 sites that are proximate to PSBA. The mechanistic rationale is that UiO-66-(OH)2 provides a tunable intraframework H-bond network that modulates linker rotational barriers (Asset 2), while PSBA provides (i) defect stabilization at high missing-linker density and (ii) a switchable coordination/protonation manifold (inner-sphere sulfonate–Zr vs outer-sphere SO3H/ion-pair) that can reversibly reconfigure local Zr–O bonding and H-bond topology (Asset 4). This localized reconfiguration is expected to (A) generate *true cooperative gating* detectable as an adsorption-step-linked, operando structural transition (unit-cell/peak-shape evolution consistent with discrete states rather than continuous filling) and (B) modulate luminescence primarily through a *dynamics-controlled non-radiative pathway* (ring rotation / H-bond constraint), which will be validated by quantitative co-variation of ssNMR-derived rotational barriers and PL-derived non-radiative rate constants across the same samples (Asset 2). The refined approach explicitly overcomes identifiability concerns by (1) requiring coincident, reproducible signatures across adsorption thermodynamics, operando structure, and site-resolved coordination/protonation spectroscopy; (2) ruling out mesoporosity/capillary/diffusion artifacts with an orthogonal pore-architecture suite; and (3) separating “protonation” from “anion binding/damage” via controlled anion-exchange series and quantitative S/Zr tracking.
Plan:
Step 0 — Sample matrix and naming (pre-registered).
0.1 Define a factorial library with three orthogonal axes and minimum replicates (n≥3 syntheses each):
  (i) Defect density target: 0, ~2, ~4, ~6 missing linkers per Zr6 (via modulator concentration and PSBA fraction).
  (ii) PSBA state: as-made; protonated/ion-paired; anion-exchanged (Cl−, NO3−, OTf−) at fixed proton activity.
  (iii) Morphology: nanoparticles (50–150 nm), sub-micron octahedra (200–800 nm), micron crystals (1–5 µm) (coordination modulation).
0.2 Controls: (a) UiO-66-(OH)2 without PSBA at matched defect densities; (b) UiO-66-(CH3)2 analog (reduced H-bonding) at matched defect density; (c) PSBA-replaced sulfonated benzoate with reduced hemilability (reviewer-requested necessity test).

Step 1 — Morphology-controlled synthesis with defect quantification (Asset 1 + reviewer discriminants).
1.1 Coordination modulation for morphology: hold Zr:total-dicarboxylate constant; vary modulator identity and equivalents (e.g., acetic acid vs dodecanoic acid) and water content to achieve size series while preserving phase purity (PXRD) and comparable crystallinity.
1.2 PSBA incorporation as co-linker/defect modulator: synthesize Hl-UiO-66-(OH)2-x(PSBA)y by co-feeding PSBA with BDC-(OH)2. Record *absolute* feed ratios and modulator equivalents for reproducibility.
1.3 Defect density and composition quantification:
  • Digestion 1H NMR (BDC-(OH)2:PSBA:modulator ratios).
  • TGA (linker:node ratio) cross-checked against NMR.
  • ICP-OES/MS for Zr and S to obtain S/Zr as a mass-balance constraint on PSBA retention and on post-treatments.
  • XPS (S 2p) to distinguish sulfonate vs sulfonic acid vs sulfate-like environments.

Step 2 — Post-synthetic “latching” without framework damage: protonation vs anion binding (addresses H2SO4 risk).
2.1 Replace single-condition H2SO4 treatment with a controlled matrix:
  • Proton activity control: treat with acids of matched pKa/ionic strength series (e.g., HCl, HNO3, HOTf) and, separately, H2SO4 at low equivalents.
  • Time/equivalents windowing: define an upper bound where crystallinity loss (VT-PXRD) or S/Zr drift (ICP) indicates irreversible incorporation/damage; exclude those conditions.
2.2 Verify reversibility and exclude sulfate incorporation:
  • Quantitative ICP for S/Zr before/after treatment and after extensive exchange.
  • Anion exchange series (Cl−/NO3−/OTf−) performed on the same parent material to decouple “protonation” from “anion binding”.
  • Monitor Zr environment by Zr K-edge EXAFS for changes consistent with sulfate coordination vs unchanged Zr6 core.
2.3 Activation standardization: identical solvent exchange protocol and activation temperature/ramp for all samples; record residual solvent by 1H NMR of digests.

Step 3 — Hard discriminants for *true cooperative gating* vs mesoporosity/diffusion (reviewer mandatory items 1 & 3).
3.1 Pore-architecture exclusion tests (capillary/mesoporosity):
  • Ar adsorption at 87 K for micropore assessment and PSD via NLDFT/QSDFT appropriate for MOFs; compare with N2 (77 K) and CO2 (273 K) to detect diffusion-limited artifacts.
  • SAXS (preferred) or Hg porosimetry (if particle integrity allows) to quantify meso/macroporosity and interparticle voids across morphologies/defect levels.
  • Correlate any hysteresis with independent mesopore signatures; hysteresis without mesopore evidence becomes gating-candidate.
3.2 Operando structural signature requirement:
  • Synchrotron PXRD during stepwise adsorption (CO2 and a polar probe such as MeOH or MeCN): collect patterns at equilibrium loadings spanning the adsorption step.
  • Quantify: (i) unit-cell parameter evolution, (ii) peak-shape/strain broadening, (iii) appearance/disappearance of subtle superstructure/shoulders.
  • Apply two-model fitting: continuous lattice breathing model vs two-state mixture model; gating is only assigned if two-state (or discontinuous) evolution best fits and coincides with adsorption step.
3.3 Operando total scattering/PDF during adsorption (mandatory item 1):
  • Collect PDF at key points (pre-step, at-step, post-step) to detect local Zr–O / Zr–Zr distance shifts consistent with defect-site rearrangement rather than only long-range changes.
  • Compare to controls lacking PSBA and/or lacking –OH H-bonding: a gating-specific local signature must be absent or significantly reduced in controls.
3.4 Adsorption thermodynamics linkage:
  • Microcalorimetry coupled to dosing to locate enthalpy discontinuities at the step; gating claim requires coincident (PXRD/PDF) structural transition + enthalpy feature + isotherm step reproducibility.
3.5 Cycling stability:
  • ≥20 adsorption/desorption cycles with identical step position (±5% in pressure/loading) and preserved operando signature; loss indicates metastable pore filling rather than cooperative gating.

Step 4 — Site-resolved validation of PSBA–defect adjacency and coordination switching (reviewer mandatory item 2).
4.1 Isotopic labeling strategy (choose one primary + one secondary handle):
  Primary: 13C-label PSBA carboxylate carbon (and/or BDC-(OH)2 carboxylate) to enable carboxylate-specific ssNMR.
  Secondary: 17O enrichment (selective, low-level) of carboxylate oxygens for coordination-mode sensitivity (if feasible within budget/time).
4.2 2D ssNMR adjacency probes:
  • 1H–1H (e.g., RFDR) to detect proximity between –OH protons (UiO-66-(OH)2) and PSBA aromatic/sulfonate-associated protons (SO3H when protonated).
  • 1H–13C HETCOR focusing on 13C-labeled PSBA carboxylate to detect cross-peaks to –OH/µ3-OH region; strengthened contacts indicate spatial adjacency.
  • Repeat under (i) activated, (ii) guest-loaded (at gating step), and (iii) post-desorption conditions to test reversible coordination/protonation shifts.
4.3 Complementary vibrational operando:
  • In situ DRIFTS during dosing to track: (i) ν(S=O) shifts (sulfonate vs sulfonic acid vs coordinated sulfonate), (ii) –OH stretching changes, (iii) guest-specific bands.
  • Require reversibility of diagnostic bands upon desorption for gating latch claim.

Step 5 — Deconvoluting PL: dynamics-driven vs electronic/chemical mechanisms (reviewer mandatory item 4 & 5).
5.1 Quantitative PL kinetics and temperature dependence:
  • Measure absolute quantum yield (integrating sphere) + time-resolved lifetimes vs temperature (e.g., 80–350 K) under inert conditions and under controlled guest partial pressures.
  • Extract radiative (kr) and non-radiative (knr) rates from (Φ, τ). Fit knr(T) with Arrhenius/Eyring models to obtain activation parameters; dynamics-driven mechanism predicts systematic barrier shifts matching NMR-derived rotational barriers.
5.2 Rule-out electronic/protonation-only effects:
  • Anion series (Cl−/NO3−/OTf−) at same proton activity: if PL changes track anion identity strongly without corresponding NMR barrier change, then electrostatics/CT dominates; gating/dynamics claim is weakened.
  • ICP + XPS to rule out heavy-atom/paramagnetic impurities; include metal impurity screen.
  • Guest-quenching controls: oxygen/water vapor quenching under conditions where uptake is known (from isotherms) to separate diffusion-limited quenching from intrinsic knr changes.
5.3 Direct dynamics measurement linkage (mandatory item 5):
  • VT separated-local-field / DIPSHIFT ssNMR on the *same exact samples* used for PL to obtain effective dipolar couplings and rotational barriers.
  • Success requires a monotonic, quantitative correlation between (Δbarrier from NMR) and (Δknr from PL) across the matrix, with controls breaking the correlation.

Step 6 — Go/No-Go metrics (predefined, quantitative).
6.1 Gating (all must be met):
  • Reproducible isotherm step (pressure/loading) across ≥3 batches: variation ≤±5%.
  • Coincident operando synchrotron PXRD signature: discontinuous unit-cell/peak-shape change or two-state mixture behavior at the step.
  • Coincident operando PDF local-structure change attributable to defect-site environment (not present in non-PSBA or non–OH control).
  • Cycling: step position and operando signature retained after ≥20 cycles with <10% capacity loss.
6.2 Dynamics → PL (all must be met):
  • knr(T) activation parameters shift systematically with NMR-derived rotational barriers across the same sample set.
  • Anion series shows that PL modulation is not explained solely by anion binding (i.e., NMR barrier + PL changes co-vary more strongly with barrier than with anion identity).
  • Controls: UiO-66-(CH3)2 (reduced H-bonding) should show diminished barrier sensitivity and diminished PL-gating coupling.

Step 7 — Modeling constrained by discriminants (Assets 2 & 4).
7.1 Periodic DFT on representative local motifs validated by S/Zr, EXAFS, and ssNMR (do not overfit to unconstrained structures):
  • Compute linker rotation barriers under specific –OH···OH and –OH···SO3H / SO3− configurations.
  • Compute guest binding energies at defect-adjacent PSBA motifs and relative stability of “latched” coordination states.
7.2 Compare computed barrier shifts to ssNMR barriers and computed adsorption energetics to microcalorimetry step enthalpies; accept only qualitative-consistent trends, not exact absolute matching.

Deliverables timeline (indicative):
  • Months 1–3: synthesis library + defect/morphology quantification + anion/protonation matrix boundaries.
  • Months 4–6: pore-architecture exclusion suite + baseline adsorption.
  • Months 7–10: operando PXRD/PDF + DRIFTS + calorimetry.
  • Months 11–14: ssNMR (incl. labeled subset) + PL kinetics + correlation analysis.
  • Months 15–18: cycling, refined controls, DFT constrained modeling, final go/no-go decision per metrics.
Feasibility:
Empirical anchoring: UiO-66 linker dynamics are demonstrably tunable by linker substituents, with –OH increasing rotational barriers via H-bonding (Asset 2), giving a realistic handle to shift non-radiative decay pathways in a temperature-quantifiable way. Separately, PSBA-enabled hemilabile UiO-66 supports unusually high defect densities while retaining/improving thermal stability after acid treatment (Asset 4), providing precedent that PSBA can stabilize missing-linker environments rather than simply increasing collapse risk.

Addressing reviewer identifiability concerns: (i) “Gating” is not inferred from hysteresis alone; it is only claimed when an adsorption step is *synchronously* accompanied by operando synchrotron PXRD discontinuities/two-state behavior and a local PDF signature, and when mesoporosity artifacts are excluded by Ar(87 K)+NLDFT/QSDFT plus SAXS/Hg porosimetry. (ii) “Dynamics-driven PL” is not inferred from PL change alone; it is only claimed when NMR-derived barrier shifts quantitatively co-vary with knr activation parameters across the same sample set, and when anion-identity controls and impurity screens exclude alternative electronic explanations. (iii) Defect-adjacent PSBA is not assumed from bulk EXAFS/PDF alone; it is tested with site-resolved 2D ssNMR correlation enabled by targeted isotopic labeling, and with reversible operando DRIFTS signatures upon guest/protonation toggling. (iv) Acid-treatment damage/sulfate binding risk is mitigated by replacing a single H2SO4 condition with an acid/anion matrix, tracking S/Zr by ICP and S chemical state by XPS, and demonstrating reversibility via anion exchange—thereby separating intended protonation/ion-pairing from irreversible anion incorporation or node degradation.

Practical feasibility: All required measurements are standard in advanced MOF characterization workflows (digestion NMR, TGA, ICP, XPS, adsorption/calorimetry, synchrotron PXRD/total scattering, DRIFTS, ssNMR, PL lifetime/Φ). The added discriminants (Ar 87 K, SAXS/Hg porosimetry, operando scattering, labeled ssNMR subset, anion exchange series) are modular and can be staged so that expensive/limited-beamtime experiments are reserved for candidates that already pass pore-architecture and reproducibility filters. This staged, metric-gated workflow reduces risk while preserving the original concept chain (defect stabilization + H-bond-programmed dynamics + gated porosity + luminescence readout).
Critique: The engineering plan is unusually well-resolved, with pre-registered factorial sampling, explicit controls, orthogonal artifact exclusions, and go/no-go metrics that directly answer typical “hysteresis ≠ gating” and “PL change ≠ dynamics” critiques. The principal deduction is that the central mechanistic claim—localized, cooperative two-state rearrangement at missing-linker Zr6 sites proximate to PSBA—remains underdetermined even with operando PXRD/PDF, because (a) defect distributions and PSBA adjacency will likely be heterogeneous and may produce apparent two-state fits from population averaging; (b) PXRD/PDF sensitivity to small-amplitude, local coordination/protonation changes at sparse sites may be marginal without a stronger, site-specific structural reporter; and (c) the assumed causal chain guest uptake → PSBA coordination/protonation switch → Zr–O topology change → cooperative gate is plausible but not yet anchored to a quantitative thermodynamic/kinetic framework that predicts step position, hysteresis width, and dependence on defect density/anion identity. The PL–dynamics linkage is thoughtfully constrained (same-sample NMR/PL, Arrhenius/Eyring analysis), but still vulnerable to confounders common in UiO-type photophysics (defect-state emissive traps, excimer/exciplex formation, guest-dependent dielectric effects, and energy transfer to adsorbates) that may co-vary with defect density and anion content even when impurities are ruled out.

Hypothesis: Hydrostatically conditioning solvent-saturated defect-engineered UiO-type Hf-MOF monoliths/nanocrystals within a quantitatively defined sub-amorphization pressure window, and coupling this with a capillary-stress-minimized solvent-exchange/activation pathway (culminating in supercritical CO2 drying), will yield higher retained BET surface area and pore volume than conventional ambient exchange + evacuation. The operative mechanism is not defect “healing” by rebonding under pressure alone, but pressure–pathway control: (i) isotropic densification under hydrostatic load increases framework stiffness (effective bulk modulus) and reduces strain localization at defective nodes; (ii) maintaining full pore filling during compression and solvent exchange suppresses gas–liquid menisci, thereby preventing high Laplace capillary pressures and shear heterogeneity that otherwise trigger linker slippage, crack initiation, and defect coalescence during drying; and (iii) if—and only if—a chemical lever is introduced (mobile monocarboxylate or linker feed + controlled water/acid and mild thermal bias), hydrostatic pressure can be tested as a kinetic/thermodynamic bias that shifts defect speciation (modulator vs linker occupancy) toward more strongly bridging carboxylate binding, which must be demonstrated by stoichiometric mass balance (quantitative digested NMR/ICP/halide analysis) rather than inferred. Therefore, the central, testable model predicts that porosity retention scales with the ratio of predicted capillary pressure (Pc) to measured mechanical resistance (K, yield onset/amorphization threshold), and that pressure history improves outcomes primarily by reducing collapse-driving stress gradients and microcrack formation during the liquid-to-supercritical-to-gas transition.
Plan:
A. System definition and defect-state quantification (pre-registered sample set)
A1. Platforms: UiO-66(Hf) and UiO-67(Hf) with three targeted defect regimes (Low/Med/High). Defects introduced via modulated solvothermal synthesis using (i) TFA (high defect propensity) and (ii) monotopic carboxylates (formate/acetate/benzoate) to vary modulator size/pKa and binding strength. Include UiO-66(Zr) matched-defect controls.
A2. Form factors: (i) nanocrystals (20–200 nm; controlled via water content and modulator equivalents) and (ii) binder-free monoliths prepared by sol–gel/gelation of Hf-oxo clusters with dicarboxylate linker, aged to reproducible permeability (measure via solvent flow/uptake kinetics). Keep pores fully solvent-filled at all times prior to activation.
A3. Defect chemistry baseline (must be quantitative):
  • Digested 1H NMR with internal standard (e.g., dimethyl sulfone) to obtain linker:modulator ratio; report absolute mmol g−1 for each organic species.
  • ICP-OES for Hf (and Zr in controls) to close mass balance.
  • Ion chromatography or potentiometric titration for F−/Cl− if halides are present from precursors/modulators; water content by Karl Fischer on mother liquors and representative washed solids.
  • TGA to cross-check organic/inorganic ratio and estimate missing-linker vs missing-cluster trends.
A4. Structure/porosity/mechanics baseline:
  • PXRD (phase/topology, crystallite size/strain), SEM/TEM (morphology), N2 77 K isotherms (BET, micropore volume via t-plot/DFT), monolith density and open porosity.
  • Mechanical: nanoindentation (monolith modulus/hardness) and/or microcompression; for powders, compaction response (pelletization curve). Avoid mercury intrusion; use gas pycnometry + geometric density for porosity.

B. Quantitative capillary-stress model (computed + measured) and “collapse predictor”
B1. Determine pore-size distributions (PSD): DFT from N2 77 K (micropores) plus mesopore PSD from Ar 87 K or Kr as needed; for monolith interparticle mesoporosity, add SAXS or N2 hysteresis analysis.
B2. For each solvent step (DMF, EtOH, acetone or MeOH, liquid CO2 surrogate), measure:
  • Surface tension γ(T) (tensiometry or literature with verification at working T).
  • Contact angle θ on pressed MOF pellets/monolith slices (goniometry) in the relevant solvent; if unreliable, bracket with θ = 0–30° (wetting) and propagate uncertainty.
B3. Compute capillary pressure distribution Pc(r) using Laplace: Pc = 2γ cosθ / r, where r is pore radius (use PSD). Report Pc,max and Pc,median for each solvent. This produces an a priori ranking of collapse risk by solvent.
B4. Define a mechanistic figure-of-merit for each sample/condition: Π = Pc,max / Pcrit, where Pcrit is measured amorphization onset or yield proxy from HPPXRD/mechanics. Hypothesis predicts porosity retention improves when Π is minimized by (i) solvent choice/order and (ii) maintaining saturated conditions and avoiding menisci via scCO2.

C. Explicit pressure–temperature–time trajectories (no ambiguity) with two mechanistic modes
C0. General rule: pores remain liquid-filled from start of pressure conditioning through entry into supercritical CO2; no intermediate drying.
C1. Hydrostatic conditioning trajectory (P–t path, solvent-saturated):
  • Load sample in a hydrostatic medium identical to pore solvent (initially DMF or EtOH depending on synthesis washing state) to avoid osmotic gradients.
  • Apply stepped compression: 0.00 → 0.05 → 0.10 → 0.15 → 0.18 GPa, hold 45 min at each step (T = 298 K), then hold 2 h at 0.18 GPa.
  • Controlled decompression to the working exchange pressure (not ambient): 0.18 → 0.12 GPa over 30 min, then hold at 0.12 GPa for solvent exchange (Section D).
  • Safety mapping: For each defect regime, run a short HPPXRD screening to locate amorphization onset; set Pmax = (onset − 0.03 GPa). If onset ≤ 0.15 GPa for high-defect samples, set Pmax to 0.10–0.12 GPa.
C2. Optional “chemical-lever” trajectory (only if testing defect re-speciation): repeat C1 but add one controlled chemical driver during the 0.18 GPa hold:
  • Introduce a known concentration of mobile monocarboxylate (e.g., benzoic acid/acetate) or low-dose linker feed in the pore solvent plus controlled water (e.g., 0.5–2.0 vol%) and mild thermal bias (323–343 K) for 2–6 h. This is explicitly designed to supply ligands and enable exchange/reattachment chemistry; without this lever, no defect healing claim is made.

D. Pressure-assisted solvent exchange (constant pressure, defined order, quantified mass transfer)
D1. Exchange is conducted at constant P = 0.12 GPa (or the Pmax-safe value identified in C1) to maintain saturation and suppress meniscus formation.
D2. Exchange sequence (two variants to isolate order effects):
  • Sequence S1 (standard): DMF → EtOH → acetone.
  • Sequence S2 (alternate): DMF → acetone → EtOH.
D3. Implementation: 5 exchange cycles per step; each cycle replaces ≥90% of external liquid volume. Monitor exchange completion by 1H NMR of supernatant (DMF residual) and sample mass change; for monoliths, measure effective diffusivity/permeability by tracking concentration vs time in outlet.
D4. Record solvent compressibility and viscosity (literature) to interpret penetration and equilibration times under pressure; ensure equilibration criterion is met (no further DMF signal decrease in two consecutive cycles).

E. Activation paths (fully specified) and scCO2 transition
E1. scCO2 activation path (primary):
  • After final acetone exchange at P = 0.12 GPa, switch the pressure medium to liquid CO2 in-cell while maintaining pore filling (flow-through replacement, 10–20 pore volumes equivalent).
  • Increase T and P to scCO2 conditions: 313–318 K and 8–12 MPa CO2 (note: this step involves changing the pressure-control modality from 0.12 GPa hydrostatic conditioning to the scCO2 autoclave regime; the sample is never exposed to a gas–liquid meniscus in the pores).
  • Hold 4–6 h with continuous CO2 refresh, then depressurize CO2 at ≤0.2 MPa min−1 to ambient.
E2. Vacuum activation path (control):
  • After solvent exchange, depressurize hydrostatic cell to ambient while keeping sample immersed; then transfer to vacuum oven and activate under dynamic vacuum with a mild ramp (e.g., 298 → 393 K, 1 K min−1, 12 h).
E3. “Pressure-conditioning without scCO2” control:
  • Follow C1 + D (pressure-conditioning + exchange), then do only E2 (vacuum) to isolate the role of pressure history.
E4. “scCO2 without pressure-conditioning” control:
  • Perform ambient-pressure solvent exchange followed by E1 to isolate scCO2 benefit.

F. Full factorial attribution matrix (mandatory isolation of effects)
Factors (binary/ternary as feasible):
  • A: Pressure conditioning (Yes: C1 / No: none)
  • B: Activation (scCO2: E1 / Vacuum: E2)
  • C: Exchange order (S1 / S2)
  • D: Defect regime (Low/Med/High)
Minimum core matrix: A×B×C at Med-defect for each platform (UiO-66(Hf), UiO-67(Hf)) + A×B at Low/High defect for UiO-66(Hf). Include UiO-66(Zr) at Med-defect for A×B.
Replicates/statistics: n = 3 independent synthesis batches per condition for BET and NMR mass balance; report mean ± SD and use ANOVA to attribute main effects and interactions.

G. In situ / operando structural readouts aligned with the mechanistic model
G1. HPPXRD (in situ under hydrostatic medium):
  • Measure unit-cell parameter vs P, peak broadening, and amorphization onset for each defect regime (at least once per regime/platform). Extract bulk modulus (K) from equation-of-state fits in the elastic region.
  • For selected conditions, collect HPPXRD after conditioning + after exchange (still wet) to see whether pressure history changes compressibility/strain (a proxy for microcrack/heterogeneity changes).
G2. Defect chemistry change assay (unambiguous):
  • Pre- vs post-conditioning digested 1H NMR with internal standard + ICP-OES to determine whether modulator/linker occupancy changed; close mass balance within error.
  • If chemical-lever mode used (C2), additionally quantify uptake of added ligand (supernatant depletion) and verify stoichiometry.
G3. Optional advanced probes (only if access is secured and sample environments are compatible):
  • Total scattering/PDF or Hf EXAFS on a reduced subset (one platform, Med-defect, 4 key conditions: baseline, scCO2 only, pressure+vacuum, pressure+scCO2) to test whether local Hf–O disorder changes correlate with K and BET. If not feasible, de-scope without impacting core claims.

H. Primary outcomes and success criteria
H1. Primary endpoint: retained BET surface area (%) relative to solvent-exchanged but unactivated reference, plus micropore volume retention.
H2. Secondary endpoints: hysteresis changes (mesoporosity/interparticle voids), crystallinity retention (PXRD), mechanical robustness (post-activation pelletization stress test + BET), and correlation of BET retention with Π = Pc,max/Pcrit.
H3. Mechanistic decision rules:
  • If pressure-conditioning improves BET even when scCO2 is held constant (compare A=Yes vs No under E1), attribute benefit to pressure history (densification/heterogeneity reduction).
  • If benefit only appears with scCO2 (interaction A×B), attribute to combined pathway suppression of menisci + stress gradients.
  • Only claim defect “healing” if quantitative NMR/ICP/ion balance shows increased linker occupancy or decreased modulator occupancy beyond experimental error, with corresponding structural/mechanical changes.
Feasibility:
1) Addresses the reviewer’s mechanistic concern by replacing speculative defect annealing with a quantitative, falsifiable stress–stability model: capillary pressures (Pc) are computed from measured γ, θ, and PSD and are explicitly correlated against measured mechanical thresholds (bulk modulus/amorphization onset from HPPXRD; modulus from indentation). This operationalizes why the pathway should work at 0.10–0.18 GPa without invoking unlikely spontaneous rebonding.
2) Execution is attribution-focused via a factorial control matrix that isolates (i) scCO2, (ii) pressure-conditioning history, and (iii) exchange order, with statistical replication (n=3) across independent syntheses—directly addressing confounding and over-attribution risk.
3) Pressure–time trajectories are explicitly defined and internally consistent: decompression steps are only to a defined working pressure for exchange (not to ambient), and the sample remains pore-filled through the transition to scCO2, aligning with the stated goal of avoiding menisci/capillary collapse.
4) Defect chemistry is assayed with unambiguous mass-balance methods (quantitative digested NMR with internal standards + ICP-OES, complemented by halide analysis where relevant). Any claim of defect re-speciation/healing is gated behind an added chemical lever (mobile ligand + controlled water/acid + mild heat) and must satisfy stoichiometric closure, preventing chemical overcommitment.
5) High-end measurements (EXAFS/PDF) are de-risked by being optional and limited to a small, pre-specified subset; the core hypothesis can be validated using accessible PXRD/HPPXRD, adsorption, contact-angle/surface-tension data, and quantitative chemistry—ensuring feasibility even with limited beamtime access.
6) Literature alignment: hydrostatic-pressure sensitivity of defective UiO-66 provides a calibrated ‘safe window’ and failure boundary (Asset 2), while the proposal explicitly links structural integrity and porosity retention via mechanical pathway control rather than assumed rebonding (Asset 1 conceptual link). The nanocrystal/monolith form-factor focus and BET-centric validation align with known nanostructure/porosity-performance relationships (Asset 3).
Critique:
This is a strong, attribution-aware plan with unusually good experimental resolution (explicit P–t trajectories, solvent-exchange cycles, scCO2 path, and a factorial matrix with replication) and a commendable insistence on quantitative defect mass balance (qNMR+ICP+anion analysis) before any “healing” claim. The core mechanistic model—collapse driven by capillary stresses and stress gradients interacting with defect-softened mechanical thresholds—is logically coherent and testable via the proposed Π = Pc,max/Pcrit correlation.

Score deductions are primarily for (i) practical and conceptual ambiguities around measuring/using contact angle on MOF pellets/monolith slices (surface roughness, solvent uptake, swelling, and chemical heterogeneity make θ ill-defined; Π may become dominated by measurement artifacts), (ii) incomplete definition of the mechanical failure metric used as Pcrit across powders vs monoliths (HPPXRD amorphization onset, yield, microcrack initiation, and irreversible densification are not equivalent; you need a single operational definition per form factor), and (iii) feasibility/compatibility risk in executing solvent exchange at 0.12 GPa in a hydrostatic cell with repeated replenishment and analytics while maintaining identical internal/external chemical potentials—this is nontrivial and could introduce uncontrolled gradients unless the cell design and flow/exchange protocol are engineered and validated. Finally, densification increasing “framework stiffness” is plausible, but the proposal does not clearly separate reversible elastic stiffening from irreversible densification that may itself reduce accessible porosity; this needs a direct volumetric/structural quantification beyond BET alone (e.g., skeletal density and cell parameter shifts linked to porosity changes).

Hypothesis: A dynamically crosslinked, proton-conducting MOF nanopore coating covalently anchored to the inner wall of a fused-silica capillary will simultaneously (i) increase capillary electrochromatography (CEC) selectivity/efficiency for ionizable drugs and (ii) enable electrically triggered, on-column drug release, because reversible dynamic covalent bonds (hydrazone/imine exchange) can reconfigure the MOF’s pore-surface functionality and local Brønsted acidity under an applied electric field and controlled hydration, thereby modulating electroosmotic flow (EOF), analyte partitioning, and proton-hopping pathways (Grotthuss) in a coupled manner. Methodological adaptation: replace conventional static MOF coatings/monoliths with an open-tubular MOF thin film whose pore apertures are ‘gated’ by dynamic covalent linkers tethered inside the channels and whose interface is permanently anchored to silica via a catechol-silane primer, yielding a self-healing stationary phase that can be tuned in situ (pH/field/humidity) without loss of crystallinity or adhesion.
Plan:
Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select MOF backbone and channel motif: synthesize a chemically robust, 1D-channel Zr-MOF thin film (UiO-66-type) using a mixed-linker strategy: terephthalate (BDC) + aldehyde-functionalized terephthalate (BDC-CHO) at controlled ratios (e.g., 5–30% BDC-CHO) to introduce reactive sites without collapsing porosity.
1.2 Prepare capillary substrate: activate fused-silica inner wall (NaOH/HCl rinse), then deposit a catechol-silane adhesive primer (e.g., dopamine-derived silane or polydopamine + APTES) to provide (i) strong interfacial adhesion and (ii) surface amines for subsequent covalent anchoring.
1.3 Grow an open-tubular MOF film: perform solvothermal layer-by-layer (LbL) or modulated growth (benzoic acid/acetic acid as modulators) to form a 200–800 nm continuous UiO-type film on the inner wall; verify coverage by SEM (capillary cross-sections) and XRD (scraped film reference).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Install dynamic covalent ‘pore gates’: diffuse bifunctional hydrazides or diamines into the MOF to form reversible hydrazone (with BDC-CHO) or imine linkages, producing a dynamic covalent network partially spanning pore windows. Tune gate density by BDC-CHO content and linker length (e.g., adipic dihydrazide vs aromatic dihydrazide) to target pore-aperture modulation in the 0.5–1.0 nm regime.
2.2 Create proton-conduction pathways: introduce a confined proton-carrier guest (e.g., 1H-1,2,4-triazole or imidazole) by vapor/solution infiltration; co-introduce small amounts of sulfonic acid (e.g., tethered sulfonate via mono-hydrazide bearing –SO3H) to create fixed acid sites while preserving dynamic exchange at other positions.
2.3 Covalent anchoring to prevent film delamination: couple a fraction of MOF aldehydes to capillary-wall amines (Schiff base) followed by mild reductive amination (NaBH3CN) ONLY at the interface to “lock” the MOF to the substrate, while leaving internal aldehydes reversible for gating.
2.4 Implement CEC operation and stimulus control: run CEC with controlled humidity/aqueous-organic mobile phases (e.g., 10–40% ACN, buffered pH 3–8). Apply electric field (e.g., 100–400 V/cm). Modulate pH and field polarity to shift imine/hydrazone equilibria and guest protonation state; optionally apply short high-field pulses to induce transient gate opening for release.
2.5 Drug loading/release demonstration: load model ionizable drugs (e.g., propranolol, lidocaine, diclofenac) into the MOF coating under low-field conditions, then trigger release by switching to a condition that (i) protonates carriers and increases proton conductivity and (ii) shifts dynamic covalent equilibrium to a more open-pore state (acidic pulse for hydrazones; basic pulse for certain imines).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural/chemical validation: confirm dynamic covalent formation by FTIR (C=N), solid-state NMR (if feasible), and derivatization assays on aldehyde consumption; quantify guest loading by TGA and solvent extraction/LC.
3.2 Proton conduction quantification: perform impedance spectroscopy on analogous MOF films on planar interdigitated electrodes under controlled RH to extract σH+ vs RH and vs gate density; correlate σH+ with CEC EOF stability.
3.3 CEC performance metrics: measure EOF (neutral marker), plate number, resolution, selectivity factors for drug panels across pH/field/RH; compare to (i) bare silica, (ii) static UiO-66 film without dynamic gates, (iii) conventional silica C18, and (iv) polymer monolith.
3.4 Mechanistic tests: (a) gate-density series (BDC-CHO %) to link pore gating with retention/selectivity; (b) isotope effect (H2O vs D2O mobile phase) to probe Grotthuss contribution; (c) competitive guest experiments (triazole present/absent) to decouple proton-carrier contribution from mere surface charge.
3.5 Durability/self-healing: perform 200–500 run cycling, including deliberate pH shocks; track performance recovery after “damage” (drying/rewetting) to evidence dynamic covalent self-repair; inspect film integrity post-cycling by SEM.
3.6 Drug-delivery relevance: quantify on-column controlled release kinetics (peak-area vs trigger protocol), and evaluate payload protection (stability of labile drugs) by comparing degradation products with/without MOF confinement.
Feasibility:
1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: MOFs are established as high-surface-area solid stationary phases for CEC, and proton conduction in MOFs is known to be enhanced by heterocycles (e.g., triazole/imidazole) and hydration, consistent with Grotthuss/vehicular mechanisms. Dynamic covalent bonds (imine/hydrazone) provide reversible, stimulus-responsive functional reconfiguration under mild conditions compatible with organic/water mobile phases.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal uses a rational Zr-MOF (UiO-type) for hydrolytic stability, mixed-linker installation of aldehyde handles for post-synthetic dynamic covalent chemistry inside nanopores, and interfacial covalent anchoring to silica to satisfy capillary-format constraints (thin, adherent, low backpressure). The dynamic covalent network is deliberately confined to pore interiors (tunable gating) while the interface is locked, enabling a true ‘adaptive stationary phase’ rather than a degradable coating.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to static MOF/silica phases, the dynamic-gated MOF can be tuned in situ to optimize separations across diverse drug chemotypes without re-packing or re-coating. Coupling proton-conducting guests with fixed acid sites stabilizes EOF and adds an orthogonal control knob (σH+) to modulate retention and release. The self-healing dynamic covalent chemistry addresses a key limitation of MOF capillary coatings—microcracking/delamination and irreversible fouling—by allowing reversible bond exchange and functional re-equilibration after stress, improving lifetime and reproducibility.
