Chemical plausibility of Zn–O–Si tethering is addressed by (i) restricting hydrolysis/condensation chemistry to pre-formed, low-water-activity silanol oligomers, which reduces uncontrolled in-pore TEOS hydrolysis and bulk silica precipitation, and (ii) explicitly proving (or falsifying) interfacial Zn–O–Si formation using orthogonal, interface-sensitive techniques (DRIFTS, Zn K-edge EXAFS, ToF-SIMS fragments) with rigorous physical-mixture and “no-anchor” controls. Risk of MOF damage is managed by a quantified stability envelope (water-activity screening) and hard mass-balance criteria: Zn leaching (ICP of every liquor) and linker loss (solution NMR of supernatants) must remain below preset thresholds; otherwise conditions are rejected.

Spatial localization (pore-mouth skin vs internal filling) is made testable by cross-sectional metrology (FIB-SEM + STEM-EDS/EELS thickness statistics on many crystals) rather than relying on porogen intuition. The mandatory falsifiable criterion separating “gating” from “pore blocking” is built into the workflow: improved selectivity must coincide with preserved internal micropore PSD/volume (NLDFT) and a transport signature requiring a new surface barrier term (dual-resistance modeling) while maintaining intracrystalline diffusivity comparable to pristine material. If selectivity gains only occur alongside major micropore volume loss or broad PSD collapse, the mechanism is reclassified as blocking and the central hypothesis is rejected.

Acidity claims are strengthened by explicitly recognizing the reviewer’s concern that low-temperature alumination can yield extra-framework Al. The proposal therefore (i) decouples constriction (Si loading) from acid creation (Al insertion route), (ii) assigns Al coordination/speciation using 27Al MQMAS, and (iii) quantifies Brønsted sites via Hofmann elimination (or NH3-TPD), then correlates Brønsted density with Henry-regime benzene adsorption enthalpy (qst) to mechanistically connect acidity to benzene preconcentration.

Finally, thickness inference from ICP-AES is no longer underdetermined because ICP is used as a mass constraint that is cross-validated with direct thickness distributions from cross-sectional microscopy and with porosity-derived accessible volume changes; optional SAXS provides an additional independent core–shell check. Together, these upgrades satisfy the reviewer-mandated proof standard and de-risk the key assertions while preserving the original concept chain (zeolite-like gate chemistry + CUB-21 confinement) for benzene/cyclohexane separations.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in engineering resolution: it specifies a stability envelope, hard mass-balance controls, negative controls for interfacial bonding, cross-sectional localization metrology, and a mechanistically discriminating ‘gating vs blocking’ decision rule. The main scientific vulnerability is chemical plausibility/uniqueness of the claimed Zn–O–Si interfacial covalent linkage under the proposed conditions. In Zn4O-carboxylate nodes, generating persistent Zn–OH anchor sites without concurrent node hydrolysis/ligand exchange is nontrivial, and the pre-treatment (iPrOH + 200–1000 ppm H2O) may either be too weak to form a meaningful anchor population or, conversely, initiate exactly the hydrolysis pathway you aim to avoid. Relatedly, DRIFTS/ToF-SIMS are suggestive but not definitive for covalent Zn–O–Si vs strongly adsorbed/ionically bound silica; EXAFS sensitivity to a minority surface population may be marginal unless Si loading is high enough to risk blocking, creating a potential internal contradiction between detectability and non-invasiveness. The transport-model claim (new ks barrier with preserved D) is well-posed but may be underdetermined unless external film resistance, particle size distribution, and heat effects are rigorously controlled; otherwise, fitted ‘surface barriers’ can be artifacts. Finally, the acidity chain (Al speciation → Brønsted density → Henry benzene qst/selectivity) is conceptually coherent, but ensuring that measured acid sites reside at the gate (not on detached aluminosilicate particulates or external deposits) will require additional spatially resolved acidity validation beyond bulk Hofmann/TPD.

Hypothesis: A MOFomics-guided, isoreticular dual-network MOF—comprised of (i) a hydrolytically robust, high-surface-area host with 1D channels and (ii) a geometrically confined, intrachannel-only mixed-valence Cu–(quinone/catecholate)–Cu sublattice—will deliver chemiresistive sensors that simultaneously maximize analyte uptake (host-controlled) and electrical signal transduction (sublattice-controlled). The key mechanistic advance over conventional ‘conductive MOF vs porous MOF’ tradeoffs is enforced spatial separation of function: adsorption occurs predominantly on the preserved host pore surface, while charge transport occurs on a topologically constrained 1D hopping backbone whose conductivity is governed by (a) percolation/continuity of Cu–L–Cu segments and (b) a tunable thermally activated hopping barrier (Ea) linked to ligand-to-metal charge transfer energetics and effective band gap. By pre-designing docking-site topology so that only intrachannel bidentate closure is sterically and geometrically allowed (and interchannel bridging is forbidden), the in-pore sublattice is confined, periodic, and resistant to pore-blocking precipitation. The targeted ‘operational band-gap window’ (0.8–2.5 eV) is justified not as an abstract semiconductor range, but because it corresponds—via a quantified hopping/percolation model incorporating mixed-valence ratio, segment correlation length, film/contact resistance, and humidity-dependent ionic leakage—to room-temperature σfilm that is high enough to overcome contact-limited noise yet low enough to preserve high chemiresistive modulation upon analyte-induced redox/coordination perturbations.
Plan:
Step 0 — Hard design constraints (pre-synthesis) to guarantee confinement/continuity
0.1 Intrachannel-only docking geometry (exclude interchannel bridging): Select a 1D-channel host topology where (i) channels are separated by pore-wall thickness > 7 Å (through-framework distance between adjacent channel voids), and (ii) docking pockets are oriented strictly into the channel with a steric ‘backstop’ to prevent outward coordination. Implement with mixed-linker substitution where the minority docking linker bears a chelator (e.g., bipyridyl, hydroxamate, salicylaldimine-like O,N set) attached through a rigid spacer that fixes its bite vector toward the channel centerline.
0.2 Geometric acceptance rule (computational, before synthesis): For each candidate host, compute from the crystal structure:
- Intrachannel docking-to-docking distance (d_in) along the channel axis and its distribution.
- Minimum interchannel docking-pocket approach distance (d_out) through the framework.
Require: d_out − d_in ≥ 4 Å AND docking bite vectors deviate < 15° from the channel radial direction (ensures that a bidentate quinone/catecholate bridge can only close within the same channel). Reject hosts failing this.
0.3 Bridging ligand length matching: Choose quinone/catecholate derivatives with terminal coordination distances that match d_in within ±5% to suppress chain termination and off-axis coordination. Prepare a small ligand library (3–5 ligands) spanning electron-withdrawing/donating substituents (e.g., F/Cl/CF3 vs Me/OMe) while keeping the backbone length constant.

Step 1 — MOFomics dataset: descriptor provenance, size, and uncertainty strategy
1.1 Data assembly (minimum viable dataset sizes):
- Host scaffold dataset: ≥200 structures (experimental + hypothetical isoreticular variants) with measured or GCMC-predicted BET/pore volume/PSD and qualitative stability labels (water/acid/base tolerance) supplemented by computed bond valence/metal–ligand strength proxies.
- Electronic/transport dataset (label scarcity acknowledged): ≥50 frameworks/variants with experimentally measured band gap (DRS), σ(T), and/or activation energy; for mixed-valence Cu motifs include ≥20 entries with XAS/EPR-confirmed valence ratios.
1.2 Descriptor provenance (explicit):
- Measured: BET, PXRD stability, DRS band gap, σ(T), Ea, ICP-MS leaching.
- Computed: GCMC uptake/accessible surface after docking (geometric pore blocking model), DFT(+U) band edges/DOS for a *calibrated subset*, and polaron hopping barriers from cluster Marcus analysis (see Step 3).
1.3 DFT(+U) calibration protocol (to control U/spin/defects sensitivity):
- Calibrate U on Cu using a training subset where XPS/XAS valence ratios and optical gaps are measured; choose U that minimizes error in (i) band gap and (ii) Cu 2p core-level shifts/charge localization trends.
- Sample multiple charge/spin orderings for mixed valence (at least 3 orderings per structure) and propagate the spread as label uncertainty.
1.4 Model + acquisition: Use an uncertainty-calibrated surrogate (Gaussian process or GNN with conformal prediction) and a multi-objective acquisition function that penalizes high-uncertainty electronic labels unless they are within the ‘decision boundary’ for go/no-go. Maintain an external test set (≥20% of data, time-split if possible).
1.5 Candidate downselect (6–10 total): stratify by docking density (e.g., 2%, 5%, 10% docking-linker fraction) and by ligand substituent set (EWG/EDG) while holding host constant for mechanistic comparability.

Step 2 — Synthesis with engineered docking-site topology and controlled intrapore metallation
2.1 Host synthesis (robust high-area 1D channels):
- Primary host family: Ti-oxo carboxylate (MUV-10-like) for hydrolytic robustness and tunable band structure; secondary control family: Zr6-oxo carboxylate with analogous channel dimensions.
- Mixed-linker implementation: majority trimesate-type linker for rigidity + minority docking linker (2–10 mol%) bearing fixed inward chelator. Verify linker incorporation by digestion NMR and quantitative LC-MS of digests.
2.2 Crystallinity-preserving activation (SC–SC where possible): staged solvent exchange (DMF→EtOH→acetone) followed by supercritical CO2 drying; accept as ‘activated’ only if BET retention ≥80% of undocked host reference and PXRD matches within defined Rwp threshold.
2.3 Intrapore “pore-wall chelation docking” with precipitation suppression:
- Sequence: (i) pre-coordinate redox ligand to docking pockets at low concentration under diffusion-limited conditions; (ii) rinse to remove free ligand; (iii) introduce Cu precursor under conditions favoring pocket-first binding (use weakly coordinating anions, e.g., triflate) and low supersaturation.
- Confinement control: keep total Cu loading below the calculated monolayer capacity of docking sites (target 0.9–1.1 equiv per pocket) to avoid nucleation of bulk Cu–quinone phases.
- Redox control: establish mixed valence using either electrochemical poising (working electrode film) or buffered chemical redox pairs; target Cu(I)/Cu(II) or Cu(I)/Cu(III) ratios in a controlled series (e.g., 20/80, 50/50, 80/20).
2.4 Anti-crosslinking steric safeguard: include a ‘pocket cap’ design element—bulky substituent on the docking linker positioned behind the chelator—to block outward coordination. This is a design criterion in Step 0 and verified by SCXRD (if available) or Rietveld-refined PXRD + DFT geometry optimization.

Step 3 — Falsifiable engineering test plan for continuity and confinement (mandatory acceptance criteria)
3.1 Structural confinement tests (pass/fail):
(A) SCXRD / high-resolution PXRD (where SCXRD unavailable):
- Pass if electron density / refined occupancy for Cu is localized at docking pockets with no additional Cu sites in the pore center or interchannel region.
(B) XAS (EXAFS/XANES) with quantitative fitting:
- Fit Cu first-shell coordination: require ≥85% of Cu assigned to the intended pocket coordination environment (Cu–O/N distances consistent with design ±0.05 Å), and ≤15% ‘off-target’ fraction (Cu–O-only or Cu–Cu metallic-like contributions).
(C) PDF (pair distribution function) for 1D correlation length:
- Define the Cu–Cu (or Cu–ligand–Cu) axial repeat signature. Require a minimum correlation length Lcorr ≥ 4 repeats (i.e., ≥ ~4×d_in) to claim ‘continuous sublattice’ rather than isolated dimers/trimers.
- Fail if PDF indicates significant Cu–Cu distances corresponding to interchannel bridging or bulk Cu–quinone phases.
3.2 Pore preservation tests (pass/fail):
- BET retention after docking: ≥60% of host BET AND pore size distribution retains the primary channel mode (no disappearance of the 1D channel peak).
- Reject if hysteresis/PSD indicates pore blockage beyond a pre-set pore volume loss threshold (e.g., >40%).
3.3 Precipitation/external phase exclusion:
- SEM/TEM + EDS mapping: Cu signal must be spatially uniform without external nanoparticles.
- Leaching check during washing: Cu in supernatant quantified by ICP-MS must fall below threshold after final rinse (define threshold, e.g., <1% of total Cu per wash step).

Step 4 — Quantitative transport/percolation model tied to measurable targets (mandatory)
4.1 Model form (inputs → σfilm prediction):
- Treat the Cu–L–Cu chain as a 1D hopping network with site occupation probability p (fraction of docking pockets successfully metallated and bridged) and segment length distribution determined from Lcorr.
- Effective conductivity along channels: σchain(T) = σ0 · p · exp(−Ea/kT), where Ea is obtained from Marcus hopping: Ea ≈ (λ/4)·(1 + ΔG°/λ)^2; λ (reorganization) and ΔG° (driving force) are estimated from cluster calculations and experimentally constrained by optical/XPS redox energetics.
- Percolation/continuity criterion: require p above a critical value for finite-length channels; operationally enforce via Lcorr criterion in Step 3.
4.2 Incorporate film/contact resistance and humidity explicitly:
- Use a series resistance model: Rmeas = Rcontact + (L/A)/σfilm.
- Establish target σfilm range so that Rcontact does not dominate (e.g., require Rfilm ≤ 0.3·Rcontact in baseline to ensure measurable modulation; determine Rcontact empirically from transmission line method on blank electrodes).
- Humidity term: include parallel ionic leakage conductance Gion(RH) extracted from impedance spectroscopy; require σelectronic to exceed humidity-induced ionic contribution under operating RH (e.g., 20–60% RH) by a defined factor (≥5×) to maintain chemiresistive specificity.
4.3 Justify the 0.8–2.5 eV ‘band-gap window’ via targets:
- For room-temperature operation, aim for Ea ≈ 0.05–0.25 eV to obtain σfilm in ~10^−6 to 10^−3 S·cm^−1 (measurable on microelectrode films without being fully metallic). Use the calibrated relationship between optical gap / charge-transfer energy and Ea (from Step 4.1 + Step 3.2 data) rather than assuming a direct band-gap-to-σ mapping.
- Predetermine go/no-go conductivity: if σfilm(298 K) < 10^−8 S·cm^−1 (contact-limited/noise dominated) OR >10^−2 S·cm^−1 (response compression), deprioritize that candidate for sensing arrays.
4.4 Experimental extraction:
- Temperature-dependent two-/four-probe σ(T) on oriented films; fit ln(σT^n) vs 1/T to distinguish hopping vs band-like transport.
- Impedance spectroscopy vs RH to separate electronic/ionic components.

Step 5 — Redox/humidity stability protocol and decision tree (mandatory)
5.1 Cycling protocol (quantified):
- Redox cycling: 100 cycles between defined potentials (or chemical redox states) corresponding to Cu valence ratio swings (e.g., 20/80 ↔ 80/20), monitoring PXRD, XAS, and σ after 1, 10, 50, 100 cycles.
- Humidity aging: 7-day exposure at 50% RH and 25 °C + 24 h challenge at 80% RH; optionally include acidic/basic vapor pulses relevant to analytes.
5.2 Leaching and structural retention metrics:
- ICP-MS on condensate/extracts: cumulative Cu loss must be ≤5% after full protocol.
- BET retention after cycling/aging: ≥70% of post-docking BET.
- PXRD similarity: predefined threshold (e.g., peak positions retained; Rietveld residual change within set bounds).
5.3 Go/no-go decision tree:
- Go to sensor array scaling only if ALL are met: (i) confinement/continuity acceptance (Step 3.1), (ii) σfilm in target window and humidity specificity (Step 4), (iii) stability retention (Step 5.2).
- If continuity fails but porosity/stability passes: increase docking density or improve ligand length matching.
- If precipitation/off-target Cu fraction fails: reduce Cu activity (precursor/anion), lower loading, or strengthen pocket selectivity.
- If humidity causes ionic domination: introduce hydrophobic pore-surface modulation (minimal, to preserve uptake) or operate with RH compensation algorithm; only proceed if electronic/ionic separation is restored.

Step 6 — Sensor fabrication, mechanistic validation, and closed-loop MOFomics update
6.1 Film fabrication: oriented films on interdigitated electrodes via seeded growth or electrophoretic deposition of nanocrystals followed by mild necking; quantify Rcontact via TLM.
6.2 Sensing tests: analytes (NH3, H2S, NO2, VOCs) under controlled RH; report sensitivity, response/recovery times, drift over cycling.
6.3 Mechanistic causality: combine QCM uptake, in situ DRIFTS (adsorption site identification), in situ XAS/EPR/XPS (valence ratio shift), and in situ conductivity to verify that analyte adsorption perturbs Cu/ligand redox equilibrium and hence hopping rate.
6.4 Controls: host-only, sublattice-only analog (dense conductive CP with low area), and dual-network to demonstrate decoupling.
6.5 Feedback: update the surrogate model with measured labels and uncertainties; refine docking periodicity rules and ligand substituent selection for specific analyte classes.
Feasibility:
1) Chemical/structural feasibility is de-risked by ‘geometry-first’ confinement: docking-site topology is pre-screened so only intrachannel bidentate closure is allowed (steric backstop + inward bite vectors + d_out − d_in margin). This directly addresses the reviewer’s concern about interchannel crosslinking.
2) Off-target Cu–quinone precipitation and pore blockage are controlled by (i) pocket-first binding sequence, (ii) strict Cu loading capped to docking capacity, and (iii) explicit rejection criteria based on EXAFS off-target fraction (≤15%), PDF signatures, and microscopy. The proposal no longer assumes success; it defines what constitutes failure and how it will be detected early.
3) Continuity of the 1D sublattice is made falsifiable via a minimum Cu–Cu correlation length (Lcorr ≥ 4 repeats) from PDF plus SCXRD/PXRD site localization and XAS quantification—meeting the mandated engineering test plan.
4) The band-gap target is mechanistically justified through a quantitative transport framework: σfilm is predicted/fit as a function of docking occupation p, mixed-valence ratio, and hopping barrier Ea (Marcus), then translated into measurable Rmeas including contact resistance and humidity-induced ionic leakage. This converts the 0.8–2.5 eV ‘window’ into an operational requirement tied to σfilm and sensor SNR rather than a generic semiconducting range.
5) Stability concerns (redox cycling + humidity) are addressed with a defined protocol (cycle counts, RH levels) and hard metrics (ICP-MS Cu loss ≤5%; BET and PXRD retention thresholds) plus a go/no-go decision tree before scaling.
6) MOFomics predictive risk is bounded by explicit descriptor provenance, minimum dataset sizes, DFT(+U) calibration to experimental references, propagation of spin/charge-ordering uncertainty, and external test-set validation with uncertainty-calibrated acquisition to avoid overclaiming. This ensures that computation informs design without being treated as infallible.
Grounding in prior art from the provided assets: (i) electrically conductive coordination polymers and their sensor relevance motivate chemiresistive targets and the need for controlled doping/porous electrodes; (ii) mixed-valence Cu MOFs with non-innocent benzoquinoid ligands demonstrate feasible semiconducting transport pathways; (iii) robust Ti-oxo frameworks show high surface area and band-gap tunability via heterometal doping; (iv) MOFomics/high-throughput screening is established for adsorption and structure–property mapping and is extended here with disciplined uncertainty handling.
Critique: The proposal is unusually strong in engineering specificity: it predefines confinement geometry, explicitly rejects failure modes (crosslinking, precipitation, pore blocking) with quantitative pass/fail criteria, and ties the band-gap discussion to measurable σfilm through a hopping/percolation/contact/humidity model rather than generic semiconductor rhetoric. Main scientific risks remain: (i) achieving true periodic, intrachannel-only Cu–L–Cu chain formation at low docking-linker fractions without a large population of dead-end motifs (dimers/trimers) is still chemically nontrivial even if geometrically allowed; (ii) the Marcus-barrier parameterization (λ, ΔG°) from clusters may not transfer to the extended, defect-rich MOF environment, and the proposed ‘calibrated relationship’ between optical gap/CT energy and Ea could be weak or non-unique; (iii) the stated dataset sizes (especially ≥50 transport-labeled, ≥20 mixed-valence XAS/EPR-confirmed) are ambitious and, if not met, could make the MOFomics component underpowered or overfit despite uncertainty tooling; (iv) Ti-oxo hosts with mixed-linker chelators plus repeated redox cycling may still face slow framework degradation or pocket hydrolysis not fully captured by PXRD/BET retention alone (local defect growth can preserve diffraction). These issues temper the otherwise excellent mechanistic and execution rigor.

Hypothesis: In HKUST-1, external pressure does not directly “amplify” gas polarizability; instead, pressure increases loading and drives a coordination/packing transition in which O2 (and other quadrupolar/paramagnetic guests) increasingly populate the coordinatively unsaturated Cu(II) paddlewheel sites and their first-shell vicinity. This changes (i) site occupancy statistics, (ii) guest orientation distributions, and (iii) the local electric field magnitude and anisotropy experienced by both guest and node. We hypothesize that these loading-dependent local fields induce non-negligible polarization energy (induction + charge–quadrupole) at open Cu sites that is systematically underestimated by non-polarizable force fields, and that this polarization manifests as predictable, loading-dependent vibrational frequency shifts. Specifically, we predict two pressure-resolved adsorption regimes in HKUST-1: (Regime A) low loading where adsorption is dominated by pore-filling with weak field gradients and small induced dipoles; (Regime B) higher loading where Cu-site occupancy increases and local fields at/near Cu generate larger induced dipoles and altered Cu–O(carboxylate)/Cu–Cu force constants and guest intramolecular modes. By combining a fully specified induced-dipole (Thole-damped) polarizable GCMC protocol with a quantitative Raman linkage—mapping simulated local field/polarization energy and site populations to computed vibrational frequency shifts on representative loaded fragments—we will mechanistically separate electronic induction signatures from confounders (framework strain/compression, residual hydration/site blocking, and pressure-induced structural changes). A physically realistic comparison to zeolite NaX will be made by explicitly including Na+ cation sites and framework/guest polarizability, and by focusing on comparable observables (guest-mode Raman/IR shifts and adsorption thermodynamics) rather than non-analogous framework modes.
Plan:
Step 0 — Materials control and activation state definition (HKUST-1 vs NaX)
0.1 HKUST-1 synthesis/activation: Synthesize phase-pure HKUST-1; activate under dynamic vacuum with a temperature program (e.g., 120–180 °C) to target a controlled fraction of open Cu sites. Prepare three controlled states: (i) fully activated (max open sites), (ii) partially hydrated (controlled H2O dose), (iii) site-blocked control (e.g., low-dose NH3 or pyridine as a strong ligand at Cu) to suppress open-site adsorption.
0.2 Verify open-site fraction and residual water: (a) CO-probe IR (Cu(I)/Cu(II)–CO band intensity as site metric), (b) TGA/DSC for residual solvent/water, (c) XANES/EXAFS at Cu K-edge to confirm coordination number changes upon activation/hydration, (d) PXRD to confirm phase purity.
0.3 NaX preparation: Ion-exchange NaX to a defined Na+ population (avoid mixed cations); dehydrate under controlled conditions. Quantify water content by TGA and confirm cation distribution consistency (as feasible) by composition analysis and literature-informed site occupancy (SI/SII positions).

Step 1 — Polarizable force field choice and full polarizable GCMC specification (mandatory: one formalism)
1.1 Polarization formalism: Use an induced point-dipole model with Thole damping (not Drude) to avoid adding explicit Drude particles in GCMC moves. Assign polarizabilities to: (i) Cu centers (anisotropic tensor, αCu, reflecting open-site directionality), (ii) key node atoms (carboxylate O, selected Cu-adjacent O/C atoms) with smaller isotropic α, and (iii) guest molecules (O2, N2, H2) with literature polarizability tensors (and quadrupole moments where appropriate). Organic linker atoms otherwise retain fixed partial charges.
1.2 Total energy per configuration:
Utotal = UvdW + Uperm-elec + Upol + U3body(optional)
where
- UvdW: Lennard-Jones 12-6 with Lorentz–Berthelot mixing (or refit near Cu if needed).
- Uperm-elec: Coulomb interactions among permanent charges and guest multipoles (include at least quadrupoles for N2/O2 if using explicit multipole model; otherwise represent via charged sites consistent with validated models).
- Upol = 1/2 μ^T α^{-1} μ − μ · Eloc, summed over polarizable sites, with μ induced dipoles and Eloc the local electric field from permanent charges/multipoles and other induced dipoles.
- Thole damping: Apply Thole screening to dipole–dipole interactions and field contributions using an exponential Thole function with damping parameter a (to be fit; initial a ≈ 0.3–0.4 typical) to prevent polarization catastrophe near open Cu.
1.3 Self-consistent induced dipole solution per MC move:
- For each trial insertion/deletion/translation/rotation, solve induced dipoles by iterative SCF (e.g., successive over-relaxation or conjugate gradient).
- Convergence: max| Δμ | < 1×10−5 Debye or relative change in Upol < 1×10−7 per polarizable site; cap iterations (e.g., 200) with fallback to rejected move if not converged.
- Use predictor: initialize induced dipoles from previous accepted configuration to accelerate convergence.
1.4 Long-range electrostatics:
- Periodic boundary conditions with Ewald summation for permanent charges/multipoles.
- For induced dipoles: use Ewald for dipole–dipole interactions (polarization Ewald) with Thole damping applied in real space; reciprocal-space handled consistently (or use a PME-like implementation if available in chosen code).
- Validate convergence with respect to Ewald parameters (real-space cutoff, κ, reciprocal vectors).
1.5 Ensemble and sampling:
- Perform polarizable GCMC for O2 (primary), and N2/H2 as mechanistic comparators, across 1–50 bar and multiple temperatures (e.g., 298 K and one higher/lower T).
- Compute: excess uptake, absolute uptake, site-resolved occupancy (Cu-site vs pore), isosteric heats Qst via fluctuation formula and via Clausius–Clapeyron across temperatures.
- Output mechanistic descriptors vs loading: (i) Cu-site occupancy fraction, (ii) induced dipole magnitude distributions on Cu and guests, (iii) local electric field distributions at Cu (vector magnitude and axial component along Cu open-site direction), (iv) polarization energy partition (Cu vs guest vs node).

Step 2 — Parameterization and tiered validation set (beyond isotherms)
2.1 Ab initio training set (cluster + periodic checks):
- Cluster models: Cu2(O2CR)4 with truncated benzoate/acetate ligands and an axial open site; generate geometries with O2/N2/H2 at multiple distances/orientations (including side-on/end-on for O2) and with/without co-adsorbates to mimic higher loading.
- Compute DFT binding energies, energy decomposition proxies (e.g., induction via SAPT on reduced models where feasible), and electric field/induced dipole response; extract anisotropic polarizability tensor at Cu site (or effective tensor fit) consistent with observed coordination environment.
- Periodic benchmark: a small set of periodic DFT single-point adsorption energies and charge response (e.g., Bader/CM5) at representative loadings to verify transferability.
2.2 Force field fitting targets:
- Match DFT binding energies at Cu site (low coverage) within ~1–2 kJ/mol.
- Match distance/orientation dependence of adsorption near Cu (potential energy surface).
- Match induced dipole magnitude trends and field response (effective polarizability) from DFT.
2.3 Experimental validation tiers:
Tier 1 (thermodynamics): high-pressure isotherms up to ≥30 bar (HKUST-1 benchmarked to known performance; connect to Asset 1 methodology) and Qst vs loading.
Tier 2 (site populations/structures): where feasible, use in situ PXRD or neutron diffraction (or literature data) to validate Cu-site vs pore filling populations; alternatively, use in situ XAS under gas pressure to track coordination changes at Cu.
Tier 3 (spectroscopy): Raman/IR guest-mode shifts and framework-mode shifts vs pressure/loading, with controls for hydration and site blocking.

Step 3 — Explicit pressure-to-loading-to-field mechanism and framework strain control
3.1 Pressure affects loading/packing: Convert pressure to chemical potential in GCMC; compute adsorption isotherms and occupancy transitions; identify pressures at which Cu-site occupancy sharply increases.
3.2 Framework mechanics/strain handling:
- Primary approach: justify rigid lattice for baseline by citing HKUST-1 structural robustness under cycling/high pressure (Asset 1) and confirm by in situ PXRD cell-parameter tracking under pressure.
- Add a correction/uncertainty analysis: incorporate an effective compressibility model by repeating GCMC on two to three lattices with cell parameters adjusted according to measured (or literature) compressibility; quantify impact on (i) uptake, (ii) Cu-site occupancy, (iii) predicted Raman shifts.
- Distinguish strain vs induction: if Raman shifts correlate with measured cell contraction rather than simulated local-field metrics, attribute accordingly; use blocked-site and hydrated controls to decouple.

Step 4 — Quantitative Raman linkage (mandatory mapping, not qualitative)
4.1 Define Raman observables:
- HKUST-1 framework modes sensitive to node environment: Cu–Cu stretch and Cu–O(carboxylate) vibrations (track both frequency and linewidth).
- Guest modes: O–O stretch (for O2) and N–N stretch (for N2) where detectable; if Raman weak, supplement with IR for guest modes.
4.2 Compute vibrational frequency shifts from representative loaded configurations:
- From polarizable GCMC, select statistically representative snapshots at multiple loadings (e.g., low, mid, high) and with defined Cu-site occupancy counts.
- Build embedded fragments: Cu2 paddlewheel + first coordination shell + nearest linker atoms, with external point charges/dipoles taken from the GCMC snapshot (electrostatic embedding including induced dipoles) to reproduce local field.
- Perform DFT vibrational frequency calculations on these fragments to obtain Δν for Cu–Cu, Cu–O, and guest intramolecular modes as a function of (i) Cu-site occupancy, (ii) computed local field component along the adsorption axis, and (iii) polarization energy Upol.
4.3 Establish a predictive correlation:
- Fit a regression/physics-informed model such as Δν = A·Eloc,ax + B·Upol(Cu) + C·nCu-guest + D·ΔV/V (strain term) to explicitly separate induction vs strain contributions.
- Use this to generate predicted Raman shift vs pressure curves by mapping pressure→loading (GCMC)→(Eloc, Upol, occupancy)→Δν.
4.4 Experimental Raman under pressure:
- Conduct in situ high-pressure Raman with controlled temperature; record spectra during adsorption/desorption to check reversibility and hysteresis.
- Compare measured Δν(P) and linewidth changes to predicted Δν(P) and to occupancy transitions; apply blocked-site and hydrated controls to verify that signatures vanish/shift as predicted when Cu sites are unavailable.

Step 5 — Realistic NaX comparison (mandatory: physically correct polarization + comparable observables)
5.1 NaX polarizable model:
- Include explicit Na+ cations at crystallographic sites with fixed +1 charge; represent framework (aluminosilicate) with fixed charges consistent with known NaX force fields.
- Add induced dipoles on oxygen atoms (and/or Si/Al if needed) with Thole damping; optionally include guest polarizability as above.
- Do not claim “delocalized polarization” without explicit induced-dipole sites; polarization is local on framework O atoms and interacts with strong static fields from Na+.
5.2 Comparable spectroscopic observables:
- Focus on guest vibrational shifts (O2/N2) in NaX rather than framework modes that are not symmetry-analogous to HKUST-1 node modes.
- Supplement with IR if Raman sensitivity is low in NaX; track how guest-mode shifts correlate with Na+ site occupancy and local fields predicted by GCMC.
5.3 Water/cation confounders:
- Maintain matched dehydration protocols and quantify residual water; perform a controlled “wet” NaX condition to show the effect of water on cation sites and guest-mode shifts.

Step 6 — Deliverables, robustness, and decision points
6.1 Deliverables:
- A validated polarizable GCMC workflow for HKUST-1 and NaX with full energy decomposition and occupancy statistics.
- Pressure-resolved mechanistic map: pressure→loading→Cu-site occupancy→local field/polarization energy→Raman/IR shifts.
- Clear discrimination criteria: (i) disappearance of induction-driven Raman signatures upon Cu-site blocking/hydration, (ii) distinct guest-mode shift–loading correlations in HKUST-1 vs NaX.
6.2 Robustness tests:
- Sensitivity to Thole parameter a, Cu polarizability tensor anisotropy, and partial charge set.
- Replicate simulations with alternative initial cation configurations in NaX to bound variability.
- Cycling experiments (adsorption/desorption) and post-cycling PXRD/XAS to ensure no irreversible structural change is misassigned to polarization effects.
Feasibility:
Mechanistic specificity (pressure→loading→field): The revised premise removes the incorrect implication that pressure directly increases polarizability. Pressure increases chemical potential, raising loading and Cu-site occupancy; this changes local electric fields and induced dipoles, which we will compute explicitly (field and Upol distributions) and connect to spectroscopy via embedded fragment vibrational calculations. This directly addresses the reviewer request for a quantitative chain from loading-dependent fields/coordination to vibrational shifts while separating strain terms.

Algorithmic completeness of polarizable GCMC: The proposal now specifies a single polarization formalism (Thole-damped induced dipoles), explicit energy terms, SCF convergence criteria per MC move, polarization-catastrophe prevention (Thole damping), and long-range electrostatics (Ewald for charges and dipoles). These are standard, implementable components in modern polarizable simulation frameworks and are sufficient to evaluate transferability across loadings.

Transferability and validation beyond isotherms: Parameterization is tied to a tiered validation set: DFT adsorption energies and effective anisotropic polarizabilities at Cu sites (cluster and selected periodic checks), Qst vs loading, and experimental site populations (XAS/PXRD/neutron where feasible). This reduces the risk that fitted parameters only reproduce macroscopic isotherms while missing the correct microscopic mechanism.

Confounder control (hydration, compression, structural changes): Residual water and partial site blocking are treated as explicit experimental states and modeled conditions, enabling falsifiable tests of the open-site polarization hypothesis. Framework strain is handled by in situ PXRD checks plus a controlled lattice-parameter sensitivity analysis, allowing Raman shifts to be decomposed into induction vs compression contributions.

NaX comparison made physically fair: NaX is modeled with explicit Na+ cations (dominant source of static fields) and induced-dipole polarization on framework oxygens with Thole damping, avoiding an oversimplified “delocalized” description. Spectroscopic comparison is restricted to guest-mode shifts (Raman/IR) that are genuinely comparable across HKUST-1 and NaX, minimizing symmetry/selection-rule confounds.

Alignment with prior evidence: The plan leverages established high-pressure adsorption methodologies (up to ≥30 bar) and the known robustness and oxygen-storage relevance of HKUST-1 (Asset 1), modern reticular design understanding of node-centric function (Asset 2), and the demonstrated necessity of polarization/induction terms for correctly capturing confined-gas behavior and spectroscopic signatures (Asset 3).
Critique: The proposal is technically strong and unusually explicit for polarizable GCMC, including SCF tolerances, damping, and long-range electrostatics. The mechanistic chain (pressure→loading→Cu-site occupancy→local fields/Upol→vibrational shifts) is logically coherent and directly addresses the “pressure amplifies polarizability” misconception. Main weaknesses are (1) parameter identifiability and transferability: fitting anisotropic Cu polarizability, Thole a, near-Cu LJ, and charge model to limited cluster DFT risks non-unique solutions that still reproduce isotherms/Qst but mispredict fields and Raman slopes; (2) spectroscopic forward model risk: embedded-fragment DFT frequencies can be highly sensitive to fragment boundary choice, functional, spin treatment for O2, and the electrostatic embedding representation of induced dipoles—this could dominate the claimed induction signatures; (3) framework flexibility: a 2–3 lattice-parameter sensitivity study may not capture local paddlewheel distortions and adsorbate-induced relaxation that directly affect Cu–Cu/Cu–O force constants and could masquerade as “induction”; (4) experimental discriminants: blocked-site controls (NH3/pyridine) change local electrostatics and vibrational signatures beyond merely eliminating open sites, complicating “signature disappearance” as a falsification test.

Hypothesis:
A Zr6-based MOF containing (i) spatially anchored Brønsted acid equivalents (–SO3H/–SO3−···H+ paired with imidazole/imidazolium and/or phosphate) arranged as short, percolating hydrogen-bond segments inside 1D channels and (ii) proximate, acid-tolerant xylose-binding motifs will increase furfural selectivity at fixed conversion by shifting the kinetically relevant step from non-selective, bulk-like protonation/polymerization to a confined proton-transfer (PT) event that is coupled to bound-xylose dehydration. The falsifiable mechanistic claim is: under liquid-phase reaction conditions, the turnover frequency (TOF) for xylose→furfural is controlled by a bound-state PT step whose rate constant kPT scales with in-pore proton mobility (μH+) measured operando in the same solvent composition, while humin formation scales with the fraction of “free,” unconfined Brønsted acidity (aH+,free) and with xylose residence time outside binding pockets. 

Microkinetic/transport framework (explicit, testable):
(1) Uptake/binding: X (xylose) + * ⇌ X* (equilibrium Kads; * = pocket site; X* is pore-confined, H-bonded to framework).
(2) Rate-determining proton transfer to bound xylose: X* + Hwire ⇌ XH+* + wire− (forward kPT; reverse k−PT). This is the Grotthuss-enabled step; Hwire denotes a proton on the wire segment (imidazole/phosphate/water network) rather than a freely solvated acid.
(3) Fast dehydration sequence to furfural precursor + regeneration: XH+* → F* + H2O (kchem,fast) and F* ⇌ F + *.
(4) Competing humin pathway occurs predominantly from free/solvated protonation: X (or intermediates) + H+free → oligomers (khumin ∝ aH+,free·[X]n).

Predicted rate law at low conversion (diagnostics):
If PT is rate-determining and binding is quasi-equilibrated: rF ≈ kPT·θX*·[Hwire], with θX* = (Kads[X])/(1+Kads[X]+…); thus rF shows saturation in [X] and positive dependence on [Hwire] but weak dependence on total acid equivalents once wire sites are filled.
Operando mobility correlation: kPT ∝ μH+ (or 1/τH+), where μH+ is extracted from liquid-compatible impedance/dielectric spectroscopy and/or QENS/PFG-derived residence/diffusivity metrics for the protonic species; therefore TOF should correlate with μH+ across a designed series where total Brønsted acidity is held constant but wire continuity changes.
Isotope prediction: primary kinetic isotope effect KIE(H/D) > 2 when replacing H2O with D2O (and/or deuterating imidazole) if PT is rate-determining; if chemistry/dehydration is rate-determining, KIE approaches ~1–1.5.
Rectification (de-risked claim): we do not require diode-like rectification. The testable requirement is anisotropic, high-frequency PT along confined H-bond segments that increases kPT for bound X* relative to kPT in controls lacking anchored proton relays. Any directional bias (if observed) will be treated as an emergent property, not a prerequisite for catalytic benefit.
Plan:
A. De-risked material architecture (prioritize robustness + measurable structure–property series)
A1. Framework choice and channel dimensions (address diffusion critique):
- Start from robust Zr6 UiO-67-type and/or Zr6 MOFs known to tolerate functionalization and to exhibit larger channels than UiO-66. Target 1D channel apertures of 8–11 Å (not 5–7 Å) to ensure access of partially solvated xylose in GVL/H2O while still enabling confinement. 
- Implement “localized wire segments” by placing proton-relay functionalities on a subset of linkers lining the channel, rather than enforcing full-pore occupancy. This preserves transport while still enabling PT coupling near binding sites.
- Decision gate (by Month 6): if PFG-NMR and breakthrough tests show Deff(xylose) < 10−11 m2/s or uptake < 0.2 mmol g−1 under reaction solvent, increase aperture via longer linkers (UiO-68 analogues) or introduce hierarchical mesoporosity (modulated synthesis/templating) while keeping wire density constant.

A2. Sulfonate introduction without Zr poisoning (contingency-first):
Path A (preferred for crystallization reliability):
- Synthesize a parent UiO-67/UiO-68 analogue using non-coordinating sulfonate-protected linkers (e.g., sulfonate ester/protected sulfonate) or a mixed-linker strategy where the sulfonated linker fraction is kept low initially (1–5 mol%) to avoid Zr-node poisoning.
- Post-synthetic deprotection/ionization to generate –SO3− after framework formation.
Path B (if protection is infeasible):
- Use post-synthetic sulfonation on an aromatic linker (carefully controlled to avoid over-sulfonation/defects). Quantify defect density via TGA, 1H NMR of digested samples, and missing-linker analysis.
Success metric: retain crystallinity (PXRD), BET area within ≥60% of parent, and <10% Zr leaching in hot GVL/H2O stability test.

A3. Stepwise installation of proton relays (avoid high-risk “periodic order” requirement):
- Prepare a matrix series with identical framework but systematically varied relay composition:
  S0: no sulfonate, no relay.
  S1: sulfonate only (Brønsted acid after protonation).
  S2: sulfonate + imidazole (neutral) loaded by sorption/ion pairing.
  S3: sulfonate + tethered imidazolium–imidazole cation (ion-exchanged into sulfonate sites).
  S4: sulfonate + tethered imidazolium–imidazole + phosphate (stepwise exchange to H2PO4−/HPO42−).
- Use tethered imidazolium–imidazole (one fixed cationic head for anchoring; one neutral imidazole for shuttling) but do not assume crystalline long-range order. Instead, quantify spatial proximity and confinement.

A4. Spatial distribution / proximity verification (required by reviewers):
- STEM-EDS/EELS mapping for P and N across single crystals/particles to confirm internal (not external) localization; compare before/after extensive solvent washing.
- Solid-state NMR: 31P and 15N (labeled where needed), including 15N{31P} and/or 13C/15N REDOR distance constraints to demonstrate nm-scale proximity between phosphate and imidazole and between relay and sulfonate-bearing linkers.
- PDF analysis to detect local ordering of relay species even without SCXRD-level periodicity.

B. Replace boronic acids with acid-tolerant binding motifs (address chemical fragility)
B1. Binding pocket strategy (two-pronged, acid-compatible):
- Primary: exploit Zr-node Lewis acidity and adjacent μ3-OH groups as reversible diol/H-bond binding sites by controlled defect engineering (modulators such as formic/acetic acid; targeted missing-linker sites capped with –OH/H2O). This provides diol coordination/H-bonding without hydrolytically fragile boron.
- Secondary (optional): incorporate neutral H-bond donor/acceptor pockets on linkers (e.g., urea/amide or hydroxyl arrays) positioned to bind xylose via multipoint H-bonding under acidic conditions.
B2. Map binding vs dehydration requirements explicitly:
- Measure xylose adsorption isotherms and heats of adsorption (microcalorimetry) as a function of water activity (GVL/H2O 0–30 wt%) and temperature (80–160 °C). Select operating window where Kads is sufficient (θX* measurable) while wire remains hydrated enough for PT.

C. Operando transport + kinetics coupling (core mandatory directive)
C1. Liquid-compatible proton mobility measurements under identical solvent composition:
- Use broadband dielectric spectroscopy / impedance in sealed liquid cells containing MOF pellets soaked in the exact reaction medium (GVL/H2O ratio, phosphate loading, xylose present/absent). Extract effective protonic mobility proxies (conductivity σ, relaxation times) and activation energies under liquid-phase conditions.
- Complement with QENS (where feasible) to characterize confined water/proton dynamics, and with 1H/2H NMR relaxometry to quantify bound vs mobile water fractions.

C2. Xylose diffusivity/accessibility early gate (mandatory):
- PFG-NMR to obtain Deff(xylose) in the MOF pores (GVL/H2O). 
- Dynamic breakthrough curves in a packed bed (xylose in solvent) to extract uptake capacity, mass-transfer coefficients, and residence time distribution.
- Gate: proceed to catalysis optimization only if uptake and Deff meet the thresholds defined in “success metrics.”

C3. Microkinetic testing plan designed to falsify the PT-control claim:
- Conduct initial-rate measurements at low conversion (<10%) varying:
  (i) [xylose] (to test saturation consistent with X* formation),
  (ii) wire density/continuity (S1–S4 series) at fixed total acid equivalents,
  (iii) water activity (controls wire hydration and PT),
  (iv) added salt/ionic strength (to perturb free-acid activity vs anchored-wire sites).
- Measure KIE: repeat kinetics in D2O-containing solvent and/or with deuterated imidazole (where incorporated). Prediction: KIE > 2 only in wire-containing samples if PT step dominates.
- Measure reaction orders: distinguish rF dependence on σ(liquid-cell) vs total titrated acidity. Acceptance criterion: within the S2–S4 series, TOF correlates more strongly with μH+/σ (R2 ≥ 0.8) than with total acid equivalents.

C4. Direct protonation-state / bound-intermediate evidence:
- In situ/operando ssNMR in swollen state (e.g., 1H/13C/15N MAS with labeled xylose where possible) to detect formation of protonated sugar/intermediate signatures and to quantify fractions of protonated relay species under reaction conditions.
- ATR-IR/DRIFTS in solvated environment (where possible) to observe changes in imidazole/phosphate bands upon xylose loading and during turnover.

D. Catalysis platform and controls
D1. Reaction systems (aligned to diffusion + separation):
- Test xylose dehydration in: (i) GVL/H2O (10–30 wt% water) and (ii) biphasic H2O/2-MTHF with controlled phase ratio to extract furfural.
- Prefer continuous-flow packed-bed once stability is shown, because it sharpens leaching/deactivation diagnosis.

D2. Controls that discriminate “wire-mediated” vs “bulk acid”:
- Parent MOF (no sulfonate/relay), sulfonated only (S1), imidazole-only (S2), tethered cation-only (S3 without phosphate), phosphate-only physically adsorbed (no sulfonate anchoring), and conventional sulfated zirconia at matched accessible acid equivalents.
- Additionally: same total acid equivalents but different wire continuity (vary phosphate loading and imidazole density) to decouple acidity from mobility.

E. Stability, leaching, and phosphate risk mitigation
E1. Phosphate handling:
- Treat phosphate as an adjustable co-relay, not required. Build a “phosphate-free wire” baseline (imidazole-only relays) and introduce phosphate only if it increases μH+ without suppressing activity (i.e., without decreasing kPT[Hwire] effectively via buffering).
- Quantify phosphate retention under flow by ion chromatography; set a strict leaching threshold (see metrics). If leaching exceeds threshold, switch to tethered phosphonate groups on the linker (covalently fixed) to provide similar H-bond/proton reservoir behavior without mobile anions.

E2. Hydrothermal/solvent stability:
- 100 h continuous-flow test at target temperature with periodic PXRD, N2 sorption, and ssNMR post-mortem.
- ICP-OES for Zr and IC for phosphate at each time point.

F. Quantitative success metrics (explicit go/no-go)
F1. Transport/accessibility:
- Xylose uptake ≥ 0.2 mmol g−1 in reaction solvent at 120 °C equivalent conditions (corrected for swelling), and Deff(xylose) ≥ 1×10−11 m2 s−1.
F2. Catalytic performance (normalized and comparable):
- Report TOF normalized per accessible Brønsted acid equivalent (acid titration + accessibility correction), and per mass of catalyst.
- Target: ≥2× TOF vs sulfonated-only control (S1) at matched acid equivalents, and furfural selectivity ≥70% at 30% xylose conversion in GVL/H2O or biphasic.
F3. Deactivation/leaching:
- Deactivation rate constant kd reduced by ≥2× vs S1 and sulfated zirconia; cumulative Zr leaching < 50 ppm and phosphate loss < 5% of initial inventory over 100 h.
F4. Mechanistic validation thresholds:
- KIE(H/D) > 2 for wire-containing catalysts and ≤1.5 for non-wire controls.
- Across S2–S4 series at fixed acid equivalents: TOF vs μH+/σ correlation R2 ≥ 0.8; TOF vs total acidity correlation significantly weaker.

Deliverables timeline (high level):
- Months 0–6: build framework + sulfonate introduction; prove uptake/diffusion gates; assemble relay series S0–S4.
- Months 6–12: operando mobility measurements in liquid cells; initial-rate kinetics + KIE; refine channel size if needed.
- Months 12–18: continuous-flow, long-term stability, full carbon balances/humin quantification; finalize structure–mobility–activity map.
Feasibility:
1) Mechanistic falsifiability (addresses critique i): The proposal no longer assumes that humid-gas EIS represents catalytic PT. Proton mobility will be measured operando in sealed liquid-compatible cells using the identical GVL/H2O composition (±xylose), and explicitly linked to a microkinetic model where a bound-state proton-transfer step is rate-determining. The model yields clear diagnostics: saturation kinetics in [xylose], a strong KIE when the wire is present, and—most critically—a quantitative TOF correlation with μH+ (or σ) across a controlled series where acidity is held constant but wire continuity changes.

2) Synthesis de-risking and contingency (addresses critique ii): Rather than relying on one-pot crystallographic ordering of mobile ion pairs (high risk), the plan starts from a known robust UiO-67/UiO-68-type Zr6 scaffold and introduces sulfonate sites via protected-linker or post-synthetic routes to avoid Zr poisoning. Proton-relay species are introduced stepwise by ion exchange/sorption into anchored anionic sites, and their spatial distribution is verified by STEM-EDS/EELS and ssNMR distance constraints (REDOR), so catalytic interpretation does not depend on long-range periodic order or SCXRD.

3) Transport realism (addresses critique iii): Channel apertures are deliberately moved to 8–11 Å and validated early via xylose uptake, PFG-NMR diffusivity, and breakthrough curves. A predefined redesign trigger (larger linkers/hierarchical porosity) prevents committing to a pore size that inadvertently excludes solvated xylose or becomes phosphate/water-blocked.

4) Binding pocket chemistry under acidic, hot, aqueous media (addresses critique iv): Boronic acids are replaced/augmented with acid-tolerant motifs: defect-engineered Zr-node Lewis sites and neutral H-bonding pockets. This avoids protodeboronation/hydrolysis liabilities and removes the pH-compatibility conflict between diol binding and dehydration.

5) Phosphate risk managed by design-of-experiments (addresses critique v): Phosphate is treated as an optional mobility enhancer/buffer whose net effect is measured, not assumed. Leaching is quantified under flow, and a built-in fallback (covalently tethered phosphonate functionality) preserves the “proton reservoir/H-bond network” concept while eliminating mobile anion loss.

6) Discriminating ‘wire-mediated’ vs ‘bulk acid’ pathways: The control matrix (S0–S4 plus conventional sulfated zirconia) and normalization per accessible acid equivalents allow separation of (a) activity from simple acid density, (b) selectivity from confinement/uptake, and (c) humin suppression from reduced free-acid pathways. Carbon balances and humin quantification are mandatory outputs to ensure selectivity claims are not artifacts of undetected insoluble products.
Critique:
The proposal is unusually strong in mechanistic falsifiability and de-risking: it defines a microkinetic scheme, prespecifies diagnostics (saturation kinetics, KIE, TOF–mobility correlations), and builds a materials series explicitly designed to separate “acid density” from “proton mobility.” The transport/accessibility gates (PFG-NMR, breakthrough) and contingency plans (UiO-68/hierarchical porosity; phosphonate fallback) are technically credible and address common MOF catalysis failure modes.

Key deductions arise from (i) an incomplete closure between the measured proxy (pellet-scale σ/relaxation in soaked pellets) and the claimed molecular rate constant kPT at the catalytic pocket: conductivity may be dominated by percolating water/ions in defects, external surface films, or interparticle pathways rather than the specific near-pocket wire segment population that controls turnover; (ii) potential confounding between “wire continuity” and local acid strength/availability—adding imidazole/phosphate can change pKa, buffering, and effective [Hwire] and can also alter xylose adsorption or water structuring, making a TOF–σ correlation non-unique unless additional controls directly quantify pocket proton activity and bound-state populations; (iii) the requirement that xylose (partially solvated) accesses 8–11 Å channels in GVL/H2O at 120–160 °C is plausible but still borderline—diffusion and competitive uptake of water/phosphate could suppress θX* and invalidate the assumed quasi-equilibrated binding regime; (iv) the concept-chain mismatch: the proposal does not address HMF and is not framed as a metal-oxide composite beyond a Zr-node MOF, so grounding to the target chain is incomplete.

Overall, the scientific plan is high-resolution and logically cohesive, but the central causal link (μH+ → kPT → TOF) needs stricter, more local, pocket-specific validation to avoid an appealing but potentially spurious structure–property correlation.

Hypothesis:
A vapor-phase, single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC–SC) linker-exchange-by-sublimation (LES) protocol can achieve true Zr6–carboxylate linker substitution—without bulk dissolution/amorphization—if the dry-state exchange is deliberately catalyzed by a metered, volatile “bond-dynamics activator” (ppm–0.1% H2O and/or a volatile monocarboxylic acid modulator such as formic/acetic acid) that transiently lowers the barrier for Zr–O(carboxylate) bond rearrangement while remaining far below the threshold for solvated Zr–carboxylate fragment formation. Mechanistically, LES proceeds via (i) surface adsorption of a sublimed anhydride/diacid, (ii) activator-assisted formation of a transient mixed-ligand Zr6 node (labile Zr–OH/Zr–O2CR/μ3-OH microenvironment) enabling associative interchange, and (iii) inward propagation by surface-to-core diffusion, producing controlled spatial gradients because the rate is diffusion-limited rather than solution-equilibrated. Using an anionic Zr6 framework preloaded with charge-balancing alkylammonium guests provides SC–SC stabilization against node detachment; however, exchange kinetics and accessible porosity will be preserved by (a) tuning guest loading to a quantified “stability window” (partial occupancy) and (b) using activator levels that promote bond dynamics without generating a continuous condensed phase.

Functionally, gradient installation of (1) polar/quadrupolar-binding linkers (e.g., fluorinated/anhydride-derived) and (2) demonstrably sublimable donor–acceptor (D–A) chromophore linkers (or volatile protected precursors unmasked in-pore) will (a) improve gas-separation selectivity by programming a 1D channel distribution of binding motifs, and (b) produce illumination-dependent heterogeneous electron-transfer (HET) kinetics on supported MOF films that is attributable to photogenerated charge-separated states increasing interfacial carrier density (lowering charge-transfer resistance and increasing k0 for an outer-sphere redox couple), rather than to photothermal heating, mass-transport changes, or nanoparticle catalysis.
Plan:
Step 1 — Platform selection, baseline dynamics, and “stability window” mapping
1.1 Choose an SC–SC-capable Zr6 MOF with accessible node dynamics and crystallinity suitable for single-crystal XRD (SCXRD) where feasible. Primary choice: a MOF-808-type Zr6O4(OH)4 cluster framework (high connectivity, robust) engineered to be anionic by incorporating a fraction of sulfonated/isophthalate-derived linkers or mixed-linker strategy that produces net framework charge requiring pore cations. Prepare both (i) single crystals (for SCXRD) and (ii) microcrystalline batches (for adsorption/electrochemistry). Confirm net anionic character by: elemental analysis (S content if sulfonated), zeta potential (dispersed crystallites), and cation content from digestion 1H NMR/ion chromatography.
1.2 Establish the pore-cation “stability vs accessibility” window. Load tetrabutylammonium (TBA+) and smaller alkylammoniums (TEA+, TMA+) by ion exchange in rigorously dried MeCN. Prepare a loading series (e.g., 0, 25, 50, 75, 100% of charge-balance equivalents). Quantify: (i) cation uptake (digestion 1H NMR with internal standard), (ii) free volume loss (N2 sorption at 77 K; BET; pore volume), (iii) framework integrity (PXRD line shape, SCXRD on selected crystals, SEM). Down-select a loading that preserves ≥70% parent pore volume while improving thermal/processing robustness.

Step 2 — Mechanistically credible LES with metered activator co-dosing
2.1 LES reactor architecture and moisture/activator metering. Use a dual-zone sealed ampoule or stainless Swagelok-type reactor with separate temperature control zones and a calibrated micro-reservoir for activator delivery.
  2.1.1 Zone A (MOF bed): 80–130 °C (chosen below any onset of linker decomposition and below framework collapse; confirm by variable-temperature PXRD).
  2.1.2 Zone B (linker source): temperature set to achieve measurable vapor pressure (see Step 3 prescreening), typically 120–220 °C.
  2.1.3 Activator dosing module: (i) H2O delivered as controlled ppm–0.1% in carrier gas (N2/Ar) using a humidity generator or permeation tube; and/or (ii) volatile modulator vapor (formic/acetic acid) delivered via a temperature-controlled bubbler/permeation source. Inline capacitive humidity sensor (for H2O) and gravimetric calibration (for acid) to quantify delivered amounts.
2.2 Kinetics mapping vs activator level (mandatory mechanistic proof). For a single, well-behaved sublimable anhydride linker (e.g., tetrafluoroterephthalic anhydride or a rigid fluorinated anhydride/diacid with verified volatility):
  2.2.1 Run LES at fixed linker dose/time while varying activator: H2O = 0 ppm (ultradry), 50 ppm, 200 ppm, 1000 ppm, 0.01%, 0.05%, 0.1%; and separately modulator vapor (e.g., 10–500 ppm equivalent).
  2.2.2 For each condition: quantify exchange fraction and rate (digestion 1H/19F NMR with internal standard; see Step 4), crystallinity (in situ PXRD during dosing if possible), and amorphous fraction (total scattering/PDF). Identify an operational “exchange-without-amorphization” window where exchange fraction increases monotonically with activator, but PDF/PXRD shows no growth of amorphous signatures and no loss of Bragg intensity beyond a pre-set threshold (e.g., <10% decrease).
  2.2.3 Mechanistic signature of activator catalysis: demonstrate negligible exchange at 0 ppm, strong acceleration with ppm–0.1% activator, and a failure regime at higher activator (or longer exposure) where amorphization begins—thereby establishing the kinetic/thermodynamic rationale for minimal activator co-dosing.
2.3 Pulsed LES protocol (gradient-enabled) within the validated activator window.
  2.3.1 Use iterative pulses: 0.5–2 h exposure (linker + activator) followed by 2–12 h anneal/rest under activator-free dry N2 at Zone A temperature to allow diffusion inward without continuous reaction at the surface.
  2.3.2 Gradient control parameters: crystal size (e.g., 20, 50, 200 µm), pulse number (1–20), and partial pressure of linker. Predict diffusion length scales from time/temperature and fit to measured depth profiles (Step 4.4).

Step 3 — De-risk volatility and chemical integrity of linker delivery
3.1 Pre-screen all candidate linkers/precursors for (i) vapor pressure, (ii) decomposition/polymerization, and (iii) chemical identity after sublimation.
  3.1.1 Vapor pressure determination: Knudsen effusion (preferred) or TGA-based vapor pressure estimation under inert gas. Require a measurable vapor pressure at ≤220 °C (or below MOF stability limit) and stable mass-loss behavior consistent with volatilization rather than decomposition.
  3.1.2 Thermal stability: DSC/TGA to ensure no exothermic decomposition below intended source temperature; reject candidates showing early decomposition.
  3.1.3 Identity of sublimed species: collect condensate on a cold finger and analyze by LC–MS/GC–MS and NMR. Require matching to intact precursor.
3.2 Redesign D–A linkers toward demonstrably sublimable precursors.
  3.2.1 Replace low-volatility NDI diacids with smaller, rigid, and/or fluorinated anhydride precursors or “volatile protected” derivatives. Example strategy: deliver an anhydride/diester that is sublimable, then unmask carboxylates in-pore via the same minimal-activator chemistry (trace H2O) to generate the coordinating diacid in situ. Gate criterion: successful sublimation with intact recovery plus in-pore conversion evidenced by solid-state NMR/IR.
  3.2.2 Use modular D–A installation: first exchange a sublimable acceptor-bearing linker (e.g., compact diimide-like acceptor surrogate with verified volatility), then a donor-bearing linker in a second LES step; or co-dose if no cross-reaction is detected in condensate analytics.

Step 4 — Unambiguous proof of true linker substitution and SC–SC retention
4.1 Quantitative digestion NMR (mandatory): digest MOF under conditions that fully solubilize node/linkers; quantify linker ratios using an internal standard (e.g., dimethyl sulfone or a fluorinated standard for 19F). Provide full mass balance: incorporated linker + recovered linker from traps + remaining source.
4.2 Solid-state NMR to rule out mere guest inclusion: 13C ssNMR (carboxylate shifts), 19F ssNMR for fluorinated linkers, and 1H–13C CP/MAS to distinguish coordinated vs free acid/anhydride. Look for coordination-induced shifts/broadening and disappearance of anhydride carbonyl signatures upon incorporation.
4.3 SC–SC validation:
  4.3.1 Where single crystals survive: collect SCXRD pre/post LES to demonstrate retained space group/topology and locate (even partially occupied) new linker electron density or changes in node coordination environment.
  4.3.2 For microcrystals: Rietveld refinement against PXRD plus pair distribution function (PDF) analysis to verify preserved local Zr6 cluster structure.
4.4 Spatial gradient verification (quantitative depth profiles):
  4.4.1 Confocal Raman/IR mapping across crystal cross-sections.
  4.4.2 FIB-SEM cross-section plus EDS mapping when a halogen handle exists (F/Cl/Br) or use ToF-SIMS for depth profiling of diagnostic fragments.
  4.4.3 Fit profiles to diffusion-reaction models to extract effective diffusivities and reaction rates under different activator levels.

Step 5 — Gas separation: link gradient chemistry to adsorption/selectivity under realistic conditions
5.1 Adsorption: single-component isotherms (CO2, N2, C2H2) at 273/298 K; compute Qst (Clausius–Clapeyron) and perform microcalorimetry where available.
5.2 Mixture performance: IAST selectivity plus dynamic breakthrough for CO2/N2 and C2H2/CO2 under dry and humid feeds. Explicitly compare: parent MOF, LES-exchanged uniform samples (long anneal), and gradient samples.
5.3 Binding-site mechanistic probes: in situ DRIFTS with CO2/C2H2; 13CO2 ssNMR to identify binding motifs and correlate with depth-profiled linker distribution.

Step 6 — Electrochemistry: strict causality for photo-modulated interfacial electron transfer (no ORR dependence)
6.1 Electrode architecture: grow a thin, adherent MOF film on FTO or glassy carbon via seeded growth; then perform LES directly on-film to preserve contact.
6.2 Use a purely outer-sphere redox probe with matched charge to the anionic framework to avoid adsorption artifacts and inner-sphere chemistry. Preferred: a ferrocene/ferrocenium derivative tethered to a cationic group (e.g., Fc–CH2–NR3+), ensuring partitioning into pores while remaining outer-sphere at the electrode. Confirm probe uptake and location by UV–vis (if chromophoric) and digestion NMR.
6.3 Report true electron-transfer kinetics: obtain k0 via Nicholson or Laviron analysis from cyclic voltammetry over scan-rate series; corroborate with EIS (charge-transfer resistance Rct) under identical conditions.
6.4 Mandatory controls to isolate photocarrier effects:
  6.4.1 Temperature control: measure electrode temperature at the film surface (micro-thermocouple or IR thermometry) and enforce identical light/dark temperature (use heat sink or chopped illumination with duty cycle control).
  6.4.2 Chromophore controls: (i) acceptor-only linker, (ii) donor-only linker, (iii) D–A non-charge-transfer analog (sterically/electronically disrupted CT), each installed by the same LES protocol and at matched exchange fraction.
  6.4.3 Transport controls: measure film porosity/accessibility to the redox probe before/after illumination (no permanent changes), and verify identical probe loading in all samples.
  6.4.4 Mechanistic quench test: introduce a pore-confined electron (or hole) scavenger that selectively quenches the CT state without altering porosity; show loss of light-induced k0 enhancement.
6.5 Photophysics-to-electrochemistry correlation: measure UV–vis-NIR (CT band), transient absorption, and light/dark EPR (radical signatures) on the same films; correlate radical yield/lifetime with k0 and Rct changes.

Step 7 — LES vs SALE benchmark (amorphization and performance)
7.1 Perform conventional SALE on the same parent MOF and linker targets (as solubility allows) under best-practice conditions from literature. Quantify: crystallinity retention (in situ PXRD), amorphous fraction (PDF), and linker incorporation (digestion NMR).
7.2 Explicitly compare batch variability (exchange fraction distribution, crystallinity metrics) between LES and SALE to support the central claim of reduced amorphous by-products.

Step 8 — Modeling tightly coupled to measured mechanisms
8.1 Compute activator-assisted exchange energetics: periodic DFT or cluster models of Zr6 nodes comparing (i) dry anhydride/diacid approach, (ii) water-assisted proton shuttle, and (iii) monocarboxylate-assisted ligand interchange; predict rate trends vs activator and compare to measured kinetics.
8.2 Simulate adsorption in gradient pores: GCMC with spatially varying interaction parameters constrained by measured gradient profiles; predict breakthrough and compare to experiment.
Feasibility:
Mechanistic credibility in the dry state is established by explicitly introducing a controlled, minimal activator that is known to mediate Zr–carboxylate bond dynamics (trace H2O/protic modulator) while maintaining the central LES advantage: absence of bulk solvent that enables dissolution–reprecipitation and amorphous by-products (a key limitation highlighted for SALE/BBR). The proposal now contains a required kinetics-vs-activator map that will empirically identify a quantitative operational window where exchange proceeds but amorphization remains below a defined threshold (in situ PXRD + PDF), directly addressing the reviewer’s primary risk.

Volatility risk is reduced by front-loaded vapor-pressure and decomposition screening (Knudsen/TGA vapor pressure, DSC, and chemical identity checks of sublimed material). The D–A component is redesigned around demonstrably sublimable precursors or volatile protected linkers that can be unmasked in-pore using the same minimal-activator chemistry, rather than assuming NDI diacids will sublime cleanly at MOF-safe temperatures.

SC–SC and true substitution are made unambiguous by combining quantitative digestion NMR (with internal standards and mass balance) with solid-state NMR signatures of coordination and, where possible, SCXRD before/after exchange—explicitly ruling out mere guest inclusion. Spatial gradients are verified by multiple orthogonal depth-profiling methods (confocal mapping, FIB-SEM/EDS/ToF-SIMS) and interpreted with diffusion-reaction models.

Electrochemical causality is tightened by avoiding ORR (and any nanoparticle-catalysis ambiguity) and instead measuring true heterogeneous electron-transfer rate constants (k0) for a well-defined outer-sphere ferrocene/ferrocenium derivative designed to partition into the anionic framework. Photothermal and mass-transport artifacts are controlled by enforced isothermal light/dark conditions, matched probe loadings, and inert chromophore control frameworks (donor-only/acceptor-only/non-CT analog). Light-induced changes in k0/Rct are mechanistically anchored to independently measured CT-state formation and lifetimes (transient absorption, light/dark EPR), creating a closed causal chain from linker photophysics to interfacial electron-transfer kinetics.

Overall, the refined plan preserves the original concept chain (LES → suppressed amorphization + gradient programming → gas separation + photo-coupled electrochemistry) while adding the specific chemical parameters and mandatory controls required to make the exchange mechanism, volatility, SC–SC proof, and electrochemical interpretation reviewer-proof.
Critique:
Methodologically, the proposal is unusually detailed and addresses the principal LES failure modes (volatility, decomposition, guest inclusion vs true substitution, and amorphization) with appropriate orthogonal measurements (digestion NMR mass balance, ssNMR coordination signatures, PDF, in situ PXRD, SCXRD where possible, ToF-SIMS/FIB-EDS depth profiling). The activator-window kinetics map is a strong, falsifiable centerpiece.

Key weaknesses are (i) platform risk: an “anionic MOF-808-type” with partial sulfonated linkers may compromise SCXRD quality, defect chemistry, and node lability in ways that confound mechanistic attribution (anionicity/guest loading/defectivity are coupled variables). (ii) Mechanistic ambiguity remains around the claimed dry-state associative interchange at Zr6 nodes: even sub-0.1% H2O plus acid vapor can generate localized condensed phases in micropores at 80–130 °C (capillary condensation/strong adsorption), recreating a quasi-solvated microenvironment; the plan measures outcomes (PXRD/PDF) but does not directly bound “no condensed phase” beyond indirect inference. (iii) The gradient claim is plausible but diffusion-limited propagation is not independently validated against alternative explanations (surface-only exchange + defect-mediated penetration; fracture/microcracking during thermal cycling). (iv) The electrochemistry section is strong on artifacts, but it explicitly de-emphasizes ORR while the concept chain includes Tafel slope; as written, there is no kinetic current–overpotential regime, no separation of charge-transfer vs mass-transport polarization, and thus no place where Tafel slopes are interpretable.

Overall: high engineering resolution and rationale; logic is mostly coherent but with remaining untested assumptions about micro-condensed phases and coupled variables; evidence grounding is reduced mainly by the unused “Tafel slope” concept.

Hypothesis: We hypothesize that enzyme-like bifunctional catalytic microenvironments can be created in UiO-66(Zr) by (a) engineering missing-linker point defects to generate coordinatively unsaturated Zr sites and (b) installing Boc-protected primary amine monocarboxylate caps in a defect-density-dependent manner, followed by mild, quantitatively monitored Boc deprotection to yield proximal primary amines adjacent to open Zr Lewis acids. The key mechanistic refinement that overcomes prior ambiguities is explicit decoupling of (i) defect density (number of missing-linker sites per Zr6 node) from (ii) cap identity (TFA vs installed monocarboxylate): we will (1) first create a defect series using TFA modulation, then (2) implement a standardized cap-exchange protocol that replaces residual node-bound TFA with a spectroscopically trackable, isotopically labeled amine-bearing monocarboxylate, and (3) close mass balances via digestion NMR + ICP-OES/TGA. Enzyme-like cooperativity will be asserted only when distance-sensitive solid-state NMR (15N-based, not 91Zr-dependent) demonstrates node-proximal amines (through heteronuclear dipolar couplings to node/carboxylate signatures) and when catalytic rate enhancements exceed adsorption/diffusion controls and are selectively attenuated by site-poisoning of either the Lewis-acid Zr sites or the base/nucleophile amines. Thus, activity is mechanistically attributed to defect-localized, co-localized Lewis acid–base pairs rather than to non-specific pore functionalization or residual modulator effects.
Plan:
Step 0 — Platform selection and defect-series design
0.1 MOF: UiO-66(Zr) as the primary platform (robust Zr6O4(OH)4 nodes; well-studied defect chemistry). Target 3–4 defect levels spanning low to high missing-linker density while preserving crystallinity/porosity.
0.2 Defect modulation: synthesize UiO-66(Zr) using trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) as modulator at defined equivalents (e.g., 0, low, medium, high) chosen to span the literature-relevant defect window; replicate syntheses to quantify batch variability.

Step 1 — Quantitative defect density and cap speciation (explicitly separating “missing-linker density” from “cap identity”)
1.1 Initial cap/speciation quantification (as-synthesized materials):
  - Digest each MOF in a standard Zr-dissolution mixture (e.g., DCl/D2O + DMSO-d6 or HF-free alternative validated for complete dissolution) and quantify:
    (i) linker (BDC) by 1H NMR,
    (ii) residual TFA by 19F NMR (external standard for absolute quantitation),
    (iii) any other monocarboxylate species if present.
  - Independently quantify Zr by ICP-OES to convert NMR integrals into “caps per Zr6 node” and “missing-linkers per node” using stoichiometric constraints.
  - TGA/DSC to cross-check organic/inorganic mass fractions and provide an orthogonal constraint on cap/loading.
1.2 Cap-exchange to standardize cap identity across the entire defect series:
  - Perform post-synthetic cap exchange (PSCE) under conditions that preserve the UiO-66 lattice (mild temperature, controlled water activity) using a single, spectroscopically trackable monocarboxylate cap (see Step 2) in large excess.
  - Iterate exchange until digestion 19F NMR shows residual TFA below a defined threshold (e.g., <5% of initial cap count or below quantitation limit). This explicitly removes “TFA-as-cap” as a confounder while retaining the defect topology.
1.3 Post-exchange quantification and mass-balance closure:
  - Repeat digestion 1H/19F NMR + ICP-OES + TGA on exchanged samples to obtain: (a) missing-linker density (per node), (b) cap identity distribution (installed cap vs any residual), and (c) total cap loading.
  - Acceptance criterion for proceeding: defect series shows distinct missing-linker densities, while cap identity is matched (same installed cap; minimal residual TFA) across all samples.

Step 2 — Defect-targeted installation of Boc-protected primary amine caps with isotopic labels (testable NMR claims)
2.1 Cap molecule design (monocarboxylate, Boc-protected primary amine):
  - Use a Boc-protected amino-alkyl benzoic acid (or analogous monocarboxylate) engineered to: (i) bind Zr nodes via carboxylate, (ii) present a Boc-protected primary amine toward the pore.
  - Isotopic labeling: synthesize 15N-labeled amine (15NH2 before Boc protection) and optionally 13C-label at the carboxylate carbonyl to enable 13C–15N correlations and REDOR distance measurements. The TFA history remains trackable by 19F NMR during/after exchange.
2.2 Thermodynamic/kinetic basis and explicit controls for “defect targeting”:
  - Rationale to be tested (not assumed): monocarboxylate binding occurs at under-coordinated Zr sites associated with missing-linker defects; therefore uptake should scale with missing-linker density when cap identity is standardized.
  - Controls:
    (i) Low-defect UiO-66 (near-stoichiometric) subjected to identical exchange conditions.
    (ii) Competitive capping: co-dose labeled Boc-amine monocarboxylate with an unlabeled competitor monocarboxylate of similar pKa/sterics to test whether binding is defect-limited and site-competitive.
    (iii) Time-course uptake to distinguish kinetic trapping vs equilibrium binding.
2.3 Quantify selective uptake vs defect density:
  - Digest 1H/15N (solution NMR if feasible for label), 19F NMR (to confirm TFA removal), and ICP-OES to report “installed cap per Zr6 node” and correlate with “missing-linkers per node.”
  - Expectation/decision rule: a monotonic relationship between installed cap loading and independently quantified missing-linker density; absence of scaling in low-defect control indicates non-specific adsorption is minor.

Step 3 — Controlled Boc deprotection with node/cap integrity monitoring (avoiding collapse and decoupling from TFA confounds)
3.1 Deprotection strategy:
  - Use vapor-phase TFA (or very dilute solution-phase TFA in anhydrous compatible solvent) under carefully limited exposure to minimize framework hydrolysis and avoid re-capping by TFA.
  - Immediately follow with rigorous evacuation and solvent washes, then repeat PSCE if necessary to remove any reintroduced TFA (verified by 19F NMR after digestion).
3.2 Verify deprotection without cap loss:
